Notes on home coffee roasting — hardware setup, roast logging, and profiles.
The setup here uses Artisan roaster scope software running on a headless Ubuntu server with a Phidget VINT Hub for thermocouple input, controlled remotely from a Mac on the same network.
data.equipment#Equipment: Roaster: FreshRoast SR800 Sensor hub: Phidgets HUB0002_0 VINT hub Thermocouple input: Phidgets TMP1101_1-4x (4-channel K-type) Probe: MECCANIXITY K-type thermocouple, 1.5×100mm, 9.8 ft wire, 0–1100°C (32–2012°F), stainless steel Probe fitting: Evolution Sensors 1/8 NPT stainless steel compression fitting, for 1/16" (0.0625") diameter thermocouple probes Fitting ferrule: Evolution Sensors PTFE ferrule, for 1/16" diameter RTD/thermocouple compression fittings

data:
How to set up a headless Ubuntu server as a Phidget sensor hub, so that Artisan running on your Mac can read the VINT thermocouples as if they were plugged in locally.
Architecture: the Ubuntu server runs the Phidget Network Server — a lightweight daemon that makes all attached Phidget devices available over the LAN via WebSockets on port 5661. The Mac’s Phidget22 library discovers it automatically, and Artisan sees the remote sensors transparently. No Artisan instance, no virtual display, and no VNC needed on the server.
[Phidget VINT Hub] --USB--> [Ubuntu server] | phidget22networkserver (WebSocket, port 5661) | LAN/WiFi | [MacBook] Artisan + Phidget22 (reads sensors as local)
data.1-install-the-phidget22-library-and-netw:
Phidgets provides an apt repository for Ubuntu.
# Add the Phidget repo curl -fsSL https://www.phidgets.com/downloads/setup_linux | sudo bash # Install the library and the network server daemon sudo apt-get install -y libphidget22 libphidget22extra phidget22networkserver If you prefer not to run the setup script, download the packages directly from phidgets.com/downloads.
data.2-usb-permissions-udev-rule#2. USB Permi:
By default, USB devices are only accessible to root. Add a udev rule so the network server process can reach the Phidget Hub without running as root.
sudo tee /etc/udev/rules.d/99-phidgets.rules <<'EOF' SUBSYSTEM=="usb", ACTION=="add", ATTR{idVendor}=="06c2", MODE="0664", GROUP="plugdev" EOF sudo udevadm control --reload-rules # Add the user that will run phidget22networkserver to plugdev sudo usermod -aG plugdev $USER Log out and back in (or reboot) for the group change to take effect.
Plug in the VINT Hub, then verify USB enumeration and permissions:
# Device should appear lsusb | grep -i phidget # Expected: Bus 00X Device 00X: ID 06c2:XXXX Phidgets Inc. # Your user should be in plugdev groups $USER | grep plugdev # Quick permission check — should print the device file with group rw ls -la /dev/bus/usb/$(lsusb | grep 06c2 | awk '{print $2,$4}' | awk '{printf "%s/%03d\n", $1, $2+0}' 2>/dev/null) 2>/dev/null || \ echo "check dmesg | tail -20 if device not found" If lsusb doesn’t show a Phidget, try a different USB port, check dmesg | tail -20 immediately after plugging in, or try a different cable.
data.4-run-the-phidget-network-server#4. Run:
The phidget22networkserver package installs a systemd unit. Enable and start it, open the firewall port, then verify the server is listening:
sudo systemctl enable phidget22networkserver sudo systemctl start phidget22networkserver sudo ufw allow 5661/tcp sudo ufw reload sudo systemctl status phidget22networkserver ss -tlnp | grep 5661 # Expected: LISTEN 0 ... 0.0.0.0:5661 The server listens on port 5661 and publishes all connected Phidget devices over a WebSocket interface. It also advertises itself via mDNS/Bonjour so the Mac’s Phidget22 library can discover it without needing a static IP.
data.auto-discovery-same-lan-mdns#Auto-discov: If your Mac and the Ubuntu server are on the same subnet, the Phidget22 library discovers the network server automatically via Bonjour. No further config needed — just press ON in Artisan’s toolbar and you should see live ET/BT readings within a few seconds.
data.confirming-everything-works#Confirming E:
On the Ubuntu server:
# 1. Phidget hub is enumerated lsusb | grep 06c2 # 2. Network server is running and listening systemctl is-active phidget22networkserver ss -tlnp | grep 5661 From the Mac:
# 3. Port is reachable from the Mac nc -zv 5661 # Expected: Connection to port 5661 [tcp] succeeded! In Artisan (Mac):
Press ON — ET and BT should populate within a few seconds. The status bar should show the Phidget device name without an error icon. Wiggle a thermocouple gently — the temperature reading should respond. Troubleshooting:
Symptom Check lsusb shows no Phidget `dmesg networkserver fails to start journalctl -u phidget22networkserver — likely a permissions issue; verify plugdev group Port 5661 not reachable from Mac sudo ufw status; confirm server IP is correct Artisan shows no readings Confirm Phidget22 drivers installed on Mac; try phidget22admin -a to force address ET/BT swapped Swap channel assignments in Config > Device
data.hardware#Hardware: Ubuntu server (22.04 or 24.04 LTS, headless) Phidget VINT Hub (e.g. HUB0000_0) connected via USB Thermocouple module(s) in VINT ports — e.g. TMP1101 (4-input K-type) or TMP1100 (single) Mac on the same local network
data.install-the-phidget22-drivers-on-your-ma:
The Mac needs the Phidget22 library to talk to the network server. Download and install the macOS package from phidgets.com/downloads.
You do not need to physically attach any Phidget to the Mac.
data.manual-server-address-if-mdns-doesnt-wor:
If auto-discovery fails (e.g. across VLANs, or mDNS is blocked), set the server address explicitly. Open a terminal on your Mac and add the server:
# Run once — registers the server address persistently with the Phidget22 library /usr/local/bin/phidget22admin -a Or set it within Artisan: Config > Device, look for a Server or Remote field and enter :5661.
data.open-artisan-and-configure-the-device#Op: Launch Artisan on your Mac. Go to Config > Device. In the device list, select the Phidget module that matches your thermocouple board — e.g. Phidget TMP1101 for a 4-input K-type board. Set the channel assignments for ET (environmental/drum temp) and BT (bean temperature) to match how your thermocouples are wired to the VINT ports. Click OK.
data.server-ip#Server IP:
Note the server’s LAN IP — you’ll need it if mDNS discovery doesn’t work on your network:
ip addr show | grep 'inet ' | grep -v 127.0.0.1

data: How to export a roast from Artisan and add it as a page on this site.
data.creating-a-roast-page#Creating a Roast P:
Each roast gets its own Markdown file under content/docs/coffee-roasting/.
hugo new docs/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe.md
data.keeping-pages-ordered#Keeping Pages Orde:
Use weight in front matter to control sidebar order. Lower numbers appear first. A convention that works well:
Section _index.md: weight: 100 Individual roast pages: use the date as a weight, e.g. weight: 20250115 for 2025-01-15 This keeps roasts sorted chronologically from oldest (top) to newest (bottom). Reverse it by assigning descending weights.
data.page-template#Page Template: --- title: "2025-01-15 Ethiopia Yirgacheffe" date: 2025-01-15 weight: 200 --- **Bean**: Ethiopia Yirgacheffe, washed **Source**: [Roaster name] **Green weight**: 250g | **Roast out**: 210g (16% loss) ## Roast | | Temp | Time | |---|---|---| | Charge | 195°C | 0:00 | | Turning point | 92°C | 1:45 | | First crack | 196°C | 9:30 | | Drop | 207°C | 11:00 | ![Roast curve](/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png) ## Notes Notes on the roast — airflow adjustments, gas changes, anything that went well or needs adjustment next time. ## Cup Tasting notes after resting 5–7 days.
data.publishing#Publishing:
Add the new page and static files, then push to main — CI deploys automatically.
git add content/docs/coffee-roasting/ static/static/coffee-roasting/ git commit -m "roast: 2025-01-15 Ethiopia Yirgacheffe" git push
data.roast-curve-image#Roast Curve Image:
After the roast completes (or during):
File > Save Graph — saves the roast curve as a .png (also offers PDF and social-media-sized exports). For a clean export, use View > Full Screen first so the graph fills the window before saving.
data.roast-data-artisan-alog#Roast Data (Arti:
File > Save As — saves the full roast as an Artisan .alog file (JSON format), including every temperature sample, event marker, and the Roast Properties entered above. Keep this file alongside the page as a data archive even if you don’t embed it in the site — it’s the only copy of the raw curve data, and it’s what ArtisanViewer or a future Artisan version would need to re-open the roast.
Optional: Artisan’s Autosave feature (Config > Autosave) can write both the .alog and a rendered image/PDF automatically at the end of every roast, using a filename template built from the roast date and bean name — worth setting up once instead of doing the File > Save Graph / File > Save As dance by hand every time.
data.roast-phase-buttons#Roast Phase Buttons:
Artisan’s toolbar has one button per roast phase — press each the instant it happens. Use the trier (the little sampling scoop on the roaster) to judge color for Dry End, and listen for the cracks:
Button Press it when… CHARGE Beans go into the roaster. This is the zero point everything else is measured from — no CHARGE, no ∆BT curve. DRY END The beans finish drying and start browning (Maillard) — pull a sample with the trier and watch the color shift from green to tan/yellow. FC START First crack audibly begins — a popcorn-like popping. FC END First crack’s popping tapers off. SC START Second crack begins, if roasting past first crack — a faster, higher-pitched crackle than first crack. SC END Second crack’s crackling tapers off. DROP Beans come out of the roaster into the cooling tray. Turning Point isn’t a button. Artisan auto-detects it as the lowest bean-temp reading shortly after Charge — the moment the cold beans stop dragging the temperature down and it starts climbing. That makes it the one phase mark that can go wrong even when you press every button correctly: if the probe glitches right after Charge, like on the first roast logged here, the auto-detected TP is meaningless even though every button-marked event on the same roast is fine.
data.what-to-capture-per-roast#What to Captur:
Enter bean and weight data straight into Artisan’s own Roast Properties dialog (Roast menu, or click the roast title above the graph) as you go — it’s saved into the .alog file automatically, so there’s nothing to transcribe later:
Roast tab: Beans (origin, variety, processing — e.g. “Ethiopia Yirgacheffe, washed”), Green Weight, Roasted Weight (Artisan computes weight loss % from these two) Title: batch identifier, shown on the graph itself Notes tab: roasting notes during the session, cupping notes once it’s rested Charge, turning point, first crack, and drop don’t need writing down either — mark each one live with Artisan’s phase buttons/hotkeys as it happens, and the exact time and temp land on the graph and in the saved profile on their own.
data.where-to-store-files#Where to Store File:
static/static/coffee-roasting/ └── YYYY-MM-DD-bean-name/ ├── roast-curve.png ← exported graph image └── roast.alog ← Artisan data file (optional, for archiving) Example:
static/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png The file will be served at:
/static/coffee-roasting/2025-01-15-ethiopia-yirgacheffe/roast-curve.png

data:
Trip prep for the Transylvania County trout country around Brevard, NC — the self-styled “Land of Waterfalls” — plus everything a short drive east and west: DuPont State Recreational Forest (east, toward Hendersonville), Rosman and the French Broad headwaters (west), and the higher Cashiers / Highlands plateau (southwest). This is the densest concentration of public trout water in the Southern Appalachians, and you can fish a technical tailwater-style spring creek, a stocked delayed-harvest run, and a native brook-trout headwater all in the same day.
The headline: two things dictate this trip — the delayed-harvest calendar and the state of Helene recovery.
1. Delayed Harvest (DH) calendar. NC’s DH waters (French Broad East Fork, DuPont’s Little River, the Tuckasegee, and others) fish catch-and-release, single-hook artificial-only from Oct 1 through the first Saturday in June. That window is the whole point — heavy fall/winter/spring stockings, no harvest, and the best numbers of the year (50-fish days on the Tuck are real). From the first Saturday in June through Sept 30 those same waters flip to hatchery-supported harvest regs, get hammered, and thin out. If you have any say over dates, come in the DH window.
2. Hurricane Helene (Sept 2024) recovery. The storm reshaped these watersheds — sedimentation, blown-out access roads, bridge replacements, and shifted stocking points. As of 2026, most water is fishable but access is the live variable: e.g., Davidson River Rd (FS 475) has had segments closed for bridge work, and NCWRC has moved some stocking locations. Re-check the Pisgah Ranger District closures page and ncwildlife.gov/trout in the days before you go — that’s the one thing that changes this plan.
data.a-short-history-of-the-regions-flies#A s:
The Southern Appalachians tie their own tradition, older and more homespun than the Western tailwater canon. The mountain patterns began as wet flies and hair-wings meant for tumbling, tannic pocket water and unsophisticated wild fish — durability and floatation over exact imitation.
Yallarhammer — the oldest and most storied of them, an old-timers’ wet fly (later fished as a dry) originally tied with the barred wing and tail feathers of the yellow-shafted flicker, the “yellowhammer” of mountain speech. When the flicker came under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, tyers moved to dyed-yellow substitute feathers, but the name and the reputation stuck — brookies hit it so hard it earned the nickname “skull crusher.” Tellico Nymph — named for the Tellico River on the Tennessee side of the range, this yellow-bodied, peacock-and-brown nymph is the region’s true breakout, the one homegrown pattern that went national and now sits in fly boxes far from Appalachia. Thunderhead — a dry fly from Fred Hall, a legendary Great Smoky Mountains tyer; a gray-brown-and-white, Adams-Wulff-ish attractor built to ride high through bubbly plunge pools. Named for Thunderhead Mountain in the Smokies, it remains the go-to high-country brook-trout dry. Sheep Fly — created by Newland Saunders of Lenoir, NC in the 1950s and popularized in the 1980s by Don Howell of Brevard, who said if he could fish one fly forever it would be this. It anchors the local canon alongside Don’s own ties like “Don’s Pet,” and the Howell family’s shop keeps it in the bins today. Green Weenie — the modern outlier: a simple chartreuse inchworm/caterpillar imitation adopted region-wide for reasons nobody fully explains. It just works, especially in summer, and no local box is without one. Other names you’ll still hear in the deep hollers — the Jim Charley, the Smoky Mountain Forked Tail, the Tennessee Wulff — round out a living tradition that Don Howell’s 1999 book helped set down before it faded.
data.chattooga-river--wild--scenic#Chattooga:
A federally designated Wild and Scenic River on the NC/SC/GA line; remote, pristine, and challenging, with wild brown, rainbow, and brook trout. Fish it for the setting and the wild fish, not the numbers.
Yallarhammer (#10–14) — the traditional “skull crusher” Thunderhead, Adams Wulff (#12–16) Tellico Nymph, Prince nymph (#12–16)
data.cullasaja-river-highlands--scenic-roadsi:
Waterfalls (Dry Falls, Bridal Veil Falls on US-64), deep pools, and long glassy runs, with easy pull-offs between Turtle Pond Bridge and Gold Mine Bridge. Wild-ish and stocked trout; approachable.
Parachute Adams, Elk Hair Caddis (#14–18) Pheasant Tail / Hare’s Ear dropper Green Weenie in summer
data.davidson-river-pisgah-national-forest--t:
Regularly ranked among the top 100 trout streams in the country, and the reason people drive here. The wild, catch-and-release, fly-fishing-only water runs from the headwaters down to Avery Creek; the stretch right below the Bobby N. Setzer State Fish Hatchery (the state’s largest) holds outsized, pellet-conditioned rainbows and browns that have seen every fly in the shop. Clear, cold, and technical — this is a small-flies-and-long-leaders game.
Midges: Zebra Midge (black/red), WD-40, disco midge (#18–22) Sulphurs (#16–18) — the signature late-spring/early-summer hatch Blue-Winged Olive dry/emerger (#18–20) — overcast days Hendrickson, Quill Gordon, March Brown (#12–16) — the early-spring parade Pheasant Tail / Hare’s Ear nymphs (#16–20) Below the hatchery only: San Juan worm, egg pattern, mop fly — the pellet-fed fish key on them 5x–6x tippet; downsize before you think you need to
data.early-summer-terrestrials-mid-june--mid-:
DH waters are now harvest regs and pressured — pivot toward freestone pocket water and the plateau. Terrestrials come online; Yellow Drakes and Isonychia show on the bigger water in the evenings. Mornings and evenings; midday slows.
Confidence: Yellow Stimulator (#12–16), foam beetle / flying ant (#14–16), Isonychia (#12–14), Green Weenie (#12–14), Tellico Nymph (#12–14)
data.east-dupont-state-recreational-forest#Ea:
10,000+ acres straddling Transylvania and Henderson counties, best known for its waterfalls (Hooker, Triple, High, and Bridal Veil Falls — the Hunger Games and Last of the Mohicans filming locations). The Little River, from the Lake Dense outflow down to Hooker Falls, is delayed-harvest water (C&R Oct–May, harvest June–Sept). Five lakes in the forest are inland public fishing waters — Cascade Lake and Lake Julia among them, worth a bank/float session for bass and stocked trout.
DH stockers: Y2K/egg, Squirmy worm, Pat’s Rubber Legs, small Woolly Bugger Green Weenie (#12–14) — regional confidence fly, inexplicably good Elk Hair Caddis, Parachute Adams (#14–18) Pheasant Tail / Prince nymph (#14–18) Two hard DuPont rules: no fishing within 300 feet of the top of any waterfall, and no night fishing anywhere on the forest game lands. Both are actively enforced.
data.east-fork-french-broad--the-dh-workhorse:
A roadside stream that has become one of WNC’s most popular delayed-harvest waters, stocked along ~4.75 miles of East Fork Road. In the Oct–June C&R window this is the high-numbers day.
Squirmy worm, egg patterns, Pat’s Rubber Legs (#8–12) Green Weenie (#12–14) Zebra Midge, Pheasant Tail, Copper John (#16–20) Small Woolly Bugger / sculpin on cloudy days
data.eating-mid-tier-and-budget#Eating: mid-t: Brevard Mid-tier: The Square Root (New American, downtown); Jaime’s Creole Brasserie Budget: Rocky’s Grill & Soda Shop (1940s soda fountain); The Falls Landing; brewery kitchens (Oskar Blues, Ecusta) Pisgah Forest / Mills River Mid-tier: Sierra Nevada Taproom (Mills River) Budget: Hawg Wild BBQ; the Pisgah Fish Camp counter Cashiers Mid-tier: Cornucopia; The Orchard Budget: Buck’s Coffee Cafe; Slabtown Pizza Highlands Mid-tier: Wolfgang’s Restaurant; Ristorante Paoletti Budget: The Highlander; Mountain Fresh Grocery (hot bar/deli) Plateau towns (Cashiers/Highlands) are heavily seasonal — a lot closes or goes limited-hours outside summer/leaf season. Confirm hours before counting on any of these.
data.fall-reset-dh-reopens-sept--oct#Fall res:
Oct 1 flips the DH waters back to C&R with fresh, heavy stockings — the single biggest date on the calendar and prime numbers season. Brown trout stage toward their November spawn, so the streamer bite turns on. Fall BWOs on gray days. Arguably the best all-around window of the year.
Confidence: egg / Squirmy / Pat’s Rubber Legs (#8–12), sculpin & Woolly Bugger streamers, BWO dry/emerger (#18–20), Green Weenie (#12–14)
data.fly-shops-and-local-figures#Fly shops an: Davidson River Outfitters (Pisgah Forest, at the mouth of the Davidson) — the anchor shop for the Brevard core, with a deep guide staff. Owner Kevin Howell is regional fly-fishing royalty: a Fly Fishing Masters champion and son of the late Don Howell, who with his brother Dwight ran the shop’s forerunner and wrote the definitive regional guide, Tying & Fishing Southern Appalachian Trout Flies (1999, with Kevin contributing). If a name comes up here the way Harrop’s does on the Henry’s Fork, it’s Howell. Headwaters Outfitters (Rosman, right at the French Broad confluence; second location in Brevard) — 30+ years running, the practical hub for the French Broad forks and the go-to for paddling/tubing shuttle logistics too. Brookings Anglers (Cashiers) — the plateau anchor, guiding the Tuckasegee, Chattooga, Whitewater, Panthertown, Cullasaja, and the small private/wild creeks. Best current intel for the Highlands/Cashiers leg. Hookers Fly Shop (Sylva, west of the plateau) — additional Tuckasegee and Smokies-side coverage if you push farther west. Worth knowing: the region has its own homegrown fly canon — the Yallarhammer (originally tied with feathers from the yellow-shafted flicker), the Thunderhead (Great Smoky Mountains tyer Fred Hall), the Tellico Nymph, the Sheep Fly, and the ubiquitous Green Weenie. A local guide will reach for these before your Western attractors.
data.fly-tying-bench-recipes-and-video#Fly-ty: The Southern Appalachian canon rewards tying your own — most of these are homespun regional patterns you won’t find pre-binned outside WNC. Below are the ones worth tying before the trip: the regional classics that anchor the fly boxes here, plus the Davidson’s two technical-water staples. Each has a hook, the standard recipe, and a video link (all verified live at time of writing). Several of these are folk patterns with no single canonical dressing — where that’s the case, the recipe below is one well-documented version, noted as such.
data.gear#Gear:
A 9’ 5wt with a floating line covers ~90% of this trip — Davidson, the DH runs, and the French Broad forks. Two sensible additions:
A 7'6"–8’ 3wt or 4wt for the small native brook-trout headwaters on the plateau and upper Pisgah — tight, rhododendron-choked casting where a 9-footer is a liability. A 6wt or a heavier leader/streamer rig if you’re chasing West Fork browns or throwing sculpins on the Tuck in higher water. No stillwater-specific gear needed unless you plan to work DuPont’s lakes (Cascade, Julia) hard — a spare intermediate line helps there. Felt-sole restrictions don’t apply in NC, but bring studded rubber for the slick plateau bedrock regardless. A NC fishing license plus the special trout privilege is required; buy online before you go.
data.green-weenie#Green Weenie:
The modern outlier — a dead-simple chartreuse inchworm/caddis-larva imitation that’s a region-wide confidence fly, especially in summer. (Actually a Pennsylvania invention, credited to Ken Igo and Russ Mowry on Loyalhanna Creek, but long since adopted as WNC’s own.) Deliberately a one-material fly.
Hook: standard 1X–2X nymph or curved scud hook, #12–14 (jig-hook/bead versions are common) Materials: fluorescent-chartreuse 6/0–8/0 thread; optional gold/brass or chartreuse tungsten bead; chartreuse Ultra Chenille / vernille wrapped full-length, with a short burnt or looped tail-tag for the inchworm silhouette. No rib, hackle, or wing. Video: Dark Skies Fly Fishing — “Fly Tying the Green Weenie, With and Without a Tail”
data.high-summer-low-water--brookie-prime-mid:
Low, clear, warm freestones — fish the Davidson (stays cold below the hatchery) and go up for native brook trout, whose high, cold headwaters are at their best now. Dawn patrol and shaded plunge pools; skip the sun-baked lowland runs when water temps climb.
Confidence: Thunderhead (#12–16), Yallarhammer (#10–14), hopper-dropper (foam hopper over a beadhead PT), Parachute Adams / beetle (#14–18)
data.late-winter--first-hatches-mid-feb--late:
Cold, often high water; DH waters are in C&R and lightly pressured — the sleeper window for big stocked fish with the river to yourself. Wild-trout streams wake up with the year’s first mayflies on the warmer afternoons. Fish midday, deep and slow.
Confidence: Zebra Midge / WD-40 (#18–22), Blue Quill & Quill Gordon (#14–18), Little Black Stonefly (#16), Pheasant Tail (#16–18)
data.looking-glass-creek--avery-creek-pisgah-:
Small, roadside, easy-access water off US-276 for an evening session. Looking Glass Falls and the Sliding Rock natural waterslide are right here, so this doubles as sightseeing water. Wild and stocked rainbows; freestone conditions.
Yellow Stimulator / Yellow Sally (#12–16) Elk Hair Caddis, tan/olive (#14–18) Parachute Adams (#14–18) Hopper-dropper: small foam terrestrial over a beadhead nymph
data.north-fork-french-broad--pocket-water#No:
Runs through a rocky gorge with several waterfalls; fast runs and dark holes holding browns and rainbows averaging ~10". Wade with care.
Heavy stonefly nymphs, streamers year-round Yellow Stimulator / Thunderhead in warm months High-floating attractor dries for the pocket water
data.peak-spring-dry-fly-april--mid-may#Peak:
The best wild-trout dry-fly fishing of the year and the Davidson’s showpiece stretch. Hendricksons, March Browns, and Grannom caddis stack up; DH water is both C&R and freshly stocked — the fullest boxes-and-bent-rods window on the calendar.
Confidence: Hendrickson (#12–14), March Brown (#12–14), Elk Hair / Grannom Caddis (#14–16), Parachute Adams (#14–18), Pheasant Tail / Hare’s Ear dropper
data.quick-confidence-box#Quick confidence bo: Category Patterns Sizes DH stockers Squirmy worm, egg, Pat’s Rubber Legs, Green Weenie 8–14 Davidson technical Zebra Midge, WD-40, sulphur, BWO, RS2 16–22 Spring mayfly (Davidson) Hendrickson, Quill Gordon, March Brown 12–16 Attractor dries Yellow Stimulator, Elk Hair Caddis, Parachute Adams 12–18 Regional classics Yallarhammer, Thunderhead, Tellico Nymph 10–16 Nymphs (general) Pheasant Tail, Hare’s Ear, Copper John, Prince 12–20 Streamers (West Fork/Tuck) Sculpin, Woolly Bugger, articulated 4–10 Native brookies (headwaters) Thunderhead, Yallarhammer, foam beetle 12–18 Season read: the delayed-harvest window (Oct 1 – first Saturday in June) is the strategic core — C&R, single-hook artificial-only, and the best numbers of the year on the East Fork, DuPont’s Little River, and the Tuck. The Davidson fishes technical and rewarding year-round; the plateau brookies want warm, bright afternoons. The one live variable is Helene-related access — re-check the Pisgah closures page and ncwildlife.gov/trout right before the trip, since road and stocking-point changes are the thing most likely to move this plan.
data.seasonal-windows#Seasonal windows: Southern Appalachian trout run on hatch timing and the DH calendar more than the four seasons. These windows are approximate — a warm February or a cold May shifts them a week or two — but they’re the rhythm a local guide plans around. Confidence flies are the ones to tie on first if you have no other intel.
data.sheep-fly#Sheep Fly:
The local Brevard classic: created by Newland Saunders of Lenoir, NC in the 1950s and made a signature fly by Don Howell — championed today by his son Kevin Howell at Davidson River Outfitters, the anchor shop for this leg. The recipe is semi-standardized; the gray-body / brown-hackle / grizzly-tip-wing character is consistent across tyers.
Hook: Kevin Howell’s version uses a Mustad 79580 (4XL) #8; commonly tied #6–14 on a 2XL nymph hook Materials: brown hackle-fiber tail; gray dubbing body (Adams gray / muskrat) palmered with brown hackle; grizzly hackle-tip wings Video: Davidson River Outfitters — “Fly Tying with Kevin Howell: Sheep Fly”
data.southwest-the-cashiers--highlands-platea: Higher, colder, and more remote — Highlands is one of the highest-elevation towns in the eastern US. This is where wild and native fish live alongside the plateau’s marquee stocked runs. Brookings Anglers (Cashiers) is the anchor shop.
data.sulphur-comparadun#Sulphur Comparadun:
For the Davidson’s signature late-spring Sulphur hatch (Ephemerella invaria / dorothea). The Comparadun — Al Caucci and Bob Nastasi’s flush-floating no-hackle dun — is the canonical way to tie it; it’s a national style, not a Davidson original, but it’s the right tool for that glassy hatch water.
Hook: standard dry-fly, Tiemco TMC 100 / 100SP-BL, #16–18 Materials: pale-yellow/cream thread; fine deer-hair wing, stacked and fanned ~180° upright over the thorax; split hackle-fiber or Microfibbett tails (sulphur/dun); slim pale-yellow/sulphur dry-fly dubbing body (Superfine Sulphur/PMD); no hackle (the defining Comparadun feature) Video: Tightline Productions — “Sulphur Comparadun”
data.sulphurs--the-dh-handoff-mid-may--first-:
The Davidson’s signature Sulphur hatch peaks — evening dry-fly fishing at its best. This is also the last of the DH C&R window before it flips to harvest, so hit the East Fork, Little River, and the Tuck hard before the first-Saturday-in-June changeover thins them out.
Confidence: Sulphur dun/emerger (#16–18), Light Cahill (#14–16), Yellow Sally (#14–16), Green Weenie (#12–14) on the stocked DH runs
data.tellico-nymph#Tellico Nymph:
Named for the Tellico River on the Tennessee side of the range — the one homegrown Appalachian nymph that went national. Originator is anonymous; a “Blackburn Tellico” variant is also common.
Hook: 1X–3XL nymph, commonly Tiemco TMC 3761, #12–16, weighted with a wire underbody Materials: black 6/0–8/0 thread; brown/ginger/furnace hackle-fiber tail; bright yellow floss body; peacock-herl rib wound over the body (counter-rib with fine gold wire for durability); ringneck pheasant-tail shellback/wingcase; brown hen hackle collar Video: Mad River Outfitters — “Fly Tying the Tellico Nymph (w/ Ian Rutter)”
data.the-strategy#The strategy: Match the water type to the day, not the other way around. Three distinct games live within 45 minutes of Brevard: technical wild/C&R water (Davidson), numbers-y stocked DH runs (East Fork, Little River, Tuck), and small-stream native brookies (high plateau headwaters). Davidson is the technical anchor — it fishes clear and cold year-round below the Setzer hatchery, holds big, pellet-conditioned, famously picky trout, and rewards small flies and long leaders. Treat it like a spring creek. DH runs are the confidence water in the Oct–June window — go here when you want bent rods and a guide-friendly day. Native brook trout are the reward — the high, cold headwaters of the Highlands/Cashiers plateau and upper Pisgah hold the South’s only native trout (“specks”). Small water, dry-dropper, bluebird afternoons. Southern Appalachian fly boxes are their own dialect — the Yallarhammer, Thunderhead, Green Weenie, and Tellico Nymph are regional standards a local guide will actually reach for. Carry a few even if your Western boxes cover the rest.
data.thunderhead#Thunderhead:
Fred Hall of Bryson City’s high-floating dry — essentially an Adams color scheme given a bushy divided calf-hair wing for buoyancy in bubbly plunge pools. The go-to high-country brook-trout dry.
Hook: standard dry-fly, #12–16 Materials: gray or black 6/0–8/0 thread; white calf-tail wing, upright and divided (Wulff-style); mixed brown + grizzly hackle-fiber tail; medium-gray dubbing body (muskrat / Adams gray); mixed brown-and-grizzly rooster hackle, Adams-style Video: Savage Flies — “Thunderhead Dry Fly”
data.town-notes#Town notes: Brevard (core base) — Transylvania County seat, home of the Brevard Music Center (summer institute since 1936) and famous for its white squirrels (there’s a festival). Compact, walkable, brewery-dense downtown; the practical grocery/gear/lodging hub for the whole trip. Pisgah Forest (just north of Brevard) — the gateway up US-276 into Pisgah National Forest and the Davidson; Sierra Nevada’s East Coast brewery is nearby in Mills River, and Oskar Blues is in Brevard proper. Rosman (west, French Broad hub) — a small former timber/rail town; nearby PARI (Pisgah Astronomical Research Institute) is a former NASA/NSA tracking station turned observatory, an unusual rainy-day stop. Cashiers (plateau) — a crossroads resort village at ~3,500 ft; upscale, seasonal, the practical stop for the Tuck/Chattooga leg. Highlands (plateau) — one of the highest incorporated towns in the eastern US (~4,100 ft), a genteel, cool-in-summer resort town with good restaurants and a waterfall-lined approach on US-64.
data.tuckasegee-river-the-tuck--numbers-king#:
The largest river in the Highlands-Cashiers area and the region’s premier delayed-harvest float/wade. In the DH window, 50-fish days happen, and the “Tuck Slam” (rainbow, brown, brook in one day) is genuinely likely. This is the confidence water of the whole trip.
Egg patterns, Squirmy worm, Pat’s Rubber Legs (#8–12) Green Weenie, Copper John, Pheasant Tail (#12–18) Zebra Midge under an indicator in the deeper runs
data.waterfalls--non-fishing-sights#Waterfall:
The “Land of Waterfalls” tag is earned — pair a bluebird afternoon with a drive:
Looking Glass Falls & Sliding Rock (US-276, Pisgah) — roadside 60-ft falls and a natural waterslide, both right on the Davidson corridor. DuPont’s falls (Hooker, Triple, High, Bridal Veil) — the Hunger Games / Last of the Mohicans set; short hikes, huge payoff. Whitewater Falls (near Cashiers) — one of the highest falls in the eastern US (~411 ft). The Cullasaja Gorge (US-64, Highlands) — Dry Falls (you can walk behind it) and Bridal Veil Falls, drive-through waterfalls on the way to the Cullasaja water.
data.wd-40#WD-40:
Mark Engler’s emerging-midge/Baetis pattern — a technical-tailwater staple that earns its keep on the Davidson’s picky, pellet-conditioned fish. A “loose” pattern: hook and whether you add thorax dubbing vary by tyer.
Hook: short-emerger or standard nymph, #18–22 (Dai-Riki 125 or TMC 2487/2488) Materials: light-olive (or gray/brown) 70-denier thread forming a slim tapered abdomen; one bunch of mallard or wood-duck flank does double duty — tips left short as the tail, butts pulled forward over the thorax as the wingcase/flared collar (the pattern’s signature move); fine dubbing thorax behind the collar Video: Charlie’s Fly Box — “WD-40 Fly Tying Instructions by Charlie Craven”
data.west-fork-french-broad--big-brown-sleepe:
Produces some of the region’s biggest browns each year. Trout-farm effluent in the headwaters makes it fecund and buggy, with unpredictable but heavy burrowing-mayfly hatches. Fewer fish, larger average size — a streamer-and-big-nymph stream.
Sculpin / articulated streamers, olive & brown Large stonefly nymphs, Pat’s Rubber Legs (#6–10) Big mayfly nymphs when the burrowers are active
data.west-rosman--the-french-broad-headwaters: The North, East, West, and Middle forks converge near Rosman to form the French Broad — one of the oldest rivers in the world, and one of the few in North America that flows north. Rosman is the western hub; Headwaters Outfitters sits right at the confluence.
data.whitewater-river-panthertown-valley--hea:
Small, high, cold native brook-trout water — Panthertown (“the Yosemite of the East”), Whitewater, and the countless unnamed feeders. Short season, bluebird afternoons, dry-dropper on a short rod. Handle specks gently; they’re the South’s only native trout.
Thunderhead, Yallarhammer, Yellow Stimulator (#12–16) Foam beetle / ant, Parachute Adams (#14–18) Small beadhead dropper (Pheasant Tail, #16–18)
data.winter-dh--midge-season-nov--mid-feb#Win:
The connoisseur’s window: DH water is stocked, cold, and nearly empty of anglers. Browns are on/finishing the spawn (leave redds alone). Small-fly, deep-nymph, slow-swing fishing on the warmest hours of the day; midges do most of the work.
Confidence: Zebra Midge (black/red, #18–22), midge larva / WD-40 (#20–22), egg pattern (#14–16), small streamer on the swing
data.yallarhammer#Yallarhammer:
The most storied mountain fly — a swung/drifted wet (also tied as a nymph) whose origin is genuine Appalachian lore, with no verifiable single inventor. Named for the “yellowhammer,” the local word for the yellow-shafted flicker whose golden quills were the original wing. That bird is now protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so its feathers are illegal to use.
Hook: #10–14, 2XL–3XL nymph (e.g. TMC 5262 for the wet version); model is tyer-dependent Materials: brown or black thread; golden-pheasant-tippet or yellow-grizzly tail; yellow floss or wool body (weighted with lead-free wire for the nymph); the wing/hackle is a mourning-dove or bobwhite-quail primary feather dyed golden-yellow (the legal flicker substitute), soaked, stem split and pith scraped, then palmered forward so the barbs spin in the current Video: Ronnie McKee — “Fly Tying the Yallar Hammer Fly”

/docs/fishing/2026-brevard-dupont-highla.title: 2026 Western NC Dossier: Brevard, DuPont & the Highlands Plateau

data:
Trip prep for Sept 7–25, 2026: Heaton Bay Campground, Frisco (Sept 7–10 and 21–25), with Carbondale (Sept 10–21) in between. Heaton Bay sits on Dillon Reservoir in Summit County — not Lake Granby/Grand Lake, easy to confuse by name.
The headline: 2026 is a historic drought year. Colorado’s water-year snowpack ranked 45th of 46 years on record, and as of mid-August exceptional drought — the worst category — is centered on Pitkin, Eagle, Summit, Lake, and Park counties, which covers both legs of this trip. Statewide rivers were running ~59% of normal in August. CPW has active full-day voluntary closures (not just noon–midnight — upgraded from partial-day back in July) on the Colorado, Eagle, and Crystal rivers, in effect since July 17 with no lift date; the Roaring Fork’s afternoon-only closure was lifted Aug 20 after cooler temps and increased Ruedi Reservoir releases. September’s seasonal outlook leans above-normal temps and below-normal precip, so don’t assume normal fall cooling fixes this fast. Re-check the CPW weather and drought closures page in the days before departure — it’s the one live variable that changes this plan.
data.barrs-bwo-emerger#Barr\u0026rsquo;s BWO:
John Barr’s Blue-Winged Olive emerger (documented with Charlie Craven in Barr Flies) — the go-to for the overcast-day BWO windows on both tailwaters.
Hook: Tiemco TMC 2487 or a 2X-short emerger (Dai-Riki #125), #20–22 (range #18–24). Daiichi equivalent: Daiichi 1130 (down eye, fine wire, 2X-wide, 2X-short, curved) Materials: olive or dark-brown 8/0 thread; brown/ginger hen-hackle-fiber tail and trailing shuck; olive-brown Superfine dubbing abdomen; wood-duck flank wingcase and legs; gray or gray-olive Superfine thorax Video: Tightline Productions — “Barr’s Emerger BWO”
data.beadhead-flashback-pheasant-tail#Beadhea:
The Americanized flashback beadhead lineage of the pheasant tail (peacock thorax, pearl-flash wingcase) — Charlie Craven’s canonical tie. General searching nymph that covers mayfly nymphs on every water this trip touches.
Hook: Tiemco TMC 5262 (down eye, 2X-heavy, 2X-long nymph), #16–20 (recipe range #12–18). Daiichi equivalent: Daiichi 1710 (down eye, 2X-heavy, 2X-long) Materials: rusty-brown 8/0 thread; brass/copper or tungsten bead sized to hook; lead-free wire underweight; ringneck pheasant-tail tail and abdomen; fine copper wire rib (counter-wrapped); pheasant-tail wingcase topped with pearl Flashabou; peacock-herl thorax; wingcase butts folded back for legs Video: Charlie’s Fly Box — “Flashback Pheasant Tail”
data.blue-river-silverthorne-tailwater-below-:
Your most reliable water on this leg — a true tailwater, cold and clear year-round, unaffected by the drought the way freestones are. Technical: small flies, long leaders, 5x tippet. Trout see everything here.
Mysis shrimp patterns (#14–16) Zebra Midge, black/red (#20–22) RS2, gray/olive (#20–22) Small BWO nymph Egg patterns if kokanee are running up from the reservoir
data.bonus-water-maroon-bells-maroon-lake--ma:
Not part of the core plan, but a worthwhile side trip out of Carbondale (Maroon Bells sits above Aspen, roughly 45 min–1 hr from Carbondale) if you want a high-alpine session alongside the scenery — the Maroon Bells are among the most photographed peaks in the country, so this doubles as the trip’s best non-fishing sight.
Access requires a reservation. Private vehicles need a timed parking permit; otherwise it’s the RFTA shuttle bus from the Aspen Highlands Welcome Center (~15 min each way). Book ahead at visitmaroonbells.com — walk-up access during the day is not guaranteed in season. Maroon Lake: stocked rainbow and brook trout, with native cutthroat also possible. Bank fishing only — wading and boats/float tubes are not allowed in the lake. Standard Colorado license and bag limits apply. Maroon Creek, below the lake, is the better dedicated-fishing option if you want to actually work water rather than just sight-cast the lake edge. Crater Lake — a 1.8-mile (one-way) hike above Maroon Lake — adds a second, quieter high-alpine lake if you want to turn the visit into a half-day hike-and-fish. Overnight camping past this point (Crater Lake, Four Pass Loop) needs a separate wilderness permit from recreation.gov; day fishing doesn’t. Given this is high alpine water (starts around 9,600 ft), expect a short season and cold mornings even in September — pair it with a bluebird-afternoon day rather than dawn patrol.
data.colorado-river-glenwood-springs-confluen:
Warmest, most drought-affected water on this trip; treat as a last resort unless flows recover.
Streamers early/late if fishing Hopper-dropper if flows come back up
data.corn-fed-caddis-tan--olive#Corn-fed Cadd:
Lance Egan’s high-floating CDC caddis — the dry to reach for on the caddis-heavy Fryingpan. Tan is the default; tie olive to match darker bugs.
Hook: Tiemco TMC 100 (wide gape, down eye, 1X-fine standard dry-fly), #14–16 (range #12–18). Daiichi equivalent: Daiichi 1100 (wide gape, down eye, 1X-fine) Materials: tan (or olive) UTC 70 thread; white/tan Antron trailing shuck; tan (or olive) Superfine dubbing abdomen; natural dun CDC underwing; white poly-yarn overwing (high-float indicator); natural CDC collar/head Video: In the Riffle — “Corn Fed Caddis”
data.crystal-river-carbondale--backup-only-cl:
Extremely low and warm as of late August; voluntary noon–midnight closure in effect. Confirm status before fishing — if open, dawn-only in shaded riffles.
Small attractor dries, terrestrials Nymph rigs fished in shade/riffle water only
data.dillon-reservoir-stillwater#Dillon Reser:
~3,200-acre reservoir right at the campground; stocked rainbow, brown, kokanee salmon, and arctic char, plus lake trout. Fair-to-good in August, improving into fall as shallow water cools and fish push out onto points, humps, and rocky structure. Bank and float-tube access is workable near the marina and inlet seams.
Woolly Bugger, olive/black (#6–10) Leech patterns, black/maroon (#6–10) Pheasant Tail / midge pupa nymphs, drifted at inlet current seams Small streamers stripped along drop-offs as water cools
data.eating-mid-tier-and-budget#Eating: mid-t: Frisco Mid-tier: Tavern West (New American, craft beer); Ollie’s Pub & Grub Budget: Butterhorn Bakery & Cafe (breakfast institution, 40+ years) Silverthorne Mid-tier: Bamboo Garden (Thai/Chinese/sushi, running since 1997); Windy City Pizza & Pub Budget: Sunshine Cafe (breakfast/lunch); Bluebird Marketplace (food-hall counter service) Carbondale Mid-tier: Izakaya Carbondale; Village Smithy Restaurant Budget: 502 Diner (burgers); Dos Gringos Burritos; White House Pizza Basalt Mid-tier: The Tipsy Trout (Fryingpan River view); The Brick Pony Pub Budget: Two Rivers Cafe (diner); CC’s Cafe (breakfast/coffee) Small-town rosters here turn over as fast as the Yellowstone-circuit towns — confirm hours before counting on any of these, especially off-season.
data.egans-frenchie-pink--hot-orange-hot-spot:
Lance Egan’s competition-born jig nymph — basically a pheasant tail on a jig hook with a hot-spot collar, and a fine general-searching pattern for the tailwaters and freestones alike on this trip.
Hook: Firehole 315 or TMC 2499SP-BL (barbless jig hook, standard length, wide gape), #14–18. No confirmed Daiichi cross-reference for this jig style — Daiichi’s closest barbless jig options are the 1120 (curved nymph/jig wire) or the newer 1920 series, but match gape/wire specs yourself before buying rather than trusting an equivalence here. Materials: slotted tungsten bead sized to hook (black nickel or copper); tan or brown UTC 70 thread; ringneck pheasant-tail fibers for tail and abdomen; small copper Ultra Wire rib; pink or hot-orange Ice Dub hot-spot collar; peacock herl thorax Video: Fly Fish Food — “Fly Tying Tutorial: Egan’s Frenchie”
data.fishing-industry-figures-and-shops#Fishi: Frying Pan Anglers (Basalt) — founded 1986 by Roy Palm on the bank of the Fryingpan; 2026 is its 40th season. One of the oldest full-service shops in the region, with one of the largest fly selections in Colorado (6,000+ patterns) and a weekly Monday river report worth checking before this leg. Ownership passed to Taylor Thackston in 2023. Taylor Creek Fly Shops (Basalt) — also on the Fryingpan, marketed as western Colorado’s oldest guide service/fly shop (~50 years running). Cutthroat Anglers (Silverthorne, on the Blue River) — opened 1999 by the late Trapper Rudd, known locally as “The Clubhouse”; now run by Ben McCormick, carries 100,000+ flies, and has been voted Summit County’s best fishing outfitter for a decade running. The obvious stop for current Blue River / Dillon Reservoir intel on Leg 1/3. Roaring Fork Conservancy (Basalt, founded 1996) — the watershed’s standing advocacy/conservation group, born from a Roaring Fork Club and Town of Basalt partnership; runs water-quality monitoring and fishery studies on the Fryingpan and Roaring Fork specifically — the Henry’s Fork Foundation equivalent for this valley. Both the Fryingpan and Roaring Fork carry Colorado Gold Medal Water designation; the Fryingpan’s 14-mile Gold Medal stretch runs from Ruedi Dam (built 1968, the reason the tailwater exists) down to the Basalt confluence. Colorado fly-fishing writer John Gierach (based in Lyons, CO, not local to this valley) has written about the Fryingpan among many Colorado waters — worth knowing the name if a guide brings it up, though he’s not a Roaring Fork Valley local the way Harrop is to the Henry’s Fork.
data.fly-tying-bench-recipes-and-video#Fly-ty: The tailwater game here (Blue below Dillon, Fryingpan below Ruedi) rewards a handful of small, well-tied confidence flies over a big fly box. These are the ones worth tying yourself before the trip — each with a hook, the standard recipe, and a video link (all verified live at time of writing). Sizes below lean to the small end for the low, clear 2026 water.
data.fly-tying-travel-kit-consolidated-packin:
Everything below covers all 9 bench patterns. Consolidated by overlap — e.g. one curved-emerger hook style covers three flies, one Superfine dubbing dispenser (if it comes in multi-color wallets) covers four colors. Pack this, not a full bench.
Hooks (7 sizes/styles total)
☐ Hook Daiichi equivalent Description Size Used for ☐ TMC 200R 1270 (length/wire match only — not curved) 3XL, standard wire, straight eye #16–18 Mysis Shrimp only ☐ TMC 2487/2488 (Dai-Riki #125 same niche) 1130 Down eye, fine wire, 2X-wide, 2X-short, curved (“scud hook” shape) #18–24 Zebra Midge, Mercury Midge, Barr’s BWO Emerger — covers 3 patterns, buy the widest range in this one style ☐ TMC 101 1110 Wide gape, straight eye, 1X-fine #20–22 RS2 ☐ TMC 5262 1710 Down eye, 2X-heavy, 2X-long nymph #16–20 Pheasant Tail ☐ TMC 100 1100 Wide gape, down eye, 1X-fine standard dry #14–16 Corn-fed Caddis ☐ Firehole 315 or TMC 2499SP-BL No confirmed match — closest is 1120 or the newer 1920 barbless series; verify gape/wire before buying Barbless jig, standard length, wide gape #14–18 Frenchie — same hook style also fits the jig Perdigons below, one size run covers both ☐ Firehole 315/318 or Hends BL 454 Same caveat as above Barbless jig #14–18 Perdigon-style jig nymphs Beads
