data:
Notes on growing food hydroponically through the winter in an unheated-ish garage — built around a 3D-printed Vertical Garden: Large Hydroponic Vegetable Tower (archive) from MakerWorld.
The model page blocks automated fetching, so the tower details here come from a PDF printout of the page (captured 2026-11-01), summarized in The Tower. The model’s own page is the authority on parts and print settings.
data.pages#Pages: The Tower: Parts, Pot, and Pump — what the MakerWorld design needs besides printed parts, pot and pump requirements, assembly order, print notes, and what its commenters changed Hydroponics 101 — how a tower works, how often to run the pump and feed, pH/EC targets, weekly upkeep, and the best crops to start with Seed Starting for Hydroponics — rockwool and plug starts, germination temperatures, lighting, and when to move seedlings into the tower Garage Grow Setup — lights, heat, timers, meters, and a shopping list for a winter garage

data: A winter garage changes three things: there is no sunlight, it is cold, and there is moisture around electricity. All three have fixes.
data.heat#Heat:
Unheated garage lows will drop the reservoir towards freezing, which stops growth and can split pumps and fittings.
Insulate — wrap or place the reservoir in foam board or a cooler-style enclosure; keep it off the cold concrete floor on a pallet or foam. Aquarium heater (adjustable) in the reservoir, set about 68 °F, plugged into a GFCI. This is the single most useful heat item. It must stay fully submerged: a heater exposed by a falling water level gets very hot very fast. Freeze protection for everything else — the reservoir heater only protects the tank. The tower column, tubing, net-cup roots, and pump all sit in garage air. If the forecast is near 32 °F, bring the tower inside or drain the column and lines, and keep the plants somewhere warm. Room-level heat — insulation plus the reservoir heater is the preferred plan. If you add an electric space heater, plug it directly into a wall outlet (never a power strip or extension cord), keep 3 ft of clearance, use one with tip-over shutoff, and don’t leave it running unattended; NFPA advises unplugging it when you leave. No fuel-burning heaters in the garage (carbon monoxide), and keep fuels and solvents away from any heater. Seedling heat mat with a thermostat for germination.
data.light#Light:
Garage windows will not do it. Plants need a dedicated light.
Seedlings: roughly 100–200 µmol/m²/s (PPFD) at the canopy, 14–16 h/day. Leafy greens and herbs in the tower: roughly 200–400 µmol/m²/s, 14–16 h/day. Fruiting crops (tomatoes, peppers, strawberries): considerably more, 400+ (a rule of thumb; not checked against a source). A light delivering ~300 µmol/m²/s for 16 h works out to a daily light integral of about 17 mol/m²/day, a good target for lettuce. Without good airflow, aim a little lower (13–14) to avoid tip burn.
The tower stands up to 180 cm (about 6 ft) with all three pot sizes stacked, so you want light that covers its height, not just the top. A 1 m bar covers roughly half of a full-height column; use two per side, or build the tower shorter. A commenter built LED strips into the optional support rings. Options:
Full-spectrum LED bars or strips mounted vertically alongside the tower, one per side. This is usually the best fit. Full-spectrum LED panel or bar above the seedling tray for the starting area. T5 high-output fluorescents — work well for seedlings, cheaper but bulkier and less efficient. Look for a manufacturer-stated PPFD (or PAR) figure at a stated distance, not just “equivalent to 1000 W” claims. Give the light its own timer (14–16 h on). The pump runs its interval cycle around the clock on a separate timer.
data.meters-and-supplies#Meters and supplies: pH meter (digital pen type) with calibration solution (pH 4 and 7); calibrate regularly and store as directed. Cheap pH test drops or strips work for rough checks only. EC meter — buy EC, not just TDS. TDS is calculated from EC with a 0.5 or 0.7 factor, so ppm readings from different meters don’t match. pH Down (and pH Up) — small bottles last a long time. Complete hydroponic nutrient — a two- or three-part set designed for leafy greens. Seed-starting tray, humidity dome, heat mat, rockwool or plugs — see Seed Starting. Small clip-on fan for airflow. Seedlings need it, and grown lettuce needs it too to prevent tip burn and damp mold, especially in a closed tent. Measuring syringes or a graduated cylinder for doses. Opaque tubing and a lid on the reservoir to keep out light and algae. Print or paint the tower parts opaque too (check the model for PETG vs PLA; PETG copes better with a cold, wet garage).
data.shopping-list#Shopping list:
Grow lights below don’t list a PPFD figure at a distance (see the Light section). Archive links are omitted where the Wayback Machine has no snapshot of a product page yet. Links and prices were checked against each product page on 2026-11-01. On the same day the list was re-checked against the tower’s own parts list (see The Tower): the pump was replaced with the designer’s Sicce (the earlier pumps could not lift to the top), the light counts were sized to the 180 cm height, the TriPart nutrient was added, and rows were added for the reservoir pot, center pipe, screws, filter foam, net pots, and grow media. Prices change; no links are affiliate links.
Item Pick Why / key spec Price (2026-11-01) Vertical LED grow lights Spider Farmer SF600 (archive), one per side
or Barrina T5 2 ft, 5000K, 4-pack (archive) SF600: 39.4″ × 5.9″ bar (100 cm), ~74 W, 2.3 µmol/J, hanging kit included; not daisy-chainable. It is a European product and no US retailer was found, so FloraSeries is the practical US stand-in. Its FAQ says its feed charts use a lower EC than GH’s US charts. The page does not give the plug diameter, so check it against the tower’s net cups. For rockwool (the designer’s choice), see the rockwool row below. $25.96 Tray + humidity dome Bootstrap Farmer 1020 tray, no holes (archive)
+ Bootstrap Farmer 1020 humidity dome (archive) Thick tray, 2.5″ deep, no holes, for bottom watering. Dome is 5.4″ tall with two vents and rests on the rim. Both made in the USA. Tray $6.69; dome $8.19 Outlet timers Lights: Autopilot 7-day digital timer (TM01715) (archive)
Pump: Autopilot analog dual-outlet timer (TM01015D) (archive) The digital timer only allows 8 on/off cycles a day, fine for lights but too few for a 15-on/15-off pump. The analog timer has 15-minute pins for the full 24 h, so it can do 15/15 or 15/30–45. Both grounded, 15 A, UL listed, indoor use. List price $25.19 (digital) / $19.94 (analog) GFCI adapter Southwire 14650013-6 single-outlet GFCI adapter (archive) 120 V/15 A, trips at 4–6 mA, manual reset (stays off after a power cut until you reset it, so check the pump after outages). Skip it if the garage outlet is already a GFCI that passes its test button. Not shown (dealer list) Air pump + airstone EcoPlus Eco Air 1 Plus
+ AquaVita 2″ cylinder airstone Single outlet, 2 W, 44 GPH; plenty for a small reservoir. Keeps the water oxygenated when the pump is off. Add airline tubing and a check valve; keep the pump above the water line. Pump $12.03; stone $3.11 Tower pump Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (archive) (designer’s pump)
or Sicce Syncra Silent 1.5 (archive) for a shorter tower
Specs: Sicce Syncra Silent page (archive) Size by lift, not flow: flow falls to zero at max head. Lift is the height from the pot’s water surface to the sprinkler, about 1.4–1.6 m on a full 180 cm tower (assuming the 180 cm includes the 40 cm pot). 2.0: 568 GPH, 6.5 ft (2.0 m) max head, 35 W, ¾″ outlet (US 120 V listing); Sicce’s own page (230 V/50 Hz) gives 2150 L/h, 200 cm, 32 W. 1.5: 357 GPH, 6 ft (1.8 m), 23 W, ½″ outlet; Sicce gives 1350 L/h, 180 cm. At full height the 2.0 runs near 80% of its max head (low flow, but the designer’s tower works), and the 1.5 would be marginal. Shorter build: measure the lift and pick a pump whose max head is comfortably above it (aim for about 1.3–1.5× lift; a rule of thumb, not from a source). With a 1.2 m lift the 1.5 has that margin. The printed base is built around the Syncra outlet, so check the fit if you use a different pump. The cheaper pump with a commenter’s connector (MakerWorld 1625658) could not be checked, so it is not listed. data.timers-and-power#Timers and power: A timer for the lights (14–16 h on) and a separate timer for the pump (15 min on, 15–45 off, around the clock) so the schedules are independent. GFCI outlet or GFCI adapter — not optional. Surge-protected power strip mounted above the water line (for the lights and timers, not for a heater). Low-water protection — as the tank drops, the pump can run dry (which damages it) and the heater can end up in air. Check the level daily; a float switch or low-water cutoff is cheap insurance.
data.water-and-mixing#Water and mixing: Know your tap water. Check your utility’s water-quality report. Very soft water (Asheville’s runs about 24 ppm alkalinity) starts near zero EC and has little pH buffering, so pH swings fast, and some nutrient formulas need a Cal-Mag supplement. Chlorine is fine; chloramine is not removed by letting water sit. Well water needs a water analysis first. Mixing: add each nutrient part to the water separately and stir; never combine the concentrates. Measure EC first, then adjust pH. pH Down is acid: wear gloves and eye protection.

data: The short version of what a vertical tower needs: water + dissolved nutrients, oxygen at the roots, light, and a stable temperature. Everything else is detail.
data.common-problems#Common problems: Symptom Likely cause Pale new leaves pH out of range, or EC too low Brown, slimy roots Water too warm or low dissolved oxygen (root rot, often Pythium) Brown leaf tips on lettuce Usually a calcium-delivery problem from fast growth under strong light with poor airflow: add a fan and ease the light. Very high EC causes a different, general leaf-edge burn Algae in the tank or on the cups Light reaching the solution; cover the tank and use opaque parts Tall, floppy plants Light too weak or too far away Lettuce bolting (flower stalk) Heat or very long days
data.feeding-ph-and-ec#Feeding: pH and EC:
pH — keep the solution at 5.5–6.5 (aim ~5.8–6.0). Outside that range, plants cannot take up some nutrients even though they are in the water. EC (electrical conductivity, how strong the nutrient mix is) — the one number that tells you when to add nutrients. Measured in mS/cm. Crop group pH EC (mS/cm) Lettuce, arugula, bok choy 5.5–6.5 1.2–1.6 Basil, other herbs 5.5–6.5 1.0–1.6 Kale, chard 5.5–6.5 1.2–2.0 (the same solution as lettuce works) Strawberries 5.5–6.2 1.8–2.2 Dwarf tomatoes 5.8–6.3 2.0–4.0 Peppers 5.8–6.3 lower than tomatoes, roughly 0.8–1.8 Start seedlings at roughly a quarter to half strength and work up. (Commercial growers feed seedlings at full strength; weak is the cautious choice for a first run.)
Routine for a small tower:
Daily — look at the tank level and the roots. Top off with plain water (plants drink water faster than nutrients, so topping off with plain water keeps EC from creeping up). Daily for the first few weeks, then every 2–3 days once readings are stable — check pH and EC at the same time of day. Adjust pH after measuring EC. Adjust pH with small doses of pH-down (or up); add nutrients if EC has dropped below target. Every 2 weeks — drain, rinse, and refill the whole reservoir with fresh solution. Top-offs cannot fix an unbalanced mix. As needed — wipe slime off the pump intake and any drip points. Use a complete hydroponic nutrient (two- or three-part) rather than garden fertilizer, and follow its label for the dilution. Miracle-Gro and similar lawn-and-garden products are not formulated for this.
data.good-first-crops#Good first crops: Crop Why it works Roughly seed to first harvest Loose-leaf and butterhead lettuce Fast, low EC, tolerates cool temperatures; cut-and-come-again 5–8 weeks Basil Loves the tower, lots of leaf; needs warmth 5–7 weeks Arugula, bok choy Fast and forgiving 4–6 weeks Kale, Swiss chard Cold tolerant; good for a cool garage 6–8 weeks Mint, parsley, cilantro Mint grows like a weed (give it its own spot); cilantro bolts quickly 6–10 weeks Strawberries (day-neutral) A reasonable second project; buy bare-root crowns, not seed months The tower is built for more (the designer lists tomatoes, cucumbers, broccoli, kohlrabi, peppers, and eggplant, with an optional ring support for heavy crops) and offers three pot sizes: GrowBig4 for large crops, Grow8 for radishes and small salad, GrowSmall4 for head lettuce, herbs, and flowers. For a first winter in a garage, fill it with the leafy crops above: fruiting crops need much stronger light and more heat than a winter garage gives them. Dwarf cherry tomatoes and peppers are a step-two project once the routine is working.
data.how-a-vertical-tower-works#How a vertica:
The tower in these notes (see The Tower) has a submersible pump in a 40+ L pot at the base. The pump pushes solution up a 20 mm center pipe to a sprinkler head at the top, and it rains down through the stack of grow pots, past the roots of plants held in net cups, and drains back through the pot floors into the reservoir. Roots get water, air, and a shallow standing layer in each pot between cycles; one commenter on the model found roots look healthier this way than in designs that drain dry.
t p [ [ o i c c p p u u p e p p u s ] ] m p | [ [ p r p p i o o n t t t k ] ] a l [ [ n e c c k r r u u a p p i ] ] n d p o o o n w t n s t h s e t a p c i k p e A bigger reservoir is more forgiving: pH and nutrient concentration drift more slowly. This design’s 40+ L pot is a good size.
data.how-often-to-run-the-pump#How often to r:
The model page gives no pump schedule, and the designer calls the system low-maintenance, so treat these as starting points borrowed from university-extension trickle towers, then adjust by watching the roots:
Stage Pump schedule (lights on) Notes Seedlings just transplanted 15 min on / 15 min off Roots are short; keep them damp Established plants 15 min on / 30–45 min off Cut back if the cups stay soggy or algae shows Lights off Keep cycling, e.g. 15 min on / 45 off Don’t leave a trickle tower dry overnight; the pump runs 24 h on its own timer, separate from the light timer Use a plain mechanical or digital outlet timer. Watch the roots, not the clock: white and fuzzy is healthy; slimy, brown, or smelling bad means too wet, too warm, or too little oxygen. Wilting at midday with a dry cup means run it more often.
A pump that fails while the lights are on can kill a tower in hours, so check it the first thing every day.
data.safety#Safety: Water and mains power share a space. Plug everything into a GFCI-protected outlet, use drip loops on cords, and keep power strips and timers well above the reservoir.
data.water-temperature-important-in-a-garage#: Keep the reservoir around 68–72 °F; treat 75 °F as the ceiling. Warmer water encourages root rot (often Pythium) and holds less oxygen; much colder water slows growth. In an unheated garage in winter, the problem is cold, not hot — see Garage Grow Setup.

data: Seeds start in a small plug of growing medium, under light, then the whole plug drops into a net cup in the tower. No soil is involved.
data.germination-quick-reference#Germination: Crop Germination temp Days to sprout Lettuce 60–70 °F 2–7 Arugula, bok choy 60–75 °F 3–7 Kale, chard 60–75 °F 4–10 Basil 65–75 °F (best ~70) 5–10 Cilantro 60–70 °F 7–21 Parsley 65–80 °F 12–21+ Peppers 80–85 °F 7–14 Tomatoes 70–80 °F 5–10
data.mediums#Mediums: Medium Notes Rockwool cubes (1″) Cheap, standard. Needs a pre-soak: saturate in nutrient solution at pH ~5.5 until the air bubbles stop (a few minutes), drain, and don’t squeeze. Wear gloves and avoid breathing the dust; the fibers irritate skin. Rapid Rooter / peat-based plugs Easy, no pre-soak pH step; pop the seed in and keep moist Coco coir plugs Good water retention; rinse if not pre-buffered Oasis cubes Foam; works but holds a lot of water For a first try, rockwool or plugs are the least fiddly. Whichever you pick, it has to fit the tower’s net cups.
data.staggering#Staggering: Sow a few new plugs every 1–2 weeks. A tower planted all at once gives one big harvest and then nothing; staggered sowing gives a steady supply, and a spare seedling ready when a plant fails.
data.step-by-step#Step by step: Soak the plug in pH ~5.5 solution and let the excess drain. It should be damp, not dripping. Sow 1–2 seeds per hole (3 for tiny seeds like lettuce, thinned later). Do not bury light-dependent seeds such as lettuce; barely cover them. Cover the tray with a clear humidity dome until the seeds sprout. Warm — most crops want 65–75 °F at the plug. In a cold garage, a seedling heat mat under the tray does more good than a space heater. Lettuce germinates poorly above ~80 °F; peppers and basil like it warmer. Light as soon as they sprout — take the dome off and put a light a few inches above the seedlings, 14–16 hours a day. Raise it as they grow. Too far away means stretched, leggy seedlings. Water from below — keep an inch of very weak nutrient solution (a quarter of the label strength, EC ~0.4–0.8) in the bottom of the tray. Do not let the plugs dry out. Transplant into the tower when roots show out of the bottom of the plug and the seedling has 2–3 true leaves (not counting the first pair), usually 2–3 weeks for lettuce and herbs (longer under dim light).
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Nothing sprouts — too cold, too dry, or old seed. Check the plug is damp and the temperature is within the range above, ideally mid-range. White fuzz or mold on the plug — too wet and too still. Vent the dome and lower the moisture. Seedlings fall over at the base — damping off, usually from wet, cool, stagnant conditions. Add airflow (a small fan on low) and let the surface dry a bit. Leggy seedlings — light too far or too weak.

data: Notes from the Vertical Garden: Large Hydroponic Vegetable Tower (archive) page on MakerWorld, designed by Structales (released 2025-04-21). Summarized from a PDF printout of the page; the filament list at the page break and the video were not captured. Check the model page for anything you are about to buy or print.
data.assembly-order-in-short#Assembly order,:
The designer says don’t use an electric screwdriver or overtighten: it cracks the printed and plastic parts.
Base — screw together the base lid parts (12 M5 screws and nuts), put the pump in the pot, and make sure the pump output sits dead center in the pot (measure it). Lid and filter — route the cable through the square hole; drill two holes on each side of the pot to line up with the lid (they hold the rods); nuts in the small holes; foam filter with a center hole and a slit facing away from the filter flap. Structure — the 2 m pipe goes in the center and must line up with the pump outlet; two rods go through pot and base; fill remaining lid holes with the cover parts; put the GrowBig4 on top. Final — stack the pots, then the black sprinkler on top. Test — fill the pot halfway. If no water comes out the top, the pump is too weak or the pump-to-pipe connection leaks (add a sealing ring). Screw the grow pots to each other, then fit the lids. If the water gets too warm, use the white cap on the top; take it off on colder days to warm the water. To clean the pot, remove the top lids, pull the two base rods, and lift the whole tower aside so the pipe slides out; the plants stay in place.
data.at-a-glance#At a glance: Type Pump-fed “rain” tower: pump in a sealed pot, 20 mm center pipe, sprinkler at the top Height Up to 180 cm with all three pot sizes stacked Footprint Pot 38 × 38 cm (printed lid 36.8 cm square) Pot sizes GrowBig4 (large crops), Grow8 (radishes, small salad), GrowSmall4 (head lettuce, herbs, flowers); each big pot is about 18 × 18 × 20 cm Print time Main tower profile: 72 h over 14 plates (P1S shown). Optional support rings: 15 h, 6 plates. Alternatives and options: 41.5 h, 4 plates Filament Lots of it. Designer: use PETG, smooth plate recommended Track record Tested outdoors for 5 months, wind-resistant per the designer
data.implications-for-the-garage#Implications: Pump: the 180 cm tower needs a pump with enough head to push water 2 m up. Pick by max lift, and don’t assume a cheap pump has it; see the shopping list. Reservoir heat: the sealed pot is a good place for a 50 W aquarium heater, and the white cap stays off in winter per the designer. Freeze risk: the pot’s water is insulated by the lid, but the 20 mm pipe, pots, and net cups are full of water in cold air. Drain the pipe before a hard freeze. Light: 180 cm of tower needs lights along its whole height; see Garage Grow Setup.
data.what-commenters-found#What commenters fo: Algae at seams. Each level snaps together, and one commenter got algae from water seeping at the seams, so they printed a cover that snaps inside to hide it. The designer says their own tower ran two months indoors on parquet without a spill. Leak at the pump diaphragm. One builder found the diaphragm isn’t airtight and sealed it with gaffer tape. Print problems. A builder had trouble at the grow pot’s connector; the designer says to use the “BigTower with connector supports” print profile. Water temperature. A commenter running two towers reports the high flow rate keeps the water temperature stable even in high ambient heat. Add-ons. A TPU cover cap for the plant holes (MakerWorld model 1526313) and a “Hydroponic tower light kit” from another designer.
data.what-to-buy-besides-the-printed-parts#Wh:
From the designer’s list:
A large plant pot, at least 40 L / 10 gal, square, thick upper rim, no drainage holes, plastic (preferably polyethylene), with a drillable rim. The model is sized for a 38 × 38 × 40 cm pot; the page lists several European planters and notes the lid’s STEP files can be adapted. A commenter points out you can screw the lid to a board and cut it to fit any pot, and another suggests an ordinary 5-gallon bucket works. A submersible pump. The designer uses a Sicce Syncra Silent 2.0 (the 1.5 should also work). Another commenter designed a connector for a cheaper Amazon pump (MakerWorld model 1625658). 20 mm outer-diameter sturdy pipe, 2 m, cut to length (designer used aluminum; one commenter used stainless). About 28 × M4 countersunk screws, 16 mm, with nuts; 2 × shorter M4 countersunk, 8 mm, for the filter flap. 12 × M5 screws and nuts for the base lid. Nuts go into the grow pots too: 4 per big pot and 2 per small pot. 3 cm aquarium foam, cut into a filter pad for the lid. Net pots for the plants. One commenter notes that nuts can get stuck, and suggests embedded nuts instead. The designer’s growing setup: Terra Aquatica TriPart fertilizers, a pH meter and EC meter, filtered or rain water, rockwool cubes with vermiculite on top, then clay pebbles in the net pot after the roots develop.

data.pages#Pages: Six Mocktails: Coconut, Citrus, a Not-a-Mule, and Three for the Beach — a coconut colada, a blood orange spritz, an alcohol-free Moscow mule, plus a watermelon mojito, a virgin paloma, and a mango chili-lime built for a beach house trip Converting a Threaded SodaStream/Drinkmate to a 5 lb CO2 Tank — parts, sourcing, and safety notes for ditching the small exchange cylinders Barrel Sauna Roof and Porch Plan — insulated roof, sealing-vs-airflow rules, a freestanding porch roof, and a heat-rated fan for an Almost Heaven four-person cedar barrel sauna

data:
Plan for an Almost Heaven four-person cedar barrel sauna with an electric heater. Goals: stop rain drips through knots and seams, add insulation for cold-weather heating, and add a covered spot to change at the door.
Note: This is general building guidance gathered from Almost Heaven’s own roof suggestions, product listings, and common practice. It is not from the Almost Heaven manual, so confirm key details with Almost Heaven or a sauna builder before committing. Product and spec claims were checked against public listings on 2026-11-04 (see Verification notes); anything still unconfirmed is marked unverified.
data.air-circulation-for-cold-feet#Air circul:
A heat-rated sauna fan can move air. Ordinary fans are not safe inside: motors and plastic can fail or become a fire risk at sauna temperatures. Check this section’s assumptions before buying; the first draft overstated what the fan does.
Product to look for: MMotors MM-S 100, a 4 inch (100 mm) sauna exhaust fan: about 105 m³/h, 16 W, IP44, rated for 140°C when running (180°C switched off) and 100% humidity, housing and back-draft damper in glass-filled polyamide. Listings include versions with a back valve. These specs come from retailer pages, not an official datasheet. Where to buy: the listings I found were European sauna shops (for example esaunashop.com and orotech.lt). The first draft named Sauna Experts, Saunainter and SaunaBee, which I could not confirm. Unverified: supply voltage. EU listings are often 230 V, so find a 120 V version or a different fan before ordering. Not the SaunaBox Flow: it is a cordless USB-C fan for SaunaBox models only (SmartSteam, Pulse PRO, Solara, Forge), and often sold out. Its “up to 30% more heat transfer” is a vendor claim. Placement: the first draft claimed a low fan near the heater pulls warm air down along the floor. I could not find support for that. The MM-S is sold as an exhaust fan, and mounting one means cutting a 4 inch hole in a stave, which may affect your warranty. Ask Almost Heaven before cutting. Try first: Almost Heaven barrels usually have a low intake vent and a high exhaust vent. If both are wide open in winter, cold air may be flooding in, so try partly closing the intake. That costs nothing. Wiring: use high-temperature (silicone) wire near the fan, and have an electrician check the wiring.
data.insulation-product-names-to-search-for#I:
All from Rockwool (formerly sold as Roxul):
Comfortboard 80: semi-rigid stone wool board, R-4.2 per inch. Thicknesses run from 1 inch up through 5 inches. Common sizes are 2 ft by 4 ft, 4 ft by 6 ft and 4 ft by 8 ft, and Rockwool’s own charts differ on which thicknesses come in which size. A Canadian retailer lists 1.5 inch as a 24 x 48 inch pack of 48 square feet (six panels) and as a 48 x 72 inch pack of 24 square feet. Check dimensions on whatever you buy; the 2 x 4 ft size is easiest to cut into strips. Comfortbatt R-15: flexible batt, 3.5 inches thick, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Easy to find, but likely thicker than you want. Safe’n’Sound: 3 inch batts, 15.25 or 23 inches wide, 47 inches long. Same stone wool, but sold for sound and fire rating in interior walls. It has no official R-value (forum guesses are R-11 to R-13), so it is a poor pick for this job.
data.open-questions#Open questions: Heater size and circuit (confirm kW rating against your model and barrel volume, and the circuit with an electrician). Barrel diameter and height at the door end, to set the porch post heights. Whether the barrel’s steel hoops need notching or shimming under the furring. Rockwool’s maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80 and sauna suitability. Whether Almost Heaven allows cutting a fan hole or fastening a roof without voiding the warranty. Local permit rules for the porch roof and the heater circuit.
data.porch-roof-at-the-door#Porch roof at the:
A separate freestanding porch roof, so you can dress and undress out of the rain and so weight stays off the barrel staves.
Size: about 4 feet deep from the door, wider than the door (about 4 to 5 feet), with room to stand, hang a towel, and maybe fit a small bench. Frame: four posts: two at the front and two beside the door at the back (this fixes the first draft, which had no support at the back edge short of resting on the barrel). Put a beam across each pair and run rafters between them. Slope: 3 inches of drop per foot (3:12), draining forward and away from the barrel. The first draft said 1 inch per foot, which is too flat: corrugated metal generally wants 3:12 or more, and asphalt shingles need at least 2:12 with extra underlayment at low slopes (one code summary says 4:12, so check your local code). Taller front posts or a steeper pitch also give you more headroom. Height: aim for about 6 ft 8 in clear under the front edge. At 3:12 over 4 ft the back edge then ends up about 1 ft higher, which is above the top of a 6 ft barrel on its base. That is fine, because the porch then sits in front of the barrel instead of under its roof. Barrel joint: keep the back edge at least 2 inches clear of the barrel and its roof overhang. Give it an upturned lip and a metal cap flashing, and do not screw anything into the staves. Measure your barrel’s height at the door end first and set the post heights from that. Lumber: cedar or pressure-treated 4x4 posts, 2x6 beams and rafters, with roof material to match the barrel roof. Set posts on piers or footings suited to local frost depth and code.
data.quick-expectations#Quick expectations: Cedar swells when wet, so small drips through knots and seams are common. A roof greatly reduces them but may not eliminate them. Almost Heaven itself says some seepage is normal. Do not caulk or foam the tongue-and-groove joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture, and rigid fill will crack or split boards. Keep some airflow at the roof edges so moisture can escape. Trapped moisture causes mold and rot. In 30°F weather, expect a longer preheat, often 60 to 90 minutes (a rule of thumb, not a measurement). A roof with insulation helps more than sealing gaps, though the ends, door and floor still lose heat. Heater: 4-person Almost Heaven barrels are commonly listed with a 6 kW Harvia (some Watoga listings show 4.5 kW; the larger Essex lists 8 kW on a 240 V, 40 A hard-wired circuit). Check the label on your own heater and put it on a dedicated circuit; have an electrician confirm the wiring.
data.recommended-build-insulated-roof-over-th:
From the inside out:
Barrel staves (existing cedar, 1-3/8 inch). Insulation strips. Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (R-4.2 per inch, so about R-6.3), cut lengthwise into strips roughly 4 to 6 inches wide and laid along the barrel like extra staves. At that width a flat strip sits within about 1/8 inch of a 6 ft diameter curve, so the board does not need to bend. Stagger the end joints. Buy one pack first and test the fit. Furring strips running around the curve (over the top from one side to the other, like hoops), spaced about 1 foot apart. They hold the insulation down and give the roof something to fasten to. Use thin, bendable strips, or rip quarter-inch plywood into narrow strips. Underlayment (roofing felt or synthetic), which keeps the mineral wool dry. Roof surface: corrugated metal or shingles, with a drip edge at the bottom so water sheds clear. Corrugated panels need to be curved with the ribs running around the barrel; shingles follow the curve more easily. How it is fastened (this corrects the first draft, which only mentioned short screws):
Furring to staves: the screw has to pass through the furring and the insulation, so use about 3 inch screws (3/4 inch furring + 1.5 inch insulation + about 3/4 inch into a 1-3/8 inch stave). Pre-drill, and test on a spare stave or a hidden spot so the tip does not reach the sauna interior. Roof to furring: 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers that stop in the furring. The original 3/4 inch screws are Almost Heaven’s advice for fastening metal straight to the staves, not through a furring layer. Cautions:
Mineral wool loses insulating value when damp, so the underlayment and roof edges must shed water cleanly. Account for the steel hoops on the barrel. The flat strips and furring can ride over them; confirm they sit flat. Wear gloves, eye protection and a dust mask when cutting mineral wool; use a serrated blade. Unverified: I could not find a Rockwool maximum service temperature for Comfortboard 80, or a statement on sauna use. It sits on the cool, outer side of the cedar, but ask Rockwool technical service before ordering a lot of it.
data.roof-options-from-almost-heavens-guidanc: Removable canvas rain jacket. Easiest, clips on with bungees, can stay on while the sauna is running, and Almost Heaven sells one (listings show roughly $245 to $280). It is a cover and not insulation. Cheap, reversible first step. Corrugated metal roof screwed on with short (about 3/4 inch) sheet metal screws. Their staves are 1-3/8 inch thick, so short screws are safe going straight into the staves. Roofing shingles over underlayment, covering as much of the top as you like. A full shelter or structure with a roof.
data.sealing-and-airflow#Sealing and airflow:
Seal the outside against rain, and leave the inside and bottom edges able to breathe. These two goals pull in opposite directions, so each gets its own rule.
Seal the outside:
Lap the underlayment shingle-style (upper layer over lower) so water sheds. Fit drip edge or flashing at the bottom edges. Seal roof fasteners and seams, since the metal or shingles are the actual waterproofing. Tuck or tape the underlayment at the ends so wind cannot blow rain up under it. Do not seal the inside face:
Do not caulk or foam the cedar joints. The wood moves with heat and moisture and will crack the seal or split boards. Do not put a plastic vapor barrier or foil directly on the cedar. It can trap moisture in the wood and cause rot. (The first draft suggested an optional foil layer under the insulation; that contradicts this rule, so it is dropped.) Leave the bottom edges open:
Sauna heat pushes moist air through the cedar into the insulation. If every edge is sealed, that moisture condenses and soaks the mineral wool and staves, leading to mold or rot. Let the roof surface and drip edge hang about 1 inch below the end of the insulation. That leaves an open pocket under the roof edge. The drip edge still sheds rain outward. Cover the opening with insect screen or mesh so wasps and mice cannot move in. Do the same at the two end walls: overhang 1 to 2 inches, drip edge, mesh.
data.shopping-list-starter#Shopping list (sta: Rockwool Comfortboard 80, 1.5 inch (one pack to test, then more as needed) Thin furring strips or quarter-inch plywood to rip About 3 inch exterior screws for the furring (pre-drill) Roofing underlayment Corrugated metal panels or shingles, plus drip edge 1 to 1-1/4 inch roofing screws with washers, and sealant for the roof fasteners Insect mesh for the open slots Metal flashing and cap flashing for the porch back edge Porch lumber: four posts, two beams, rafters; piers or footings Dust mask, gloves and eye protection for the mineral wool Optional: heat-rated sauna fan (MMotors MM-S 100, in a voltage you can use) plus high-temperature wire

data:
Swapping the tiny 14.5 oz cylinder that ships with a threaded (screw-in) SodaStream or Drinkmate for an external 5 lb tank — same carbonation, without buying $15–20 exchange cylinders every 60 liters.
This only applies to screw-in machines. The connection depends on the TR21-4 thread — the “blue label” screw-in cylinder standard shared by classic SodaStream machines and Drinkmate. SodaStream Terra and Art use a push-in quick-connect cylinder and are not compatible with this approach — they need a different adapter, if one exists at all. Confirm your machine actually screws the cylinder in before buying anything.
data.before-you-order#Before you order: Confirmed the machine is screw-in (TR21-4), not the push-in quick-connect used on SodaStream Terra/Art Cylinder ordered/sourced: new, aluminum, CGA320, current hydro-test date, filled with beverage-grade CO2 Adapter hose ordered: CGA320 → TR21-4, with gauge and bleed valve if available Tank strap or bracket sourced and installed before the tank goes anywhere near the counter Every joint leak-tested with soapy water on first hookup
data.gas-purity#Gas purity:
An in-line filter is not the real control here, and a cheap one won’t reliably catch what actually matters: industrial and welding-grade CO2 can carry compressor oil and hydrocarbon residue that a basic filter doesn’t remove. Two things that do the real work:
Specify beverage-grade / food-grade CO2 at the fill counter, every time — not the general-purpose industrial tank. Buy a new cylinder, so you’re not inheriting rust or residue from whatever the tank held in a past life. An activated-carbon in-line gas filter from a homebrew supplier is a reasonable belt-and-suspenders addition, but largely redundant if the gas source is clean — and check its pressure rating before adding it to this unregulated, full-tank-pressure line, since most are speced for regulated low-pressure use downstream of a proper regulator.
data.parts#Parts: 5 lb aluminum CO2 cylinder, CGA320 valve. Aluminum over steel — lighter, won’t rust internally. Buy new, not refurbished, DOT-approved with a current hydro-test date (5 lb aluminum cylinders in the US are DOT-3AL, hydro-tested every 5 years; the date’s stamped on the collar and a gas supplier will check it before filling or exchanging). VEVOR and Beverage Elements both make commonly-recommended 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinders. CGA320 → TR21-4 direct adapter hose, 36–60 in, braided stainless or reinforced food-grade hose, rated well above tank pressure (most listings claim 4500–5000+ psi, which is the hose/fitting rating, not an indication you need that much pressure). Get one with a gauge and bleed valve — the bleed valve lets you depressurize the line before disconnecting, which matters (see below). Grab spare nylon washers/o-rings while you’re at it. Tank strap or wall bracket. A pressurized 5 lb cylinder becomes a genuine projectile hazard if the valve gets sheared off in a fall — secure it upright, always. Upright also isn’t optional for a different reason: these adapters pass gaseous CO2 only. A tipped tank can send liquid CO2 into the machine, which the setup isn’t built for. Tools/consumables: adjustable wrench, a spray bottle of soapy water for leak-checking every threaded joint, spare washers.
data.safety-notes#Safety notes: The cylinder is the real hazard, not the gas connection. Standing, strapped, away from heat and direct sun. A cylinder is not a countertop decoration — treat it like the pressure vessel it is. CO2 displaces oxygen. It’s heavier than air and pools low in a room. This is a real risk for any large-volume leak, not just a slow one — don’t store or operate the tank in a small closed cabinet with no airflow, and if you ever smell/hear a active leak, ventilate before troubleshooting. Bleed the line before disconnecting. The gauge/bleed-valve hose exists specifically for this — open it to vent residual line pressure before you unscrew anything, rather than cracking a pressurized fitting open by hand. Leak-test every threaded joint with soapy water after assembly — bubbles mean it’s not sealed. Don’t overtighten the TR21-4 end. The washer does the sealing, not torque. Drinkmate’s own warranty generally doesn’t cover damage from third-party CO2 sources — know that going in.
data.the-core-idea-no-regulator#The core idea:
The stock 14.5 oz cylinder feeds the machine unregulated, at something like 850 psi (CO2 tank pressure is a function of temperature, not fill level, until the tank runs dry — so a “full” 5 lb tank and an almost-empty one both sit around the same pressure at a given room temperature). The machine’s own trigger valve is what meters gas into the bottle in short bursts; it’s designed for that pressure already.
That means the standard approach is a direct adapter hose — CGA320 (the tank’s valve standard) on one end, TR21-4 (the machine’s cylinder thread) on the other — with no separate pressure regulator in between. Adding a regulator dialed down to, say, 130 psi would just give weaker carbonation than stock, not a safety improvement; the machine already expects full cylinder pressure.
data.where-to-buy#Where to buy:
Cylinder — buy local if you can. A welding or beverage-gas supplier will sell a 5 lb aluminum cylinder and fill it on the spot with beverage-grade CO2, and you skip shipping a pressure vessel entirely. If ordering online, the VEVOR 5 lb aluminum CGA320 cylinder is the commonly-recommended budget option; homebrew retailers like MoreBeer and Williams Brewing carry better-vetted tanks and are reputable for this whole category.
Adapter hose:
Product Notes Soda Helper Universal CO2 Adapter Hose (OmniFizz/Aarke Carbonator 3), 60" Low-profile hose rather than a metal-shell braided one — won’t scratch counters. Spare washers included. Soda Helper CO2 Adapter Hose & Base Kit for OmniFizz Same hose plus a machine base — tidier countertop setup. GURUDAR CO2 Direct Adapter, 60" stainless Listing explicitly names DrinkMate compatibility. Label warns gaseous CO2 only, tank upright. Tiiyee CGA320 → TR21-4 with gauge and bleed valve, 60" The gauge + bleed valve combo is worth having over a bare hose. Other reputable non-Amazon sources for the hardware in general: MoreBeer, Williams Brewing, Soda Dispenser Depot, or a local welding/gas supply shop for the tank itself.

data: Six no-alcohol drinks. The first three cover different ground — creamy/tropical, bright/citrus, ginger-forward. The second three (watermelon mojito, virgin paloma, mango chili-lime) were picked to travel: each adds just one new bottle to the cooler and reuses lime, mint, agave, and soda already on the list below, rather than needing its own dedicated shopping trip. No expertise assumed on my end either — these are straightforward builds, not bartending theory.
data.blood-orange-citrus-spritz#Blood Orange:
Bright and a little tart — blood orange juice has more depth than regular orange juice, and the color is the best-looking drink of the three if blood oranges are in season (roughly winter into early spring in most US markets; regular orange juice works fine off-season, just less dramatic).
Ingredients (1 drink):
3 oz blood orange juice (fresh-squeezed if you can get blood oranges; bottled is fine otherwise) 0.5 oz fresh lime juice 0.5 oz agave syrup or simple syrup, to taste Sparkling water, to top Ice Garnish: orange wheel or twist Method: Combine the juice, lime, and agave in a glass over ice, stir, then top with sparkling water. No shaking needed — this one’s built, not mixed.
Source: One Lovely Life — Blood Orange Mocktail.
data.coconut-colada#Coconut Colada:
Creamy and tropical — the coconut mocktail to reach for over a piña colada. Full-fat canned coconut milk gives real body; coconut water alone comes out thin.
Ingredients (1 drink):
2 oz full-fat coconut milk (canned, shaken well first) 3 oz pineapple juice 0.5 oz fresh lime juice Splash of club soda or sparkling water, to top Ice Garnish: pineapple wedge or wheel, mint sprig Method: Shake the coconut milk, pineapple juice, and lime juice hard with ice — the coconut milk wants the agitation to emulsify and get that piña-colada texture. Strain into a glass over fresh ice, top with a splash of soda, garnish.
Variation: swap the club soda for a splash of ginger beer if you want more spice against the coconut.
Source: Be Well Table — Pineapple Coconut Mocktail.
data.mango-chili-lime-beach-house-ready#Mango:
Reuses the lime, mint, and salt/Tajín already on the list — a whole mango (or bottled mango nectar, if you’d rather skip peeling and pureeing one) is the one new thing to bring.
Ingredients (1 drink):
3 oz mango puree (blended fresh from a whole mango) or mango nectar 0.5 oz fresh lime juice 3–4 mint leaves Sparkling water or club soda, to top Ice Chili-lime salt (Tajín, or your own chili/salt/sugar mix) for the rim Garnish: lime wedge, mint sprig Method: Rim the glass with lime juice and chili-lime salt, same as the paloma. Muddle or tear the mint into the glass, add lime juice and mango puree, fill with ice, top with soda, stir.
Source: Aura Bora — Mango Chili Lime Mocktail, Whole30 — Mango-Chili-Lime Mocktail.
data.packing-these-for-the-5-hour-drive-down#:
This is a drive to a beach house with its own kitchen and freezer, not a cooler-only day trip — so the plan is simpler than packing for a walk to the sand:
Ice and blending both happen on arrival, not in the car. No need to haul ice down — the house has a freezer, and the blender/muddler work is easiest done in an actual kitchen anyway. Bring whole watermelons and mangoes, not pre-juiced bottles. Whole fruit travels fine at room temperature for 5 hours and blends better fresh at the house than juice that’s been sitting since before you left — this also skips worrying about fresh watermelon/mango juice oxidizing or losing flavor over the drive, which was a real concern for pre-blending, and isn’t one for whole fruit. Bottled watermelon juice or mango nectar are still fine fallbacks if you’d rather not deal with a whole watermelon at all. Pre-mix the chili-lime salt in a small shaker or travel container (or just bring a bottle of Tajín) — no different whether you’re rimming a glass at home or at the beach house. Cans of soda/ginger beer over open bottles — they hold carbonation better over a long drive and don’t go flat if the trip is bumpy. Fresh lime, grapefruit, and blood orange juice travel fine for 5 hours if juiced ahead and kept in the car’s AC rather than a hot trunk; agave, salt, and canned coconut milk don’t need any special handling at all.
data.the-not-a-mule#The Not-a-Mule:
A Moscow mule’s whole appeal is ginger heat against lime and fizz — none of that depends on the vodka, so dropping it loses less than you’d think. This is the one worth serving in a copper mug if you own them; the cold-metal thing is real, not just presentation.
Ingredients (1 drink):
4 oz good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger, well-carbonated — the quality of the ginger beer is the whole drink here) 0.75–1 oz fresh lime juice Splash of club soda, optional, for extra fizz if the ginger beer alone isn’t lively enough Ice Garnish: lime wheel, mint sprig Method: Fill a copper mug (or any glass) most of the way with ice. Add lime juice, top with ginger beer, stir gently — stir, don’t shake, or the ginger beer goes flat. Top with a splash of club soda if you want more sparkle. Garnish and serve immediately.
Source: Yummy Mummy Kitchen — Virgin Moscow Mule, Whisk Affair — Virgin Moscow Mule.
data.tools-and-stock-worth-having-on-hand#Too: Cocktail shaker (or any lidded jar/container that seals — a mason jar works) Jigger or a set of measuring shot glasses (1 oz / 2 oz) Citrus juicer or reamer — fresh juice matters a lot more than bottled here, especially for lime Muddler (the back of a wooden spoon works in a pinch) — for mint Fine strainer, if shaking anything with pulp or muddled mint Copper mugs, if leaning into the mule presentation — not required, just traditional Full-fat coconut milk (canned, not the carton beverage) and coconut water are different ingredients below — don’t swap one for the other A bottle of good non-alcoholic ginger beer (strong ginger bite, well-carbonated) and a bottle of club soda or seltzer Agave syrup (or 1:1 agave-and-water simple syrup) — shared by the citrus spritz, the paloma, and the mango chili-lime below Coarse salt or Tajín, for rimming glasses — one small shaker covers the paloma and the mango chili-lime
data.virgin-paloma-beach-house-ready#Virgin P:
Same lime juice and agave as the Blood Orange Citrus Spritz, same sparkling water as everything else on this page — the only new bottle is grapefruit juice.
Ingredients (1 drink):
3 oz grapefruit juice (fresh-squeezed if you’re juicing at home the night before; bottled is fine) 0.5 oz fresh lime juice 0.5 oz agave syrup, to taste Sparkling water, to top Ice Salt (or Tajín) for the rim Garnish: lime or grapefruit wedge Method: Rim a glass with lime juice and dip in salt or Tajín, combine grapefruit juice, lime juice, and agave over ice, top with sparkling water, stir.
Source: Sweets & Thank You — Virgin Paloma, Mingle Mocktails — Paloma Mocktail.
data.watermelon-mojito-beach-house-ready#Wate:
Reuses the lime and mint already on the list, plus club soda you’re already packing for the Not-a-Mule. The only new item is a whole watermelon — bring the fruit itself and blend at the house, rather than pre-juicing for the drive.
Ingredients (1 drink):
3 oz watermelon juice (blended fresh from the whole fruit and strained, or bottled if you’d rather skip the blender entirely) 0.5 oz fresh lime juice 4–5 mint leaves Club soda or sparkling water, to top Ice Garnish: mint sprig, watermelon wedge Method: At the house — cube the watermelon, blend, strain out the pulp if you want a cleaner drink. Muddle the mint gently in the bottom of a glass, add lime juice and watermelon juice, fill with ice, top with soda, stir once.
Source: The Merry Thought — Watermelon Mojito Mocktail, The Real Food Dietitians — Watermelon Mojito.

data.binding-cord#Binding Cord: The last part of constructing the binder is the components for holding the binding cord, its guide path, and a tensioning device. The binding cord usually comes on a spool or bobbin depending on the rodmaker’s source. I have the large industrial spool. The trick here is to let the cord come off the spool with no drag. I previously let the spool turn as I pulled the cord off. After a lot of use, the spool did not turn easily and caused drag. This increased tension on the cord and would cause the rod to twist. I solved this problem by using a 1/8 brass rod with a loop in the end that is long enough to allow the cord to freely come off the spool upwards. The rod also serves as shock absorber (like the tip of your fly rod with a delicate tippet) even if the cord drags a bit it does not cause excess tension. The cord then flows through the guides and tensioner to the last guide that allows the cord to come from behind into the drive belt and rod at approximately 45 degree angle. You do not want the cord to come directly down to where it is being bound. It must come from the same direction the rod that is being bound.
data.drive-belt#Drive Belt: How to make a knotless drive belt is easy. I use braided chalk and mason line for my drive belt. It can be found in most hardware stores. Do not choose twisted line for this purpose. To make a make the knotless drive belt you will need a large sewing needle whose eye is big enough for the line. Once you cut the line to approximate length, thread the line through the eye of the needle for about 2 - 3 inches. Because the line is braided, you can take the needle and stick it into the hollow core or the other end of the line for about 1 and 1/2 inches and then out through the line. You can now remove the needle and pull the line back until the end just goes back into the line. I now take a regular needle and thread and make a few stitches to hold the line in place with a few extras where it comes out to keep the braid from unraveling. The is just like a snake eating itself. No glue or knots are needed and you will never know when the spliced area goes around the rod. The splice is very flexible and never binds. Making this knotless belt takes very little time and requires very little effort or skill.
data.drive-wheels#Drive Wheels:
Word about drive wheels. Most wheels are too shallow and the drive belt easily jumps out of it. This is also true concerning the pulley that holds the weight. I have switched from a small one to a larger one that has a good deep wheel. I found a ready source for these at my local hardware store. I disassemble two wheeled pulleys for my guide wheels. These wheels have a standard 5/16 ID holes that fits the bolts I use as an axle.
Now for the placement of the first guide whose position is very important and its misplacement will cause problems. It should be positioned so the drive belt does not drag on the cradle. This means the angle of the drive belt to it should not be equal or greater than 180 degrees. It should be approximately 170 degrees or less, or if you prefer a clock reference, about 25 minutes pass the hour. On most diagrams of binders this point is not clear. I feel that when diagrams of the binder where made the graphic artist did not appreciate this fact and aligned the wheels to make it look neat. Wrong, this neatness has caused many problems. On my binder the angle is the maximum it could be (29 minutes pass the hour) without causing problems (dumb luck). I have seen other rodmakers who have bought binders that where made with this wheel too far left and it causes drag. This drag is one cause of problems that can cause twists in the rod. I know of one modification that uses a rod to push the belt out away from the cradle that some rodmakers use to try and correct this problem. Easiest way to remedy the problem is to move the wheel to the right.
Now for the good news, the placement of the other wheels and drive wheel are not critical. They just guide the belt. On the left side of the cradle the cord usually doesn’t drag and most rodmakers don’t have it close to the cradle.
data.feed-supports#Feed Supports: The in-feed and out-feed supports can be aligned using a wooden dowel. The out feed supports have troughs that are of a larger diameter (1 and 3/4 inches). The centers of the bottom of the support troughs need to be the same distance from the binder as the cradle trough is. On the parallel plane to the binder face centered on our reference point all guide wheels and the drive wheel.
data.tension#Tension:
You now need to tension the binding cord. You now need to tension the binding cord. The binding cord does not apply any clamping pressure to the rod. It just holds the pressure that has been applied by thedrive belt. It wraps the rod maintaining the pressure. Too much tension on the drive cord will cause a twist. Normally this will happen on the first pass and cannot be corrected on the second. What happens is the excess tension starts to pull the rod segments and this causes them to rotate them. The tension should be adjusted to allow a firm even pull on the binding cord. A good way to check to see if there is too much tension is to tie a loop in the cord and hang the weight on it. If the binding cord holds the weight, then there is too much tension. The weight should pull the binding cord easily. I know other rodmakers that use a small spring scale to measure and adjust the tension so weight and tension are even. I believe that tension should be slightly less than the weight.
With a properly tuned and adjusted Garrison binder you achieve excellent results. The only problem I have had is when the binding cord has had too much tension on it. That problem is now solved. I now have now had numerous rods that come out of gluing straight and true, requiring little or no straightening. Understanding your Garrison binder and making some subtle changes can allow you to get maximum performance out of it.
data.the-cradle#The Cradle: The cradle is the starting point from which to build the rest of the binder. Everything else is aligned relative to the cradle. The point from which all this alignment is done is the bottom of the trough (half circle) that holds the rod. The size of the trough is not important. I find a larger diameter (approximately 1" or larger) trough is easier to use than a small one (5/8"). Too small and it constrains the rod on larger sections. The space left between the two sections determines the spacing of wraps of the binding cord. This space is usually just wide enough (3/16 - 1/4") so the drive belt fits but doesn’t constrain it. This distance needs to be adjusted until you get a good working distance. This is why there are slots so it can be adjusted by sliding the cradle back and forth. I recommend only adjusting the left side since all other alignments and positioning is done from the right side. Once the cradle is in place, then all other parts of the binder will be aligned to it referenced to the trough bottom of the forward side of the cradle. This is where the drive belt comes out.
data.unlocking-the-mysteries-of-the-garrison-:
I’ve copied this content from http://www.canerod.com/rodmakers/tips/binder.html (Wayback Machine). I’ve reformatted it for reading and placed the images in-line after each paragraph.
Unlocking the Mysteries of the Garrison Binderby Chris Bogart
Hiding this ramble. Did you ever wonder why (to quote Andy Rooney) the Garrison binder is for many rodmakers the source of contentious problems while other rodmakers never seem to have problems. One of the primary reasons for the mystery the Garrison binder presents is that rodmakers often built it by following a diagram in a book and then hoped for the best. As a result, some binders worked as desired because of dumb luck and others didn’t because of bad luck. When the binder did not behave and was cantankerous to use, it was assumed that it worked that way for the master himself. I have since learned that when properly constructed and adjusted (tuned) the Garrison binder is a pleasure to operate and does a great job with little problems.
This article will discuss the how and why of constructing the Garrison binder and then how to tune it to perform at it’s best. Like most people, I first blindly followed a diagram in a book and did some things right and did some things wrong. It was initially hard for me to tell what was important and critical to its operation and what wasn’t. I have since looked at numerous other rodmakers’ binders and discussed their operation and their solutions to traditional problems. I have applied the lessons learned to my binder with great success. I have come to the following conclusions on how the Garrison binder should be constructed and why.
The Garrison binder is essentially an incredibly simple but clever device. What makes it mysterious is that there are very subtle things that are sometimes not obvious that have impact upon performance. The heart of the binder is the cradle that holds the rod, the drive belt that wraps around the rod applying pressure and the string that binds the segments together. It is here where we will analyze the binder.
data.weight#Weight: Now for the last part of tuning your binder, adjusting weights and tension. First, adjust the weight you have on the pulley that rides on the drive belt. This is the mechanism for applying pressure to the glued up rod. More weight is not necessarily better. I feel that the weight should be a little as necessary to give satisfactory results. I use a coffee jar that has old nuts and bolts in it as a weight . I can add and subtract weight easily. The first sign of excess weight is the rod will drag on the cradle. Look carefully at the rod to see if you have rounded or chipped the corners of the rod. Look also at the bottom of the cradle. I used a soft metal (Aluminum) for my binder and the bamboo will actually shave off metal if there is too much weight. So play with the weight so that you are not destroying your rod or binder. I have found that about 1 - 1.5 pounds is more than enough. This weight is based upon the glue (epoxy) I use. You may want to have one weight for butts and one for tips depending on the type of rods you build. I use the same weight for both and have had no ill effects.

data:
A Garrison-style rod binder built almost entirely from 3D-printed parts. The architecture follows E. Garrison’s original — vertical face board, cradle on the top edge with a belt gap, guide wheels and drive wheel on the face, a weight riding the belt’s slack loop, and a disc-drag cord tensioner — as documented in detail on the Garrison Binder page. Read that page first; all of its tuning guidance applies directly to this build.
Every wheel runs on two 608 skateboard bearings. All bolt holes, counterbores, captive-nut pockets, and adjustment slots are printed in place — the only drilling in this project is a handful of holes in the wooden face board.
data.1-feet-and-board#1. Feet and board: Screw the two board feet to the mounting plank ~400 mm apart, slots aligned, then clamp the plank to the bench so the board’s front face overhangs the bench edge by at least 25 mm. The belt plane runs 12 mm in front of the board face and the weight loop hangs below the board — both need clear air in front of the bench edge along the whole loop span. Drop the board into the slots and drive the pinch screws.
data.2-wheels#2. Wheels:
Press two 608 bearings into each wheel with a vise or thumb pressure. Drop a printed spacer between them (it clamps between the inner races so the nyloc can be fully torqued without binding the wheel).
Axle stack, inside to out: bolt head → washer → board → washer → bearing/wheel/bearing → washer → nyloc. Torque the nut fully — the spacer takes the clamp load and the wheel spins free.
Fasten the crank arm to the drive wheel face with two M4 × 25 screws — they self-tap into the printed pilot holes (any two opposite pilots) and stop inside the wheel, so nothing protrudes from the back face spinning next to the board. Then bolt the grip to the arm end with the M5 — nyloc snug but the grip must spin.
data.3-cradle#3. Cradle:
Drop the two cradle blocks over the board’s top edge, one each side of the belt-gap position. Each clamps with an M5 bolt through the printed slot — the hex nut sits captive in the track on the back face. The slots give ±4.5 mm of slide per block: start with a 6 mm gap between the blocks (within the article’s 3/16–1/4" range, with a little margin around the 4.8 mm belt) and close it down later only if the cord-wrap spacing demands it. The gap-facing bottom edges of each trough slab carry printed 45° relief chamfers so the departing belt clears the blocks.
The trough axis sits 12 mm in front of the board face — the same plane as the wheel grooves. This is by design; don’t shim it.
data.4-drive-belt#4. Drive belt:
Make a knotless loop from the mason line (this is the same splice described in the Garrison Binder article):
Thread one end 50 mm into the eye of a large needle. Push the needle into the hollow braided core of the other end, run it 40 mm inside, and out. Pull the tail through until the free end disappears into the splice; stitch across it twice. Route: around the rod one full turn at the cradle gap → down to guide 1 → guide 2 → across the slack loop (weight hanger + pulley riding in it) → up over the drive wheel → guide 3 → vertically back up into the gap to the rod. Splice the loop to length in place so the weight hangs with ~150 mm of travel.
data.5-cord-path#5. Cord path:
Screw the spool brackets to the face at the left end (~60 mm apart); the spool rides on the M8 axle resting in the open slots. Screw eye 1 to the face at ~130 mm from the left edge with its flange top flush with the board’s top edge (eye at rod height, guiding the spool run). Screw eye 2 at ~225 mm with its flange top ~30 mm below the edge — from there the cord rises to the bind point at roughly 50°. The tensioner goes between them at (170, 50): cord runs spool → eye 1 → down between the tensioner discs → eye 2 → up onto the rod.
Per the article, the cord must approach the rod from the in-feed side, rising at a steep angle — never straight down, and never from the out-feed side. Eye 2 sitting low and left of the cradle delivers this.
Tensioner stack on the M5 bolt: captive head in base → base → disc → cord → disc → spring → knob (captive nut, pocket facing the spring). The knob compresses the spring for fine, stable drag.
data.6-feed-supports#6. Feed supports: Cut two 1" dowels to length: measure H = bench top to the bottom of the cradle trough, then cut dowels to H − 24 mm. Push into base and head sockets, drive the pinch screws. The big 1¾" troughs end up level with the cradle trough bottom — exactly the alignment the article calls for. The base flanges have screw holes; leave them unscrewed if you want to reposition the stands between butt and tip sections.

data.tuning#Tuning:
All of the Garrison Binder tuning advice applies. The short version:
Weight: start at ~450 g (1 lb). More is not better — if the rod drags in the cradle or the corners chip, remove weight. Cord tension: must be less than the belt weight. Test per the article — tie a loop in the cord and hang the weight on it; the weight should pull cord off the spool easily. Too much cord tension twists the rod on the first pass. Spool take-off drag: cord pulling the spool round adds hidden tension upstream of the tensioner, and it grows as the spool empties — the exact problem the article describes. Its fix works here too: bend the 1/8" brass rod into a loop rising above the spool and take the cord off over the end through it; the springy rod also absorbs tension spikes. Belt clearance: if the belt rubs a cradle block, widen the gap slightly or nudge guide 1 further from the cradle — the belt leaving the rod should angle away, never scrape. With guide 1 at the drilling-plan position the belt departs at ~168° of wrap, inside the article’s ≤170° rule, and the cradle chamfers give it clear air. Bind twice, once in each direction, per standard Garrison practice.

data:
A hypothetical rod binder that inverts the Garrison principle: instead of a belt spinning the rod while the cord stands still, the rod never rotates — the cord spool orbits around it, the way a cable-serving machine or coil winder lays wire. This page is a design study: the parts are fully engineered and printable, but the machine has not been built yet. Read it alongside the Garrison Binder article and the printed Garrison binder build, which this design deliberately argues with.
This concept won a three-way design comparison against a counter-rotating twin-cord binder (fatal flaw: the wrap zone between the rotors can’t be hand-steadied, and its twist cancellation silently drifts as the friction drags wear) and a rotisserie chuck-and-leadscrew machine (fatal flaw: driving a wet 2 mm tip section from one end winds radians of torsion into it — the exact defect a binder exists to prevent).
data.design-notes#Design notes: Why a closed ring? Cable-serving machines use split rings because cables are endless. Rod sections are finite sticks — they thread through the bore end-first, so the ring can stay closed, keeping the gear teeth and V-race continuous. That continuity is what makes both features printable and smooth. Why V-in-V? The 90° ridge running in 90° grooved rollers constrains the ring radially and axially with four small contact patches — no thrust bearing needed, and roller preload is set by one slotted axle. Two drives, honestly: a 26T pinion cannot speed-multiply a 78T ring — the gear train is a 3:1 reduction, useful only as a fine drive. Production binding runs on the direct spinner knob at 1:1. (An earlier draft of this concept claimed “one crank = three wraps”; that’s the ratio backwards.) Gearing: module 2, 20° pressure angle, 78:26, tooth gaps traced on the true root circle. Each gear is thinned 0.125 mm for a designed 0.25 mm total FDM backlash; the generated profiles measure 0.252 mm working backlash and roll through mesh with zero interference at the 104 mm centre distance. Grease the mesh and run it in for a minute before first use. Roller preload: the two top roller axles sit in radial slots. Inward travel is deliberately limited to 0.75 mm — enough to take up all print tolerance in the V-race, not enough to push the standoff tubes into the orbiting gear teeth (verified: zero interference even at full preload). Balance: the spool + tensioner cluster is offset on the ring face; the counterweight cup sits diametrically opposite, filled with steel nuts until the ring has no preferred rest position. Spring drag means tension doesn’t care about orientation — balance is purely about smooth cranking. Helix-hand kinematics (the subtle one): helix hand flips when either the orbit direction or the feed direction reverses — but not both. Feeding the rod back through while cranking the same direction lays the opposite-hand helix for pass 2 with zero re-rigging. Reversing both (the intuitive move) lays the same hand again. The fairlead eye is the one surface the cord saws across under full drag. The printed eye has chamfered edges, but layer lines are layer lines: wax it, flame-polish it, or press a wire/ceramic eyelet in before binding real work.

r o d i n [ V s u [ [ p s V V = p t - - = o a r r = r n o = t c l l = ] h l l = i e e = o r ( - 1 r = n ] Ø : ] = o 9 r [ 1 b = p r r 0 o k o = l b i d n d a = a i n b o r r = t t g o - b i d = e r ] v = e e = ) = v [ [ = e V V = r - - = t r r = i o g o = [ c l [ e l = V a l p a l = l e i r e = s ) r n r = u ] i m ] p o e p n s o ] h r - t - r ] o d o u f t i n ( e 3 : c 1 r a d n o k w n ) The rod section rests in two height-adjustable V supports, passing through the ring’s Ø90 bore without touching it. The ring rides on four V-grooved rollers that engage a 90°-included V-ridge on its rim — the V-in-V contact locates the ring both radially and axially.
The ring has two drive inputs:
Primary — the spinner knob bolted to the ring face: whirl the ring directly, like spinning a valve wheel. One revolution = one wrap; a comfortable 2–3 rev/s covers a 1.3 m section in about 90–130 seconds. Fine — the geared pinion crank: a 26-tooth pinion meshing with the ring’s 78-tooth gear gives a 3:1 reduction — three crank turns per wrap. Too slow for whole sections, exactly right for creeping along a fragile 2 mm tip at low tension with full control. The spool, a disc-drag tensioner, a guide pin, and a fairlead eye all bolt to the ring’s front face and orbit with it. As you drive the ring with one hand and draw the rod through the bore with the other, the fairlead lays binding cord onto the stationary rod in a helix. Wrap pitch = feed speed ÷ wrap rate, exactly the same hand-controlled pitch as a Garrison binder.
data.open-questions-why-this-is-still-hypothe: Does cord tension alone consolidate imperfect butt strips without the belt’s kneading action? If not, the fix is a sprung follower roller — added complexity. Will printed gear mesh and race seams produce visible wrap-spacing bands? Mitigations: seam randomization, sanding, grease, run-in. Fallback: a TPU friction-ring drive in place of the gear mesh. PETG creep in the bearing pockets over months — same known issue and same reprint fix as the Garrison build.

data.pros-and-cons-vs-the-garrison-binder#Pro:
Pros
No rod rotation → no rotation-induced twist. The failure mode the Garrison article spends most of its words tuning away doesn’t exist here. No drive belt. The knotless splice, the ≤170° first-guide rule, belt drag on the cradle, and epoxy-crusted belts all disappear. Only the cord and two V-grooves touch wet glue. One tension, not two coupled ones. Garrison tuning balances belt weight against cord drag. Here a single spring-set drag does everything — and spring (not gravity) drag means tension is identical at every ring orientation. Repeatable presets. TIP/BUTT marks on the knob, instead of re-tuning a weight jar between sections. Instant opposite-hand second pass. No re-rigging — see the operating notes. Self-contained cord path. Spool → guide → tensioner → fairlead spans ~100 mm, all orbiting together. No bench-mounted spool alignment, no long cord spans to snag. Compact: ~600 mm of bench, the same ten-bearing budget as the printed Garrison build. Cons
No belt pre-consolidation. Garrison’s weighted belt kneads the strips together before the cord locks them; here cord tension alone must seat the strips. Butts may need the high preset plus a firm hand-squeeze just ahead of the wrap point. Closed ring = end-first threading. You can’t drop a section in mid-length or rescue one sideways mid-bind. A rotating assembly must be balanced. The counterweight cup is a genuine setup step; Garrison has no such requirement. Rod centring matters. More than ~2–3 mm off the ring axis and the cord payout length fluctuates once per orbit, rippling the tension. Hence the adjustable supports and the centring gauge. Garrison is completely insensitive to this. The Ø160 ring is a demanding print. Gear-tooth quality and race runout are at the mercy of printer calibration; Garrison’s plain wheels are forgiving. Small onboard spool (~15 m) must be rewound from the bulk spool. Speed cap ~3 wraps/s — beyond that the orbiting cord balloons. A Garrison binder cranks as fast as you dare.

data.setup-and-operation#Setup and operation: Mount: screw the plate feet and the two support bases to the board, supports ~200 mm each side of the plate. Rollers: bearings + spacer into each roller; bolt through plate + standoff. The two top axles sit in radial slots — snug them so the ring turns freely with no rattle. Centre the rod line: drop the centring gauge into the ring bore, slide a scrap strip into the matching hex step, and spin the support heads up their columns until the strip sits centred; lock the jam nuts. Balance: bolt on the furniture (including the drive knob), then add nuts to the counterweight cup until the ring has no preferred rest position. Calibrate: pull cord through the fairlead against a spring scale; mark TIP and BUTT knob positions. Bind, pass 1: thread the glued section tip-first through the bore, anchor the cord tail under three hand wraps, then spin the ring by its knob at ≤2–3 rev/s (= 2–3 wraps/s) while drawing the section through at ~10–15 mm/s for a ~5 mm pitch. Switch to the pinion crank (3 turns per wrap) for slow, precise work near the tip. Tie off: two half-hitches. Pass 2: drive the ring the same direction and feed the section back through — that flips the helix hand (reversing both flips nothing). Tie off, sight straight, hang to cure.
data.the-physics#The physics:
Binding pressure comes purely from cord tension. Hoop pressure on the glue-up is roughly T / (R × pitch) — tension divided by rod radius times wrap spacing. That relationship is kind to tips: a 2 mm tip at 150 g and a tight 3.5 mm pitch sees more consolidation pressure (~430 kPa) than a 10 mm butt at 500 g and 5 mm pitch (~200 kPa). So the tensioner needs only two marked presets — TIP (~150–200 g) and BUTT (~450–550 g) — calibrated once with a spring scale.
The only torque the section ever feels is cord tension × rod radius, about 2–27 N·mm across the tension and diameter range — resisted trivially by the feeding hand. Garrison’s primary twist mechanism (belt tension torquing the strips against cord drag) is eliminated by construction.

data.pulleys-for-belt-drive#Pulleys for Belt:
I have a couple of questions regarding building a binder. I’ve located some pulleys at the hardware store with ~ 1/4" channel in them, is this too wide or doesn’t it matter? What should I use for a belt? (Mark Pohl)
You can use either a round leather, or round urethane drive belt. The 1/4" wide groove shouldn’t be a problem, and you can get the belting in 1/4", too. (Martin-Darrell)
I used something similar, rollers from a patio door - got them at Lowes, brass with bushings about 1/4 inch groove. I built my binder ALA Garrison design, but have modified it per a suggestion on the list. Make a second main drive pulley and stack them together. Wind one pulley full of 50# braided nylon masons twine - I anchored the twine by drilling a small hole for a screw, sticking the end of the drive belt/string in the hole and screwing the screw in. Do the same think with the end of the belt on the empty drive pulley. Crank the pulleys backwards to rewind all of the belt onto the other pulley. Thread the belt through your pulleys and around a 1/4 test dowel, hang your weight on the belt and away you go. The benefit is NO slipping of the belt, and NO bump as the splice or knot in the belt traverses the rod. I use Polyurethane glue and run the belt back and forth through a cloth dampened with paint thinner after glue up. Use the appropriate solvent for your glue for cleanup. (Kurt Clement)

data:
A two-piece split-cane spinning rod for winter fishing on the French Broad around Hap Simpson Park in Brevard, late November through December. The joint is a spliced (scarf) joint, with a ferrule as the fallback, and both sections are milled on the standard Morgan Hand Mill bed. This is my first spinning rod, so the page also covers the spinning basics a fly-rod builder doesn’t already know: power classes, the reel seat, guides, the reel, and lures.
The spec in one line: 6'6", two piece (splice or 12/64 ferrule), hex, light power / moderate-fast action, 4–6 lb line, lures 1/16–1/4 oz (designed around 1/8 oz), sliding-ring cork grip, a 1000-size reel.
Status: design only. The taper below hasn’t been cut yet. It’s been checked against the library’s spinning rods in caneDNA (see Taper). A review on 2026-11-02 found the lower third runs stiffer than the reference rods; a trimmed variant E is proposed but not adopted.
