data.build-checklist#Build checklist: Check the taper: done in caneDNA for variant D (see Taper). Decide D vs. E before cutting (variant E); the butt-section mill table differs. Split culms into 5–6’ sections as in the class build. Stagger nodes 3×3, and keep them out of the 36–42" splice zone. Rough → heat-treat → finish each section on the standard bed. Mill the tip to 44" and the butt from 34" so both joints stay possible. Dry bind, then glue both sections. Choose the joint: cut and whip the 4.5" scarf bevels (36.75–41.25"), or trim square at 39" and fit a 12/64 ferrule. Shape the 12" cork; fit the reel foot and rings at about 8.5" from the butt. Tape the guides and do the static load test, then a casting test. Then wrap and finish. Buy the reel and line, then build the tackle box above. Before the first trip, confirm the Hap Simpson reach’s designation, the NCWRC stocking schedule, and USGS flows.
data.canedna-results#caneDNA results:
caneDNA uses RodDNA’s casting-load model. (The lure-stress and recovery numbers below carry the caveats listed after the table.) I compared this taper against the 16 bamboo spinning rods in its library, including “Spin Rod 6’ 1 pc.”, which is essentially Tyree’s 6’. For the lures, each lure was modeled as a weight at the tip with a 4× impact factor. Stress is averaged from 10" to the grip; lower stress means a stiffer rod.
Taper Stress @ 1/16 oz @ 1/8 oz @ 1/4 oz Recovery (RodDNA load) First draft (straight Tyree scale-up) 54k 67k 92k 1.87 Hz Variant D (this taper) 51k 63k 87k 2.00 Hz (75" taper) Tyree 6’ 1pc (reference) 52k 65k 91k 2.42 Hz (60" taper; not like for like) Stress level: per lure weight, the rod loads like Tyree’s proven 6’. It sits between the ultralight T&T (higher stress) and the 6–10 lb 7' spinners (lower), which fits the light rating. Recovery: the first draft was the slowest-recovering rod of any 6’+ spinner in the library. Correction (2026-11-02): the 2.42 Hz and 2.00 Hz above are not like for like. The engine integrates over the stored taper length, which is 60" for the Tyree record and 75" for D, so scaling 2.42 Hz to 78" (about 2.06) doesn’t validate D. Over the same 60" cantilever, D is 2.55 Hz against Tyree’s 2.42 (about 5% faster), and 18–19% faster than Holder’s 6’ ultralight (2.16) and Young’s Spinmaster (2.14). D matches Tyree through the top 40" but is roughly 3–16% thicker than the references from 55" to 65" (depending on which rod). See variant E. Shape: stress rises toward the butt with light lures, because the cane’s own weight dominates. It flattens at 1/4 oz. Ferrule: a ~0.2 oz 12/64 ferrule at 39" raises butt stress 6–10% between 45" and 60". That’s within the variation from one culm to the next, so the taper doesn’t change. With RodDNA’s own heavier default ferrule weight (0.53 oz) it’s about +30%. Caveats: the frequencies assume a cane stiffness (E) of 2.4 million psi, so compare them between rods rather than as absolutes. The lure-stress table above comes from a lure-at-the-tip load model that isn’t in the caneDNA repo (its stress_curve is RodDNA’s fly-line model), so those figures couldn’t be reproduced in the 2026-11-02 review; treat them as approximate. This isn’t Hexrod; Hexrod only models fly lines.

data.graphite-alternative-a-mud-hole-build#Gr: This is the same rod in graphite, built from Mud Hole parts: a weekend build that fishes this winter while the cane rod is still in the binder. Everything else on this page (reel, line, tackle, how to fish it) carries over unchanged.
data.graphite-build-order#Graphite build orde: Measure the blank’s spine and mark it; the guides go on the spine’s compression side. Ream and dry-fit the rear grip, the VSS seat on its arbor, and the foregrip. Glue them butt-first, seat aligned with the guide side. Fit the tip-top. Tape all guides on per the starting layout. Mount the reel, then do the static load test and cast test. Adjust. Wrap, finish, and cure. A graphite blank needs no varnish, just the guide wraps.
data.guides-and-tiptop#Guides and tiptop:
Line comes off a spinning spool in big coils, so the first guide (the stripper) is large and sits high. The rest step down to choke the coils into a straight line. Use light single-foot guides to keep weight off the cane tip. A rule of thumb from the bamboorodmaking page is one guide per foot of rod, plus one.
Position (from tip) Ring size Notes 0" 6 mm ring, 6/64 tube across-corners at the tip ≈ 0.092", so 6/64 (0.094") only just fits; see the tiptop note under the spec table 5" 6 mm 11" 6 mm 18" 7 mm 26" 8 mm 35" 10 mm just tip-side of the splice (36.75–41.25"), so it doubles as an alignment mark 47" 16 mm, high frame stripper, about 22" ahead of the reel foot; butt-side alignment mark These are starting positions. Tape the guides on, mount the reel, and run the line through. Then do a static load test: tie the line off and bend the rod to about 90°, then move guides until the line follows the blank’s curve without touching it. Then cast with tape before wrapping. Wrap with fine thread, same as a fly rod; spinning guides don’t need special wrapping.
data.guides-fuji-kl-h-169h-kit-kr-style#Guide:
Mud Hole’s Fuji KL-H 169H kit is Fuji’s small-reel spinning train (“spinning up to 7'6"”), with Alconite rings on stainless frames. It’s a modern KR-style train: a small, high stripper close to the reel and an early choke guide that straightens the line, followed by a row of small identical runners. That’s lighter and casts farther than the old big-stripper layout. The 4.5 runners match the blank’s 4.5 tip.
Starting layout (inches from the tiptop; reel-foot center ≈ 68" from the tip):
# Guide Ring From tip Gap to next (toward butt) tip Fuji LG micro spinning top, Alconite 4.5 ring / 4.5 tube 0 3.5" 1 KT runner 4.5 3.5" 4.0" 2 KT runner 4.5 7.5" 4.5" 3 KT runner 4.5 12" 5.0" 4 KT runner 4.5 17" 5.5" 5 KT runner 4.5 22.5" 6.0" 6 KB (transition) 4.5 28.5" 6.5" 7 KL 5.5M (choke) 5.5 35" 6.5" 8 KL 8H (reduction) 8 41.5" 6.5" 9 KL 16H (stripper) 16 48" ~20" to the reel foot This is a starting point, not Fuji’s computed layout. Fuji’s 2009 “New Concept” chart for a 6'6" spinning rod puts a bigger stripper at about 45" from the tip with seven guides. This KR kit uses a smaller stripper and nine guides, so the spacing above is my adaptation. Before wrapping:
Tape everything on. Run Fuji’s KR guide placement software (linked from Mud Hole’s KL and KT pages) with a 1000 reel and 6 lb mono. Do a static load test (bend to ~90°, line shouldn’t touch the blank). Do a cast test, watching the line cone: it should be choked to straight by guide 7. On the S782-2, keep guide 8 off the ferrule. Mud Hole doesn’t publish the ferrule location. If a guide lands within ~1" of the female ferrule, slide it.
data.handle-and-reel-seat#Handle and reel sea: The big difference from a fly rod is that the reel sits partway up the handle, not at the butt, and it hangs below the rod on a stem. Your casting hand wraps the seat with the reel stem between two fingers. The rear grip runs back along your forearm, and your index finger reaches the spool to feather the line. There’s no line hand: the reel does all the line handling.

data.morgan-hand-mill-settings#Morgan Hand Mi:
Check the form angle. These settings use the strip height as half the flat-to-flat dimension (a 60° hex). The Hand Mill’s 6-strip cutter is 61.5°, and Bob Clay’s course taper says to deduct about 2.3% from 60° dimensions when milling on it. caneDNA flags this as a possible refinement, and Rod 001 uses the same convention. Decide deliberately before cutting; at the tip it is about 0.002".
The two tables below are variant D; for variant E use the tip section below with the variant E butt table.
Oversize columns follow the class sheet: rough +0.070, Hand Mill +0.030, finish +0.003 (all per strip, i.e. added to the half dimension). The MHM Setting is the bed rise from the thickest station in each section, the same convention and station layout as Rod 001. Each section’s thin end sits at #12 with the extension at #13. The largest change between adjacent stations is 0.008", well under the bed’s 0.020" limit. caneDNA estimates hold-down hole E for the tip and hole D for the butt.
Tip section, variants D and E (shared): −5 to 45 in (finished 0–39"; long to 44" for the splice)

data.option-a-recommended-full-cork-with-slid:
The classic bamboo spinning handle (T&T, Paul Young, and the Montague-derived 6’ on bamboorodmaking all use it). It’s just a fly-rod cork grip with no seat hardware. The reel foot sits on the cork and two metal rings slide over its ends.
t i b p l a n k w 6 i c 6 n h ″ d e i c f n k r g o m t c i o p r k ~ 3 . 5 ″ r i n g r e e r l e e 1 f l 2 r o ″ e o e t c l s o - t r f e k o m o r t i n c g e ~ n 8 t . e 5 r ″ c o r k c a 7 p 8 b ″ u t b t u t t 12" Portuguese cork (78" − 12" = cork starts at 66"). Shape it as one long cigar or a straight full-wells with a slight swell under the reel. Rings: 2 nickel-silver or aluminum sliding rings sized to the cork’s diameter at the reel position, about 7/8–1". Lap the reel foot on the cork first; the rings should press it down snugly, not just touch. Reel position: about 8.5" from the butt end to the center of the reel foot, then fine-tune by balance and forearm length. Hold it the way you’d fish it: the butt end should just reach the inside of your forearm. Tradeoff: the lightest, cleanest, and most period-correct option, but rings can creep when it’s cold and wet. The fix is a strip of electrical tape under the foot or a slight taper in the cork so the rings jam.
data.option-b-skeleton-seat-modern-locks-soli:
A graphite skeleton seat (Fuji and ALPS make spinning versions in 16–18 mm) with split fore and rear grips. It’s mounted on a built-up arbor over the hex (masking tape or cork rings shaped round, epoxied).

data.power-class-ultralight-vs-light#Power cl:
Spinning rods are rated by power (how much force it takes to bend the rod; roughly, the line and lure weights it handles) and action (where it bends: fast = mostly the tip, moderate = into the middle). This is the spinning equivalent of a fly rod’s line weight.
Class Line Lures Good for Here Ultralight (UL) 2–4 lb 1/32–1/8 oz small creeks, small fish, short casts Fits the East Fork and creeks. Underpowered for the mainstem’s width, current, and the odd big brown or smallmouth. Light (L) 4–6 lb 1/16–1/4 oz small rivers, stocked trout, bass Pick this. It casts across the mainstem pools, handles a 1/4 oz spoon or jerkbait, and is still fun on a 10" stocker. Medium-light (ML) 6–8 lb 1/8–3/8 oz bigger rivers, bass-first fishing Overgunned for winter’s small, slow lures. Light wins because this rod has to cover both the wide, slow mainstem and the small DH runs, and winter lures are small (1/16–1/8 oz) but sometimes need distance. A bamboo light rod still casts 1/16 oz well, because a cane rod’s own mass helps load it. Thomas & Thomas labeled their classic 5'6" spinner “ultralight,” and a builder who measured one rated it light-to-ultralight in the hand. That’s the feel I’m after here.
data.reel#Reel:
You want a 1000-size spinning reel (Shimano 1000 / Daiwa LT 1000–2000) that’s light (≈5.5–6.5 oz) and holds ~100+ yd of 4–6 lb mono. A heavier reel will make a 6'6" cane rod feel butt-heavy.
Modern pick: Shimano Stradic FM 1000HG (SKU ST1000HGFM): ~185 g / 6.5 oz, 6.0:1 gear, 3 kg drag. It’s the trout standard: smooth, durable, and easy to get serviced. FM is the current generation (the earlier one was FL), and HG means “high gear.” Co-pick: Daiwa Ballistic MQ LT 1000: 6.2 oz on Field & Stream’s 2026 test scale. It’s the equal of the Stradic, so buy whichever is cheaper when you’re ready. Shop by spec, not by name: 5.5–6.5 oz, 1000 size, aluminum spool, a drag that’s smooth at low settings (you’ll be running about 2 lb), and a handle that swaps sides. Published weights vary by source and model year, so confirm on the maker’s spec sheet. If you can, mount the reel on a rod in a shop to feel the balance. Period-correct on cane: a vintage Mitchell 308 ultralight (the 408 is its faster-geared sibling: blue, with a screw-in handle). Check which side the handle cranks on any one you buy, because the vintage models vary. Look for a serviced one, because drags and bail springs on 50-year-old reels are the weak point. Spinning basics for a fly angler:
Spool it right. Line comes off the filler spool the same direction it goes onto the reel, or you’ll fight twist all day. Fill to about 1/8" below the spool lip. Set the drag to about 1/3 of the line test. With 6 lb line, the drag should slip at a ~2 lb pull on a scale. Casting: pin the line on your index finger, open the bail, cast, and lift your finger to release. Touch the spool rim to feather or stop the lure. Close the bail by hand, not with the crank; that’s what stops line twist and loops. Spinners twist line. Run a small ball-bearing swivel 18" ahead of any inline spinner.
data.rod-spec#Rod spec: key value geometry hex (6) rod length 6 ft 6 in (78") pieces 2, joint at 39" (spliced, or a 12/64 ferrule) power / action light / moderate-fast line 4–6 lb mono lure weight 1/16–1/4 oz (design point 1/8 oz) tip 0.080" → tiptop tube 6/64 butt (grip) 0.279–0.281" (variant D; variant E is 0.262–0.264") handle 12" full cork, two sliding rings guides 6 single-foot + tiptop (16 mm stripper) strip length ~50" per section (incl. splice overlap and cut-offs) Tiptop fit is tight. Across the corners, a 0.080" hex tip is 0.080 ÷ cos 30° = 0.0924", against a 6/64 tube at 0.09375", about 0.0013" of clearance. The tube also covers the first ~½" of the rod, where the taper is a little larger. Test-fit before wrapping and be ready to relieve the tip corners or step up to a 7/64 tube.

data.tackle#Tackle:
Everything below is single-hook or easy to convert, so the same box works on Hatchery Supported water (anything goes) and on the East Fork DH (one single hook, no bait). For DH, swap trebles for single siwash hooks with split rings and pliers, and take the second hook off a jerkbait.
Line: 6 lb mono for the mainstem; 4 lb is optional on the small DH runs. Mono is better than braid in December, because braid holds water and ices in the guides on freezing mornings. A 3’ 6 lb fluorocarbon leader is optional in gin-clear water.
Lure Size How to fish it in winter DH-legal? Marabou or hair jig (black/olive, white) 1/32–1/16 oz Dead-drift or swim slowly along the bottom of deep pools. The top pick for cold water. ✅ single hook Trout Magnet–style micro plastic on a 1/64 oz head 1/64 oz Under a small float through the slow pools. Deadly on stockers. ✅ 2" curly-tail grub / small Ned rig 1/16 oz head Hop it slowly for winter smallmouth on the mainstem’s deep bends. ✅ Inline spinner (Panther Martin, Mepps #0–1, Rooster Tail) 1/16–1/8 oz Retrieve slowly, just fast enough to turn the blade. Swap to a single hook for DH. 🔧 convert Spoon (Kastmaster, Phoebe) 1/12–1/8 oz Count it down, then flutter it back slowly. Good for long casts across the mainstem. 🔧 convert Small floating or suspending minnow (Rapala F3/F5, CD3) ~1/8 oz Twitch and pause. Big browns and smallmouth will hit it. 🔧 one single hook Nightcrawler on #8 hook + split shot — Hatchery Supported water only (bait banned on DH) ❌ Terminal kit: small ball-bearing swivels, round split shot (BB–#4), 1/2" float, #8 and #10 single hooks, single siwash hooks for conversions, a split-ring tool, forceps, a rubber-mesh net, and a small Plano box.
How to fish it: fish 11 a.m.–3 p.m., when the water is warmest. Fish slow and deep, close to the bottom of the deepest slow pools and the outside bends. Do several casts per spot before moving. Browns are spawning or just finished, so stay off redds: the clean, light-colored gravel patches.
data.taper#Taper:
No published taper matched the spec, so I designed this one from published bamboo spinning tapers on bamboorodmaking.com:
Richard Tyree’s 6’ (lures to 1/4 oz): the closest match, tip 0.079 the T&T Classic 5'6" (2–4 lb, to 1/4 oz): tip 0.072 Paul H. Young’s 6'4" Spin-Caster: tip 0.096, a heavier tip The starting point scaled Tyree’s rod to 78" with a nearly straight taper (~0.014–0.016" per 5" station). A tip at 0.080 follows Ian Kearney’s advice that a light open-face rod “needs to come down to closer to .075.” I then ran the taper through caneDNA, my RodDNA-style taper engine, and stiffened it +4% from 10" to 60", with the tip left as-is. That’s the “variant D” in the table below.

data.the-water-french-broad-at-hap-simpson-no: Where: Hap Simpson Park is a City of Brevard river access with a boat ramp and picnic tables, at about mile 21.5 of the French Broad Paddle Trail. It’s the take-out for the flat, calm ~10-mile float down from Island Ford. The Pisgah Forest access is about 5 miles downstream. What it’s like: The mainstem here is slow, sandy, deep-bend water, not freestone pocket water. In winter, fish hold in the deep slow pools, on the outside bends, and around woody cover. Expect holdover stocked trout and resident browns, plus smallmouth, redbreast sunfish and rock bass, all sluggish in cold water. Regulations (verify before fishing): A third-party county guide lists the mainstem from the West/North Fork junction down to the US 276 bridge as Hatchery Supported trout water. That reach should include Hap Simpson, but I haven’t confirmed it against the NCWRC rule text. Under Hatchery Supported rules: 7 trout/day, no minimum length, and no bait or lure restrictions. You need an NC fishing license plus the trout privilege on designated public mountain trout waters. Best fishing nearby in this window: The fresh fish are in the Delayed Harvest waters. These are the East Fork French Broad (NCWRC scheduled its fall 2026 stocking for Nov 10 after warm water cancelled October) and DuPont’s Little River. DH runs catch-and-release, artificial lures with one single hook only. Build the tackle box around single-hook lures and one kit covers both waters (see Tackle). Stocking caveat: Bobby N. Setzer hatchery, right up the Davidson, closed in late 2025 for renovation, so NCWRC now stocks from Armstrong. Check the NCWRC stocking schedule instead of assuming past patterns. Flows: USGS 03443000, French Broad at Blantyre is the closest mainstem gage below Brevard. The Brevard / DuPont / Highlands dossier has the rest of the region: shops, the DH calendar, and Helene access notes.
data.two-pieces-splice-or-ferrule#Two pieces::
The rod is two 39" sections, and the joint is chosen after glue-up: a spliced (scarf) joint or a 12/64 ferrule. Both sections fit the standard Morgan bed, so there’s no extension bed, no 89" strips, and no long heat-treating oven. The class routine (5–6’ culm sections, normal oven) applies as-is.
Mill both sections long through the joint. The tip section runs to about 44" from the tip, and the butt section starts at about 34". That covers half a 4.5" splice on each side of 39", plus cut-offs. Then pick the joint:
Splice (preferred). Cut matching 4.5" scarf bevels (on the adjustable scarf jig, set to 1:23.3) on opposite faces, across the flats, from 36.75" to 41.25". 4.5" is about 23 times the 0.193" dimension. Joined, the two bevels restore the full cross-section, so the rod bends like a one-piece and adds no weight. Whip each feather end with a few turns of thread so it can’t lift or split. At the river, lay the bevels together, line up the guides, and wrap the joint tightly with tape (cloth friction tape or self-amalgamating tape). Ferrule (fallback). Trim both sections square at 39" and fit a 12/64 ferrule. The 0.193" flats there are 12.4/64, the same fit as Rod 001’s 12/64 at 0.193". It’s convenient, but on a light spinner the ferrule outweighs the lure: a 12/64 is roughly 0.2 oz (my estimate) against a 1/8 oz lure. t s w i c h p a i r p s f e b c r o t u t i n h o s n f 3 e 6 a . t 7 h 5 e ″ r e n d 4 s 1 ; . 2 t 5 a ″ p e f r t o h m e t w h h e o l t e i p j o ( i 4 n . t 5 ″ e ) a ; c h n o o t u t t i o n g s b c u a t l t e s e c t i o n Splice 12/64 ferrule Weight at mid-rod none ~0.2 oz, more than the lure Action (caneDNA) same as a one-piece (the model ignores the tape) butt works ~6–10% harder at 45–60" Setup at the river tape it, ~1 minute push it together Failure modes feather edges chip if not whipped; align by eye stiff spot ~2.5" long; ferrule fit Other notes:
Culms and nodes: a 3×3 stagger per section, as in the class build. Keep nodes out of the scarf (36–42"), the top 6" (tiptop), and the reel-ring area. Guides near the joint: put one guide just outside each end of the splice. They double as alignment marks when you tape up.

data:
A plan and procedure for making the handle hardware of Rod 002, the 6'6" French Broad spinning rod myself: a machined reel seat (fixed hood plus a sliding threaded ring) and a cork grip built around it. The build log already covers two handle options: cork with two sliding rings (Option A) and a Fuji VSS skeleton seat on an arbor (Option B). This page is a third option: turn the seat from bar stock instead of buying it.
Status: plan only. Nothing here has been cut yet. The cane for Rod 002 hasn’t been milled either. Anything I haven’t measured or confirmed is marked to confirm, and every dimension below is a starting point, not a result.
data.bushings-and-bonding-to-the-blank#Bushin: Fit the seat to the cane first, dry. Slide the seat over the butt. It should go on freely at the corners with no rocking. Make bushings (two, one at each end of the seat): aluminum or brass rings, or turned from epoxy-filled phenolic, with a bore that matches the cane’s taper at that point and an OD that matches the seat bore. Where the bore is round and the blank is hex, either fill the gaps with thickened epoxy or turn tape-and-epoxy bushings in place. Mask the cane above and below the bonding area, and the seat’s threads and channel, with painter’s tape. Epoxy with a slow-cure (30-minute or longer) 2-part epoxy. equipment.md records a recommendation of 3M DP2216 for ferrule glue; I could use the same adhesive here (to confirm it suits an aluminum-to-cane bond; the repo only recommends it for ferrules). Use a thin film, and keep it off the threads. Align the seat so the reel hangs on the same side as the guides, then hold it square with the blank for the cure. A tape alignment mark on the butt helps. Wipe squeeze-out with denatured alcohol before it gels.
data.choosing-the-style#Choosing the style: Style How it holds the reel Pros Cons Fit for Rod 002 Sliding rings on cork (Option A in the log) Foot sits on bare cork, two rings slide over the ends Lightest; period-correct; no hardware Rings can creep when wet and cold Recommended in the log Fixed hood + threaded ring (this page) Foot sits in a fixed hood; a threaded ring winds up against the other foot Locks solid; no creep; adjustable to the reel Needs machining and exact thread fit The one planned here Hood and cap, no thread (slip-on sliding band) Same as the sliding rings but with metal-to-metal hoods Simple to make Same creep problem as rings Skip Bought skeleton seat (Fuji VSS 16, Option B) Fixed hood plus a threaded hood and lock nut Cheap, tested, ~$6 Looks modern on cane; needs an arbor Fallback A screw-lock seat (what the machined design is) beats a sliding band on a spinning rod because the reel foot takes the full pull of a hooked fish and the casting hand squeezes the seat. The band-only style is fine for light fly-style reels but is the one more likely to loosen.
Option Pros Cons Cork rings, glued up and turned Cheap; pick the best rings for the high-touch spots; any shape Takes time; voids need filling Pre-shaped cork grip (the Option B parts in the log: Fuji split fore/rear grips) Ready to ream and glue Limited shapes; sized for a particular seat I’m using rings here since the machined seat doesn’t match a commercial grip.
data.finishing#Finishing: Option Pros Cons Hard-coat or color anodize (aluminum) Tough; many colors Needs a vendor or a home kit; coat is thick, so the threads must be cut oversize/undersize to allow for it (to confirm with the anodizer) Bead-blast, then clear lacquer Easy; matte look Wears at the thread Polish (brass) Classic on cane Tarnishes; needs lacquer or regular wax Leave bare, clear-coat only on non-thread surfaces Works Needs periodic cleaning Anodizing adds a few ten-thousandths per surface, so cut the threads and fit them before anodizing, then re-check the fit. Masking the threads during anodizing is the usual alternative.
data.fitting-and-fill#Fitting and fill: Remove the grip from the mandrel by gripping it with both hands and striking the mandrel on a flat, solid surface. Ream to the blank and test-fit, then bond with epoxy, as with the seat. Put the rear grip on first against the seat’s rear edge and the foregrip against the fixed hood. Fill voids after shaping and before the final sanding: a cork dust and epoxy (or wood-filler) paste, pushed in, left proud, sanded flush. Burnish with a hard smooth surface or a very fine paper (400-grit or finer) to close the surface. (General practice, not from a cited source.) Winding check (in the log’s Option B notes: for a roughly 7.3 mm blank): fit at the front of the foregrip, then wrap and finish. Finish: leave the cork bare or seal it lightly, per taste. To confirm.
data.glue-up#Glue-up: Bore each ring to just under the blank (a tapered rattail file or reamer on a drill) and put them on a waxed mandrel or threaded rod. Rings arrive with a 1/4″ bore; the cane is 0.28–0.33″ at the grip, so ring bores should be opened slightly. Glue sparingly. Enough that the inner surface just shines; excess glue forces epoxy onto the mandrel and the grip’s outside, and the grip can become nearly impossible to remove. Press the stack: washers and nuts on threaded rod, or the printable cork press from this site. Tighten until glue just oozes between the rings. Put a low-grade ring at each end to absorb the press marks. Cure fully, overnight and a bit more. Reaming too soon makes the grip come apart.
data.machining-sequence#Machining sequence:
This is general machinist practice. I haven’t followed an opened reference for it (see Sources), so treat it as a plan to be checked on scrap first.
Lathe
Cut bar stock (6061, about 1.25″ diameter, 5″ long) with about 1/2″ extra. Chuck it, face the end, and drill and bore through to the bore diameter. Bore first so the bore and the outside are concentric. Put the body on a mandrel (or chuck on the bore) and turn the outside to OD, leaving a shoulder for the fixed hood. Turn the thread relief, then single-point the male thread. Part off. Flip, face to length. Turn the threaded ring: bore, internal thread, then knurl or a hex OD if I want grip. Test-fit the ring on the body. Fit it before any other cuts. Mill (if available)
Cut the foot channel: a flat-bottomed slot across the bed width, with a ball-end or corner radius to match the foot. Open the underside window so the reel foot can sit on the cane or bushing side. Drill any vent or pin holes (a small hole to relieve epoxy, and any set-screw I want). If I don’t have a mill: cut the channel on the lathe with a slotting setup, or file it by hand with a jig. To confirm.
data.materials#Materials: Material Pros Cons Notes 6061-T6 aluminum Easy to turn; light; anodizes well; good thread life Needs finishing to look right; will gall on its own threads if both parts are bare My default pick Brass (360 free-machining) Cuts beautifully; classic look on cane; heavy Heavier on a light rod; tarnishes unless lacquered Good for the threaded ring only Stabilized or dense wood body with brass hardware Warm look; light Wood threads wear; moisture movement Use only for the body, with a metal insert for the threads Nickel-silver The traditional bamboo-rod hardware Costly; harder to find in bar Not planned Mixing the two (aluminum body, brass ring) avoids galling, because like metals tend to seize on fine threads. Anodize or lacquer the finished parts; see Finishing.

data.parts-and-materials#Parts and materials: Qty Item Notes 1 6061-T6 aluminum round bar, about 1.25″ x 5″ For the body 1 Brass bar (360), about 1.25″ x 2″ For the threaded ring, optional 2 Bushings (aluminum, brass, or tape-and-epoxy) Sized to the cane at the seat 20–25 Cork rings, 1 1/4″ x 1/2″ x 1/4″ Spare rings for matching and for voids 1 Waxed mandrel or threaded rod, about 5/16″ Matches the bore after reaming 1 Rattail file or tapered reamer For opening the ring bores — Sandpaper, 60 to 320 grit, and a flat board Hand shaping — 2-part slow-cure epoxy Seat bonding and grip bonding — Wood glue (Titebond II or similar) Ring-to-ring — Painter’s tape, denatured alcohol, nylon washer or O-ring Masking, cleanup, ring lock — Winding check Per the log — Anodize or lacquer Finish Tools: lathe with single-point threading and a boring bar (to confirm I have this), calipers, a thread gauge, optionally a mill, the printed cork press.
data.ring-dimensions-and-count#Ring dimension: Standard ring: 1 1/4″ OD, 1/2″ thick, 1/4″ bore. That’s the size Mud Hole’s overstock cork rings list (page opened). Sizes and grades vary by maker; the “grade” label is a seller’s, not a standard. Rear grip: 7″ is the build log’s choice for the Option B rear grip, about 14 rings at 1/2″. To confirm for this rod (the handle is 12″ total in Option A). Foregrip: about 3.75″ (as in the log), about 7-8 rings. A 1 1/4″ ring leaves about 0.125–0.25″ for shaping around a 1″ seat, so grips that are bigger than the seat are possible but not by much. Larger rings exist; to confirm stock. Buy a few extras and hand-pick: put the best rings where the thumb and palm sit, and the worst at the ends where washers dent them.
data.safety#Safety: Lathe PPE: safety glasses or face shield; no loose sleeves, gloves, or jewelry; long hair tied back; chuck key out before power on. Run the lathe at a sensible speed for the stock size, and stand out of the line of the chuck. Remove burrs and sharp edges before handling parts. Threading: cut aluminum with light passes and coolant; watch for stringy chips and don’t clear them by hand. Cork dust: wear a dust mask (N95 or better) and use dust collection; work outdoors or with a shop vacuum. Epoxy: nitrile gloves and ventilation; solvents (alcohol) away from ignition sources; don’t use epoxy past its working time. Anodizing chemicals (if home-done): acids, gloves, goggles, and disposal rules. To confirm whether I’d do that or send it out.
data.sources#Sources:
I opened and read these for this page. They cover the grip and the seat sizing; I did not find an opened source for reel-seat thread specs or for turning a reel seat from bar stock, so those sections are my own plan.
Global FlyFisher: Making Grips II (archive): off-blank ring glue-up, mandrel sizing, Titebond, 60-grit to 320-grit turning, ring prices In-Fisherman: 7 Reminders for Building Custom Cork Grips (archive): waxing the mandrel, sparing glue, composite vs. standard cork, removing the grip Mud Hole: 4 Steps to Shape Custom Cork Grips (archive): spinning-mandrel shaping, reaming, bonding with epoxy Mud Hole product pages, for dimensions: Fuji VSS Standard seat (archive), overstock cork rings (archive) Back to the Rod 002 build log.
data.spinning-specific-geometry#Spinning-spec: t i b p l a n k f ( o c r o e r g k r ) i p f i [ x = e = d = = h r o f e o o e d o l t f = s o = t o = e t = m ] t h r r i e n a g d e d r g e r a i r p b u t t The reel hangs below the seat. The foot channel is open on the underside. The seat is a tube with a flat-bottomed (or slightly dished) cradle where the foot sits, a fixed hood at one end, and a threaded ring at the other that pulls the second foot tight. Seat body OD: 7/8″ to 1″ (22–25 mm) is the usual range for finished spinning seats and the size my hand is likely to want on a light rod. Finished seat sizes vary by maker, so I’ll settle on a diameter from the reel and my grip (to confirm). Reel foot gap. The distance between the fixed hood and the threaded ring at full open must exceed the foot-to-foot length of the reel, and at full closed must be less than the foot length. I’ll measure the 1000-size reel I’m going to use with calipers (to confirm) and make the channel about 1/4″ longer than that with the threaded ring’s travel at least that much. Hex under a round bore. The butt is 0.279–0.281″ across flats, so the corners are 0.281 / cos 30° = 0.325″ (8.24 mm). A round bore smaller than that cuts into the corners. Mill the bore to clear the corners, or ream the bushing bore to the corner diameter and fill the gap (see Bushings).
data.threads#Threads:
I didn’t find a published thread standard for spinning reel seat nuts. Manufacturers’ product pages (the Mud Hole pages I read) list length, ID, and OD but not the thread pitch, and different makers use different threads. So a machined seat can’t borrow a standard; I choose my own and both mating parts are mine.
Pick a common machinist thread so the tooling is on hand: 1″-20 UNEF (1″ major diameter, 20 tpi) is a good candidate for a ~1″ body. The thread depth is about 0.0325″, so the wall stays healthy. To confirm against the taps, dies, and single-point inserts I actually own. Cut the male thread on the lathe (single-point, with the lathe geared for 20 tpi) rather than with a die. A die on 1″ aluminum cuts a rough thread and leaves it off-center. Take light passes and use cutting fluid. Cut the ring’s female thread on the lathe too (boring bar or internal threading insert), then fit it to the body by sneaking up on the thread: stop when it runs freely with no radial shake. Add relief at the end of the thread, so the ring can run up against the shoulder without bottoming on a half-cut thread. Lock it: a thin nylon washer or a small O-ring under the ring’s face, or a second lock ring, so it doesn’t back off. To confirm which works.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Likely cause Fix Ring binds or won’t start on the body Thread over-cut, or chips in the thread, or the anodize added thickness Clean; re-chase; ease the thread after anodizing Ring loosens when wet No lock; thread too coarse for the load Add an O-ring or nylon washer; add a lock ring Seat wobbles on the blank Bushings oversize or too thin Re-fit; thicken the epoxy; recheck alignment while curing Seat won’t slide on over the hex corners Bore smaller than 0.325″ across corners Bore to 0.340″+ or use bushings Grip glue line shows Too much glue between the rings Use less; sand back a little Grip cracks on reaming Reamed before cure; too fast Wait; ream in steps Voids in the finished cork Poor rings Fill and sand; move low-grade rings to the ends Reel rattles in the seat Channel too long or the hood too shallow Shim with tape, or recut with a tighter channel Cork dust everywhere Dry sanding Outdoors or with a vacuum
data.turning-and-shaping#Turning and shaping: On a lathe or a drill with a support stand: true the stack to a cylinder with 60-grit on a flat board, then rough the profile, leaving a little extra, then work up through the grits. One builder ends at 320 grit. Shaping without a lathe: fold sandpaper into a firm corner and work wells into the spinning grip; a rasp for the first roughing. Calipers at the high points; stop slightly above the final diameter. Dust: cork dust is fine and gets everywhere. Work outdoors or with a shop vacuum at the grip.

data.accessories#Accessories: accessory what it does Hollow fluting cutter Hollows strip centers to cut weight (Stoner/Winston cross-section). Rollers 64/76/94° (64 std for 6-strip). Suggested wall 0.070 in (trout) / 0.085 in (steelhead-salmon). Leave the rod solid under ferrules with a ~2.5 in transition; hollow after finish-cutting, butt→tip. Hollowing loses stiffness — increase section area ~2–5% to compensate. Swelled butt kit Shims to raise the finishing anvil for a swelled butt. Max swell 0.060 in per strip / 0.120 in finished — do not exceed (anvil damage). 100 shims (0.060/0.030/0.020/0.010 in) combine in 0.020-in steps; initial rise over 2.5 in. Magic star cutter Alternate hollowing — an inverted-T with central support spokes (width 0.030–0.065 in). Square inserts remove more but leave ~80% of the triangle’s glue seam (weaker). Suggested wall 0.060–0.070 in (trout) / 0.075–0.085 in (steelhead-salmon). Extension bed 36 in bolt-on bed for one-piece rods up to ~7 ft 6 in. The strip is cut on both finishing anvils, switching once; the tip-butt transition lands between stations #7–#8. Strip length = rod + 4 in tip + 5 in butt + 2 in hold-down (e.g., 7 ft → 95 in). Enamel scraper 60°-groove anvils (with the dial-holder/shaver) to scrape enamel off beveled strips. The bed must have no taper when shaving.
data.cutter-heads#Cutter Heads:
Swappable heads for 8-, 6-, 5-, or 4-strip rods (6-strip is standard).
head included angle hold-down shoe angle 8-strip 46° — 6-strip 61.5° 61.5° 5-strip 73.5° 73.5° 4-strip 92° 91.5° Morgan uses 61.5° for 6-strip (not the traditional 60°), per Winston practice, to reduce visible glue seams.
Inserts. Two carbide inserts, 3 edges each; a set planes ~3–5 rods. Cut depth ≤ 0.010 in/pass green, 0.001–0.003 in/pass heat-treated. Regular inserts are TPGW-321, 3/8 in inscribed circle, 0.015 in tip radius; since July 2011 supplied inserts are C5 carbide (harder), 15% relief, TiN-coated relief edge, diamond-lapped top. Install with tops parallel to the pocket; rotate/pair inserts to double edge life.
data.milling#Milling: Rough on a wide roughing anvil (strip + mill stop in hole A) to a 61.5° bevel just wider than the anvil; mount the hold-down shoe once an apex forms. The stainless, spring-loaded hold-down shoe mounts in the head’s center hole and rides ahead of the cutters, so it doesn’t affect accuracy — critical for slender tips and stiff quad strips. Clean it with alcohol / dry graphite only (never oil). Then switch to a finishing anvil and set the taper. Measure strip height three ways: micrometer + height/width chart, thread-wrapped strips, or the aluminum measuring block (most accurate). Don’t measure the apex directly (leftover “fuzz”). Finish in two stages: cut ~0.015 in oversize, then install fresh sharp cutters and finish at 0.001–0.002 in/pass. Remove apex fuzz before gluing and saw off the thick held-down butt. Minimum strip width: tip 0.200 in / butt 0.250 in. Tip hold-down 2-56 (#43 drill), butt hold-down 4-40 (1/8 in), hole ~1 in from the butt. 7 ft #4 wt example (#12 ferrule): strip height 0.096 in at the ferrule (station #12), 0.033 in at the tiptop.
data.reference--further-reading#Reference \u0:
No book covers the Hand Mill itself. The manual recommends:
Garrison & Carmichael, A Master’s Guide to Building a Bamboo Fly Rod — the amateur’s “bible” Howell, The Lovely Reed Maurer & Elser, Fundamentals of Building a Bamboo Fly-Rod Ray Gould; and the Stoner / McLane encyclopedias Tom Morgan runs a private owners’ list server (join by email via troutrods.com). Free taper sources with Hand Mill station settings (including quads and pentas): RodDNA.com and hexrod.net.
Source: The Morgan Hand Mill Manual (chapters A–R, rev. 2005–2013), Tom Morgan Rodsmiths. This is a factual reference re-written in my own words; the manual is copyrighted and not reproduced here.
data.strip-preparation#Strip Preparation: Buy ≥ 10 poles (ideally 20+). Reject deep cuts, big dark splotches, and node heat marks; power fibers must run the full glued-section depth. Wall thickness: butt 5/16–1/2 in, tip 3/16–5/16 in. Node spacing: butt 9–14 in, tip 14–20 in. Common three/three node match; avoid nodes at cut ends, ferrules, and tiptop. Straighten with heat (gun 350–450 °F) and remove twist, especially the first 18 in of butts; square or slightly inward-taper the strip sides. Heat-treat to light brown (raises MOE, resists set); black = brittle. Remove maximum material before treating (harder afterward); rest treated strips ≥ 1 week to regain moisture. Rough sections ≥ 6 in over finish (+~2 in on the butt for the anvil screw); split ~1/8 in wide.
data.the-adjustable-bed#The Adjustable Bed:
A steel bar sitting on top of the base, raised above it by push/pull screws every 5 in to set the taper. The anvil sits on the bed; the strip sits on the anvil.
key value dimensions 5/8 × 3/4 × 68 in stations #0 through #13 (14 stations) on 5-in centers, spanning 0–60 in station #0 No adjusting screw, only a locking screw — always held tight against the base push screw 5/16-18 flat-head set screws pull/lock 1/4-20 cap-head screws (bed attaches to base with 14 of these) To set a taper: loosen the cap-head (pull) screw, turn the hex-head (push) set screw in or out to change the bar gap. Do not over-tighten — it warps the bed. Never adjust the bed by more than 0.020 in between adjacent 5-in stations or you may permanently damage it (matters for 3-piece / spey shim setups).
data.the-ak-hold-down-letters--the-mill-stop#:
The base has tapped holes on its right front labeled A–K; matching letters are stamped on the bed just below the finishing anvils’ 11 hold-down screws. A movable mill stop screws into one lettered hole and does two jobs: it stops the plane so the cutters can’t hit the strip’s hold-down screw, and it gives an automatic plane stop matched to the rod section’s length.
Selection rule. The strip’s tip always anchors between bed stations #12 and #13 (as close to #13 as possible) so the anvil stays widest at its tip. Choose the mill-stop letter from the bamboo hold-down screw’s position: set the mill so the cutters just clear the hold-down screw, then mount the stop just behind it — in most cases the mill-stop letter equals the hold-down letter. Untapered rough cutting uses hole A (rightmost).
Worked example (7 ft rod). The strip is fastened in hole D (4th from the right), putting the ferrule/tiptop point at station #12 with ~3 in of strip past it; the butt taper is set from station #3 (stations #2/#1/#0 left at zero).
For one-piece rods on the extension bed, use hole B for rough/finish butt and hole A for finish tip. Short (3-piece) sections may anchor farther up the anvil for support.
data.the-anvils#The Anvils:
Anvils are white HDPE with embedded brass inserts. Critically, anvils only support the strip — they do not set the taper (the bed does), so they don’t wear as the taper changes.
5 anvils shipped: butt-roughing, tip-roughing, butt-finishing, and two tip-finishing. Hold-down stations: finishing anvils have 11 lettered (A–K) positions; roughing anvils have 3 (long / medium / short — short is for ~3-piece rods). Top widths (finishing): tip ~0.150 in, butt ~0.225 in. Top widths (roughing): tip ~0.175 in, butt ~0.225 in. Truing: finishing anvils must be shaved flat between stations (with a carbide insert in the dial-holder/shaver) before use — target ±0.001 in (0.002 in TIR). Never recut the factory-installed reference anvil. Never mill an anvil narrower than the smallest strip.
data.the-base#The Base: key value what Chrome-plated cold-rolled steel bar the plane rides on — the taper reference surface dimensions 5/8 × 1¾ × 72¾ in mounting Bolts to a 2 × 2 × 3/8 in, 75 in aluminum angle at 7 points (idea from John Miller) so accuracy doesn’t depend on bench flatness capacity Two-piece rods up to ~9 ft and various three-piece rods Install the aluminum angle with a slight ~1/8 in upward bow so the plane doesn’t dip in the middle; check by rocking the plane along the base. The vertical face has 7 slots on 12-in centers for the anchor screws.
data.the-measuring-block#The Measuring Block:
A caliper-mounted 6061-T6 aluminum block that reads strip height in per-geometry grooves. Calibrate with a #38 drill blank (0.100 in).
groove constant (drill height) 61+ (6-strip) 0.152 in 73+ (5-strip) 0.140 in 91+ (4-strip) 0.123 in Add 0.100 / 0.200 in when a strip exceeds 0.100 in. Glue up ~6 measured sections to verify your own constants, since glue and pressure shift results slightly.
data.the-morgan-hand-mill--manual-reference#T:
The Morgan Hand Mill — Manual ReferenceA re-written, factual reference for the Morgan Hand Mill — the machine, its parts, and the taper-setting model — distilled from the Morgan Hand Mill Manual (chapters A–R, rev. 2005–2013) by Tom Morgan Rodsmiths (Tom Morgan & Gerri Carlson, Manhattan, MT).
Note. This page is a derived, factual digest — specs, procedures, and the taper-setting model summarized in my own words for reference and education. The manual itself is copyrighted and is not reproduced here. Source machine and maker contact: troutrods.com.
It is the human-readable companion to the caneDNA mhm_kb.json knowledge base, which grounds caneDNA’s Mill Settings and anvil-position visualizer in the actual machine.
data.the-planes-dial#The Plane\u0026rsquo;s D:
Calibrated dial reads 0–50 in 0.002-in steps; one revolution = 0.050 in of cut depth (clockwise lowers). Dial indicator travel is 0–1 in at 0.001 in accuracy. A dovetail slide + gib runs the plane; backlash is removed by a spring-loaded Teflon plug (never remove it). Nylon side pads (moly-impregnated) let it slide — set them 0.628–0.629 in apart with the supplied jig.
RodDNA caveat (from manual chapter J). Of RodDNA’s MHM Settings Report, use the Station #, Increment, Rod Dim, and Increase columns; disregard “Form Depth” (should be strip height) and “Settings” (wrong on some tapers). This is why caneDNA computes strip_depth + total_increase itself rather than porting RodDNA’s report. Free taper sources with Hand Mill station settings: RodDNA.com and hexrod.net (Frank Stetzer, with Chris Obuchowski).
data.the-taper-setting-model#The Taper-Settin:
This is the heart of the machine, and the part most often confused.
Two separate steps.
Set the taper. Using the plane’s dial indicator, raise the bed at each 5-in station to the correct height above the base. Mill. Measure the strip height with calipers / the measuring block as you cut, and stop at target. The hard stop then repeats that depth for every strip. The station “setting” is the cumulative rise of the bed at each station relative to a chosen reference (typically #2 = 0.000). It equals (half-dimension at reference) − (half-dimension at that station) = caneDNA’s total_increase. It is not the strip height. The strip height is half the flat-to-flat rod dimension at that station (one strip). It is measured during milling, never set by the bed. Reference station. Register the taper so the strip tip is near the anvil tip; for shorter rods start the taper at station #2 (or higher), not #0/#1, to avoid cutting the anvil too narrow at its tip. Extend past length. Continue the taper one or more stations past the rod’s end so strips have extra length for straight gluing (Morgan likes ≥ 5–6 in extra; min 3 in on tips).
data.what-the-machine-is#What the Machine Is:
The Hand Mill is two self-aligning parts: an adjustable plane that holds the cutters, and an adjustable bed that holds the strip. The cutters shave both sides of a strip at once at a fixed bevel; the taper is set by the bed, which raises the strip into the cutters station by station. The plane follows the grain rather than fighting it.
The redesigned plane (2004, developed with Dennis Detloff) has shipped since late 2005 and adds an adjustable hard stop (from Joe Byrd) that repeats the finish depth for every strip.

data.workflow-end-to-end#Workflow, End to End:
Split → prep / straighten nodes → drill anvil hole → rough cut (taper preset) → swap anvil → finish anvil, set taper, finish cut in many light passes.
Always mill butt → tip, and mark the butt end. Grip behind the adjusting head (never on it) with centered downward pressure; take many light passes and re-cut the first 2–3 in of each pass to full depth.

data.check-sections-for-fit#Check Sections fo:
This step is to remove glue seams (gaps) twists, and bends
Mark gaps and irregularities with a pencil Sand and straighten strips at gaps using a sanding jig This step consists of slowly working down each of the strips, starting at the butt-end of the strip, and looking for gaps surrounding the nodes. If there was a gap at the node, place arrows on the enamel-side around the node. After all nodes are inspected, place the non-enamel side up in the sanding jig and sand this side. The gap
The gap (eventually will be a glue seam) exists because there is a “scoop” in the planed face. The intent of sanding is to lengthen that scoop so that when bound again, the strip can interface properly with its neighbor strip.
data.dry-bind-strips#Dry Bind Strips:
This should be done at least once. Do this twice if time allows.
Lay out butt strips using alternating color coded ends Number the strips from 1 to 6. This is the order for the strips for the rest of the build Lay out strips on tape in order, 1 to 6 Roll strip 6 to strip 1 then work the strips together Bind butt once in a binder
data.final-planing-of-strips#Final Planing of: Plane butt strips to 0.003 over final taper dimensions This 0.003 over is to allow for enamel removal in a future step, plus moisture.
data.glue-up-section#Glue Up Section: Lay butt sections in order (1-6) on tape. Place tape at both ends of strips Spread glue with toothbrush on all surfaces of strips. Work from right to left spreading glue but skip the portions above the tape. After glue is spread everywhere, also spread onto the strips over the taped sections. Goal is to keep the tape dry enough for it to stick Roll strip 6 to strip 1 Bind butt twice in binder (once in both directions) Roll out blank on marble slab with palms, checking and correcting gaps and twists Roll out blank on marble slab with tape roller, gentle pressure down rod Hang vertically until dry, tip-side up, with a weight at the bottom to encourage straightness
data.heat-treat-strips#Heat Treat Strips: Bundle strips and place in 325 degrees oven for 45 minutes 45 minutes at 325 produces a “blond” color 20 minutes at 350 can also be used Reference needed for results of this If using a forced air oven3, flip end-to-end after approx 20 minutes
data.plane-butt--tip-strips-to-030-over#Plane: Soak butt strips in water Set up butt-finishing anvil Zero out each station True the anvil if necessary Set butt taper from spreadsheet Plane butt strips to 0.030 over final taper dimensions
data.prepare-strips-for-planing#Prepare Strip: Use froe to split & shave strips to consistent width and straightness Sand dams with disc sander Sand nodes on disc sander until flat & flush w/ enamel. Use a fancy sanding jig if you have one Drill anchor screw hole 1" from right end Separate butts and tips for separate planing Soak strips in water overnight2
data.rough-cut--bevel-butt-sections#Rough Cut: Set up butt-roughing anvil Check for trueness Set butt taper from spreadsheet Plane all butt strips to rough dimensions 0.070 over Check for and repair curves using heat gun as needed Choose 6 best strips and continue. Shelve the rest for future use
data.rough-cut--bevel-tip-sections#Rough Cut: Set up tip-roughing anvil Check for trueness Set tip taper from spreadsheet Plane all tip strips to rough dimensions 0.070 over Check for and repair curves using heat gun as needed Choose 6 best strips and continue. Shelve the rest for future use
data.sand-enamel-from-blank#Sand Enamel from:
Cut off base of butt section Sand each facet with rough and fine sanding blocks When working on tip section, measure sanding strokes on each facet to ensure even removal on all sides In class we were using Norton ProSand sandpaper in either 200 and 320 grit Common node spacings are Garrison-style, 3x3, and 2x2x2. See pg. 71 of Maurer & Elser’s Fundamentals of Building a Bamboo Fly-Rod ↩︎
An easy solution is vinyl gutters. Lowes items #279187 & #279191 combined with silicone or similar. ↩︎
Check out Frank’s Personal Waste of Time Website. If that page goes down, try the Wayback Machine archive ↩︎
data.split-culms#Split Culms: Choose culms. Bottom of the culms are used for the butts. Top of the culms are used for tips Nodes are spaced closer together at the bottom. They’re wider at the top The goal is for more power fibers at the bottom of the rod blank Cut culms to 5-6’ sections: one for bottom & one for top Inspect for depth of power fibers Split into strip with star splitter, mallet & pipe. Put the tip of the culm up Mark butt strips (B) and tip strips (T)

data:
Small shop tools for the bamboo build process. The blank-making tools tie to steps of the Morgan Hand Mill workflow; the grip, ferrule, and finishing tools serve the later stages the class notes stop short of. All are FDM-printable in PETG or PLA, generated parametrically, and validated watertight. STLs export in print orientation.
Parametric source: generate_rod_tools_stls.py — edit the parameter block (indicator stem size, ferrule bore, PVC diameter) and re-run to fit your hardware.
data.binding-cord-spool-caddy#Binding-cord sp:
For: cord payoff during binding — implements the Garrison article’s spool fix.
The bulk cord spool rides an M8 axle that drops into open cradle slots in the two uprights. The Ø3.5 socket in the base takes a 1/8" brass rod bent into an overhead loop: cord comes off the spool up through the loop, and the springy rod absorbs tension spikes instead of passing them into the wrap — the exact shock-absorber trick from the Garrison Binder article.
spool_caddy.stl · print 1 · hardware: M8 × 120 bolt (or M8 rod) + washers, ~300 mm of 1/8" brass rod, 4 wood screws
data.cork-press#Cork press:
For: gluing up a grip from cork rings.
Two Ø60 pressure discs and two six-lobed knobs with captive M8 nuts. Stack glued cork rings on a length of M8 threaded rod between the discs, spin the knobs down, and leave it to cure. Press the grip off-rod, then ream to the blank and glue it on.
cork_press_disc.stl ×2 · cork_press_knob.stl ×2 · hardware: M8 threaded rod ~300 mm
data.depth-gauge-base#Depth-gauge base:
For: checking strip dimensions over steel planing forms — the “set taper from spreadsheet” and final-planing steps.
A 70 × 40 base that rides the flats of the planing form on two end pads (the middle is relieved so bamboo dust doesn’t tilt it). A 3/8"-stem dial indicator drops through the centre bore and a printed pinch slit with an M4 cross-bolt clamps it: the socket-head bolt drives through a deep access tunnel on one side, and the nut drops into a top-loaded hex track on the other. Fit a 60° contact point to the indicator and it reads strip depth in the form groove directly.
depth_gauge_base.stl · print 1 · hardware: M4 × 35 socket-head bolt + nut, dial indicator with 3/8" stem and 60° point
data.ferrule-slitting-collar#Ferrule slitting:
For: cutting even serrations in ferrule tangs.
A collar that slips over the ferrule with six 0.7 mm saw-guide slots. The slots stop 4 mm above the base, so the jeweler’s saw bottoms out at a consistent depth and the cuts land at exactly 60° spacing. The bore is parametric — regenerate for each ferrule size you use (the included STL is Ø7.0).
ferrule_slit_collar.stl · print per ferrule size · hardware: jeweler’s saw
data.finishing-v-stands#Finishing V-stands:
For: supporting and hand-turning a blank during wrap finishing and varnish work.
120 mm-tall stands with a deep 90° V. Glue felt into the V so the blank turns without marking. Print two (or three for long butt sections) and screw them to a board at whatever spacing the section needs.
finishing_v_stand.stl ×2 · hardware: felt strip, 4 wood screws
data.node-sanding-jig#Node-sanding jig:
For: “sand nodes on disc sander until flat & flush with enamel” — the fancy sanding jig the class notes tell you to use if you have one.
A 90 mm block with an 8.2 mm channel: the strip lies enamel-down with the node proud of the face, and the printed tapered wedge presses in alongside to friction-lock it — no hardware at all. Present the jig face to the disc sander and the node sands dead flush without dishing the strip on either side.
node_sanding_jig.stl + node_jig_wedge.stl · print 1 each · no hardware
data.print-settings#Print settings: PETG or PLA, 0.2 mm layers, 3–4 perimeters, 30–40% infill. No supports on any part. The depth-gauge base benefits from a dead-flat first layer — print it alone on a clean bed.
data.related#Related: Morgan Hand Mill — the build process these tools serve 3D-Printed Garrison Binder — the binder these support Ring-Flyer Orbit Binder — design study for an orbiting-spool binder
data.strip-sanding-plate#Strip-sanding plate:
For: flattening/leveling the enamel face along a strip’s full length — the hand-sanding counterpart to the node jig above.
A 250 mm plate with a 60° V-channel down its length. The strip drops in point-down on its beveled (pith-side) edge; the enamel face sits proud above the flat rails on either side. Run a flat sanding board over the top — once the board rides the rails flush, the enamel face is level for the whole length, and the rails stop you from sanding past it.
strip_sanding_plate.stl · print 1 · no hardware
data.varnish-dip-tube-cap#Varnish dip-tube ca:
For: dust-free drying after dip-varnishing in a 1.5" PVC tube.
Caps the tube; the Ø10 centre hole passes the hanging wire so the freshly dipped section can drip and dry inside, sealed from shop dust. It prints pocket-up with zero overhang — flip it over to fit the tube. Regenerate PVC_OD if your tube measures differently.
dip_cap.stl · print 1

data:
A proposed build: a small plywood cart on locking casters for a DeWalt DW745 10" jobsite table saw, designed so the saw can live in the garage with as little dust as possible. A jobsite saw’s body is an open frame, with holes on every side and an open bottom. A box under it would only catch what falls straight down, so this cart encloses the saw body on all four sides:
a ½" plywood skirt rises from the cart top to a brush seal under the table; everything the saw throws out its sides lands inside the enclosure; a steep V-hopper below feeds a full-width slotted 4" manifold to my Rockler 650 CFM collector; a filtered inlet lets in enough air for the collector to actually pull. Several fiddly parts are 3D-printed. The saw lifts out after you lift off the front skirt panel.
Footprint: 28" W × 24" D. The DW745’s table is about 630 × 570 mm (24.8" × 22.4", per a retailer listing). Saw table height: 34" from the floor, a standard bench height, so a workbench can serve as outfeed. Enclosure: the skirt’s outside is 24" × 21". That’s inside the table’s footprint, so its top edge sits under the table, where a 1" nylon brush seals it. Inside, it’s 23" × 20" for the saw body. The front panel lifts off: its handwheel slot and switch window are open to the top edge, and printed turnbuttons hold it. Below: two ~50° ramps form a V that meets over a slotted 4" PVC manifold. The manifold exits the left side, so the cart can sit against a wall. Storage: a small drawer under the front ramp. The saw’s onboard fence and miter-gauge storage ends up inside the skirt, so hang those on printed hooks on the cart’s right side. Casters: 4 of my step-stop locking casters, plates inset 1", plus ~25 lb of ballast split either side of the manifold.
data.3d-printed-parts#3D-printed parts:
Print these in PETG or ASA, which handle garage heat better than PLA, with TPU where noted for seals and pads. Use 4+ perimeters and 30–40% infill.
Part Qty Replaces / does Foot locator cups (PETG + TPU liner) 4 Screwed to the support rails, they cradle the saw’s rubber feet. They replace the hold-down knobs, which would be unreachable inside the skirt: the saw drops in, locates itself, and stays put by its own weight. Turnbuttons 4–6 Hold the lift-off front skirt panel against a foam gasket Brush retainers 2 Channels that hold the brush strips facing each other along the handwheel slot Switch bezel 1 Frames the switch window with a foam edge Inlet filter frame + sliding shutter 1 Holds a 4″ × 5″ MERV pad on the left skirt side Rear-port adapter 1 Saw rear port (measured ~64.5 mm OD on one Type 4 saw; fit it to yours) to a 2½″ hose 4 × 4 × 2½″ wye 1 On the manifold’s 4.215″ OD stub: main line to the collector, branch from the rear port (plus a second branch for over-blade collection, if added) Manifold collar (PETG + TPU gasket) 1 Seals the pipe where it passes through the side panel’s U-notch Collector adapter 0–1 Only if your collector’s inlet isn’t a 4″ hose fit Cove / fillet strips ~6 ft On the ledge and the rail tops, so dust slides off instead of piling up Hooks 3 Fence, miter gauge, and cord on the right side Cyclone lid (optional) 1 Bucket-top separator ahead of the collector
data.above-the-table-the-part-a-cabinet-cant-:
For truly minimal garage dust, plan on four more things. The enclosure handles everything below the table, but the top of the blade still throws fine dust toward you.
Over-blade collection. A blade guard with a dust port, or an overarm guard, run on a 2½" line to a second branch on the wye. Check that one fits the DW745 before buying; the stock guard has no port. A fine filter on the collector. Single-stage bag collectors often pass the finest dust straight back into the room. Check your bag’s micron rating, and upgrade to a 1-micron bag or canister if it’s coarser. An ambient air filter running during and after cutting. A respirator for long sessions. A current-sensing auto switch for the collector is worth it too. The collector starts whenever the saw does, and the motor-cooling rule below takes care of itself.
data.build#Build:
The order matters: several parts get sealed in early.
Measure (see above) and adjust the drawings to your saw. Print the parts above. Test-fit the rear-port adapter and the foot cups on the actual saw. Bottom panel: bolt the caster plates on, inset 1″, with the heads inside. Counterbore the front pair. Manifold: cut the tapered slot along the pipe, then cut the U-notch in the left side’s bottom edge. Box: glue and screw the sides to the bottom. Slide the pipe in through the notch, at mid-depth with its slot facing up, and fit the back. Caulk the pipe to the bottom and to the right side, which caps its end. Fit the printed collar over the notch. Under the ramps: set one ballast weight on each side of the pipe. Fit the drawer-bay back, then the ramp cleats. Ramps: glue and screw them on so their feet land on the slot’s edges. Caulk every edge. Front panel, then the top: caulk the wall tops and ramp heads, then glue and screw on the top. Support rails and foot cups: set the saw on the rails, mark its feet, and screw the printed cups there. Lift the saw out again. Skirt, without the saw: fit the back and both sides with their outside cleats, and caulk them to the top from inside now, while you can reach. Cut the inlet in the left side and fit the filter frame. Front panel: set the saw in its cups, template the handwheel slot and switch window against it, then cut them open to the top edge. Fit the brush retainers, switch bezel, foam gasket and turnbuttons. Brush seal: fit the brush along each skirt top so the bristles lightly touch the underside, leaving ~1/16″ under the fence rails. Hoses: connect the rear-port adapter and its hose through the back grommet to the wye, then the wye to the collector. Test: check with incense that air is pulled in at the throat, the brushes and the inlet. Then run the blade through full bevel and height and confirm nothing rubs. Drawer and hooks: build the drawer, and fit the printed hooks.
data.buy-instead#Buy instead?: DeWalt’s DW7451 compact stand is listed for the DW745. It folds and it’s quick, but it has no dust control at all. It’s the better choice if the saw travels a lot. This cart is built for one job: a jobsite saw in a garage with the least dust that a saw like this can practically manage.

data.how-the-dust-gets-out#How the dust gets:
Side section of the DW745 dust cabinet cart, to scale: a half-inch plywood skirt on all four sides of the saw body rises from the cart top to a brush seal under the table; the saw sits on support rails over a full-size opening; below, a V-hopper of two 50 degree ramps feeds a slotted 4 inch PVC manifold that exits the side to the dust collector; a small drawer and ballast sit under the ramps.floorcasters, plates inset 1″ (c)drawerballastsupport rails (left and right) · printed foot cupsfiltered inlet (left side, high)DW745 table (34″)DW745 body: open framedust exits every side → stays inside the skirthandwheel shaftin a brushed arc slotrear port: 2½″ hose out a grommetto a printed wye at the manifold exit½″ ply skirt, all 4 sides;front panel lifts off1″ brush seal to the tableV-hopper (~50°)4″ slotted manifold →out the left side to the collectorH = 16″(example)skirt 11¾″(example)24″ deepfrontback Side section, to scale for the example (front at left). Dashed arrows show the airflow; the saw body is drawn as a dashed outline. What’s enclosed. The skirt, cart top, hopper and manifold make one sealed volume of about 4½ ft³ gross around and under the saw. The saw’s side vents, bevel slot and open bottom all empty into it.
The saw’s rear port is the best pickup point, right at the blade shroud. Don’t waste it: run a 2½" hose from it out through a grommet in the back skirt panel to a printed 4 × 4 × 2½" wye on the manifold’s exit stub.
Openings in the front skirt. The DW745’s controls are on the front:
Handwheel slot. The blade-height handwheel moves along an arc as the blade bevels. Template the arc by taping cardboard over the front of the saw, running the bevel from 0° to 45°, and tracing the shaft’s path. Cut the slot about ½" wider than the shaft and open it to the panel’s top edge, so the panel lifts straight up past the shaft. Close it with two strips of brush seal facing each other in printed retainers. Switch window. A cutout around the paddle switch, also open to the top edge, with a printed bezel and a foam edge. Bevel-lock lever. Check whether it ends up behind the skirt. If it does, extend the window to reach it.
data.makeup-air-give-the-collector-something-:
A sealed box starves the collector. With only the throat gap and brush leakage to breathe through (a few square inches), the air would have to squeeze in at over 6,000 ft/min. That costs several inches of water gauge before the hopper, slot and hose take their share, and a small single-stage collector can’t hold its airflow against it. So add a deliberate inlet:
Size: at least the duct’s area. Use a 4" × 5" opening (20 in²) high on the left skirt side, near the motor, so incoming air sweeps past the motor and down through the body. Filter: cover it with a MERV 8–11 furnace-filter pad in a printed frame. Air only flows in while the collector runs. When it stops, the filter keeps settled dust from drifting back out. Tuning: the frame takes a sliding printed shutter. Start fully open, and close it partway only if the incense test at the blade throat gets weak. The numbers.
Airflow: the collector is rated at 650 CFM free air. With the inlet, a short hose, and this box, expect 350–450 CFM. Duct and slot speed: that’s 4,000–5,200 ft/min in the 4" duct and about 3,700–4,700 ft/min through the slot. Inlet speed: about 2,500–3,200 ft/min at the inlet. Hose: keep the hose to the collector short (≤ 10 ft) and smooth-walled. Hopper and manifold.
Ramps: two ¼" hardboard ramps run from the edges of the cart-top opening down to the crown of a 4" PVC sewer & drain pipe lying across the bottom at mid-depth. They’re about 50°, well past sawdust’s 35–45° angle of repose. Slot: about 22" long, cut along the pipe’s top between the two ramp feet. Taper it from ½" wide at the exit end to ¾" at the closed end. Ends: the far end of the pipe butts the right side, which caps it. Offcuts: the slot stops larger offcuts, but thin slivers that fall through the throat can still reach a single-stage impeller. Use a zero-clearance throat insert, and consider a cyclone separator ahead of the collector. A printed bucket-lid cyclone works.
data.measure-first#Measure first:
Three measurements set the build. Take them all before cutting:
Body clearance: the saw body’s footprint below the table must fit inside 23" × 20" (the skirt’s inside) through full blade-height and 0–45° bevel travel. s: from the saw’s feet to the top of the table. g, measured along each skirt panel’s line. Mark where each of the four panels will stand (24" × 21" outside, centered under the table). At each mark, measure from the saw’s feet up to the underside of the table or fence rail directly above. Don’t measure at the table’s perimeter: the skirt is inboard of it, where the underside can be higher. Each panel gets its own height: g + 1½" − ¼", from the cart top. Carcass height H = 34" − s − c − 1½", where c is the caster height and 1½" is the support rails.
Example (yours will differ) s c H Interior Ramp angle 3" casters 12" 3.5" 17" 15.5" ~53° 4" casters 12" 4.5" 16" 14.5" ~50° 5" casters 12" 5.5" 15" 13.5" ~47° The s = 12" and the 11¾" skirt in the example are placeholders. Ramp angle = atan((interior − 4.2") ÷ 8.6").
Brush seal. Use 1″ bristle strip so it bridges uneven gaps and compresses lightly against the table’s underside. Where a panel runs under a telescoping fence rail, leave ~1/16″ between bristle tips and rail so the rails slide freely. The small leak there is just more makeup air.

data.using-it-safely#Using it safely: Never run the saw with the collector off. The DW745’s motor cools itself with air, and inside the skirt it would recirculate its own heat. The auto switch handles this. Without one, start the collector first and run it 10–15 seconds after the saw stops. Lock all four casters before you turn the saw on. Point the swivels outward as you lock them, which widens the stance. Mind the tipping point. Loaded and ballasted, the cart weighs about 125 lb, with its center of gravity centered by the split ballast. With the casters’ contact about 2¼″ in from the edges, a push of roughly 36 lb front-to-back or 43 lb sideways at table height would tip it. Support long stock with a workbench or roller stand. Removing the saw: unplug it, lift off the front skirt panel (the handwheel and switch pass out through the open slots), and lift the saw out of its foot cups. Do this to clear offcuts from the hopper. Never reach in through the blade opening. Check your collector’s specs. Rockler lists its 650 CFM Dust Right wall-mount (TADC-34WN) as ¾ hp. Measure your inlet and print the adapter to match.

data:
A proposed build — fully dimensioned and detailed, but not yet cut. A narrow wall console for an entry/hallway: drop keys and mail on top, baskets or shoes on the lower shelf. Solid cherry, hand-tool build (stock ripped and thickness-planed by machine; all joinery cut by hand).
Overall size: 42" W × 14" D × 34" H Top overhang: 1" all around the leg frame Lower shelf: ~10" off the floor, resting on the lower rails Joinery: mortise-and-tenon frame, drawbored; floating solid top
data.adjustments-to-consider#Adjustments to c: Stretch to 48" long, or drop height to 30". Add a drawer in the front apron (would change the front apron to a rail + drawer pocket). Bump legs to 1¾" square for a heavier look (still cut from 8/4).
data.build-sequence#Build sequence: Mill 4/4 down to a true ¾" in stages, resting between passes — cherry moves as internal tension releases. Leave leg blanks a hair oversized off the planer and take the last shaving by hand. Lay out and cut all mortises and tenons. Fit each tenon to its mortise before any glue-up. Glue up two end units: each = a pair of legs + short apron + short lower rail. Connect the two ends with the long aprons and long rails. Dry-clamp the whole frame and confirm the 37" and 9" shoulder distances land square before committing. Drawbore the tenons — pins pull the joints tight without clamping across the 42" span. See Drawboring below for sizes and the step-by-step. Drop the shelf onto the four lower rails. Attach the top with figure-8 fasteners or wooden buttons so the solid top can float (expand/contract seasonally). Do not glue the top down.

data.domino-option#Domino option:
A Festool Domino can cut the apron joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The plan’s 5/16″ mortise is 7.9 mm, so an 8 mm Domino matches it, and a 40 mm Domino sits 20 mm (¾″) deep in each part.
The one rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside a 1½″ leg. The hand-cut plan avoids that by mitering the tenon tips. Loose tenons can’t be mitered, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them.
Joint Domino Cut length (was) Long aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 24 mm (≈ ⅞″) below the apron’s top edge 37″ (39″) Short aprons (×2) 1 × 8×40 per end, centred 66 mm (≈ 2⅝″) below the apron’s top edge 9″ (11″) Lower rails (×4) Keep the hand-cut mitered tenons 39″ and 11″ (unchanged) With the Domino, cut length = shoulder-to-shoulder (37″ and 9″); there is no tenon allowance to add. Keep the aprons flush to the leg faces and centre each 8 mm mortise on the apron’s ¾″ thickness. The 2½″ lower rails are too short to stagger two 40 mm Dominoes at the same corner, so they stay hand-cut. Their mortises sit well below the apron Dominoes, so nothing collides. One 8×40 Domino has noticeably less glue area than the full-width tenon it replaces. That is fine for a hallway console; the lower rails and shelf stiffen the frame. Drawboring does not carry over to the Domino joints (a 1/8″ pin through an 8 mm Domino is marginal). Clamp the aprons instead, with hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you can square a 42″ frame before it sets.
data.drawboring#Drawboring:
Drawboring means the pin hole in the leg and the pin hole in the tenon are deliberately about 1/32″ out of line. A tapered pin driven through both pulls the tenon deeper into the mortise and closes the shoulder, then locks the joint mechanically. On a 42″ frame that replaces a long clamp, and the joint stays tight even if the glue ever lets go.
The blue hole is drilled in the leg; the red hole is drilled in the tenon, centered 1/32″ nearer the shoulder. The drawing is true to scale.
