data.for-this-build#For this build: Do the end units first (short, easy), then assemble the long aprons and rails into both ends together. Use hide glue or an extended-open-time glue so you are not racing the clock over 42″. Drive the pins one corner at a time. A single pipe clamp is only for starting the joints, not for holding them. Test on scrap first: make one joint in cherry with the same 5/16″ tenon and 1/8″ pin. A good result is a closed shoulder with no cracks around the pin; if the tenon splits, reduce the offset.
data.hand-tool--cherry-notes#Hand-tool \u0026: Tear-out: cherry planes beautifully but tears where grain reverses (near figure or the pith). Keep the smoother sharp and finely set, read grain direction before each pass, and keep a card scraper handy for the top glue-up and any tricky patches. Color / clamps: don’t leave clamps, tape, or stickers on exposed surfaces during glue-up or curing — cherry tans unevenly and you’ll get pale patches that never catch up. Squeeze-out: scrape off all glue squeeze-out before finishing. Finish over dried glue blocks the darkening and leaves permanent ghost lines.
data.key-reference-dimensions#Key reference d: Shoulder-to-shoulder (what actually keeps the frame square): Long aprons & long rails: 37" Short aprons & short rails: 9" The extra 2" on each part = two 1" tenons living inside the legs. Set your shoulder gauge to 37" / 9" and the tenon length falls out on its own. Mortises: ~5/16" wide × ~1" deep. Two tenons meet inside each leg corner — miter their tips at 45° so they don’t collide.
data.materials#Materials:
Species: solid cherry, clear finish. Cherry darkens dramatically with light over the first few months (pale pink → deep reddish-brown) — plan around that (see notes).
Stock Used for Rough qty (approx) 8/4 (2" rough) Legs only 5–6 bd ft 4/4 (1" rough) Top, aprons, lower rails, shelf 18–20 bd ft Only the legs need stock heavier than 4/4. A finished 1½"-square leg cannot come out of 4/4 — rough 4/4 only nets ~¾" of flat, clean stock after jointing and planing out cup/twist. Buy 8/4 and keep the legs seamless. (6/4 is too close to 1½" finished to survive jointing unless you drop the legs to ~1⅜".)
Lamination alternative: two face-glued pieces of 4/4 make a ~1½" blank, but on a 1½"-square leg the glue line lands on two visible faces and will age to a slightly different shade. On a clear-finished cherry piece, 8/4 is worth it. If you do laminate, orient the seam to a back corner.
The 4/4 estimate leaves margin for grain-matching the top and shelf glue-ups and for working around cherry’s gum streaks and sapwood.
data.sizes-for-this-table#Sizes for this tabl: Item Value Why Pin diameter 1/8″ The tenon is only 5/16″ thick; a 1/4″ pin would leave ~1/32″ of wood each side Offset 1/32″ toward the shoulder Hardwood pins this small tolerate up to ~3/64″; more can crush or split the tenon Pin position ½″ in from the leg face Mid-tenon on a 1″ tenon, clear of the end grain and of the mitered tip of the neighboring tenon Pins per tenon 2 on the 3½″ aprons (about 1″ from each edge); 1–2 on the 2½″ rails Spreads the pull across the width of the tenon Hole depth in leg Through the near wall, across the mortise, ¼″ into the far wall Blind, so no pin end shows on the far side Stagger the pins at each leg corner. Two tenons meet inside the leg, and their pins are drilled from the two adjacent outer faces. If the long-apron pin and the short-apron pin sit at the same height they cross inside the leg. Put the long-apron pins at about ¾″ and 2¾″ below the top edge, and the short-apron pin at about 1¾″ (mid-height).
data.steps#Steps: Cut and fit every mortise and tenon dry. It should seat by hand or with light taps, not with force. Drill the leg. Use a sharp brad-point bit and a backing block. Start on the leg’s outer face (so the pin dots show on the faces that are meant to be seen) and drill square through the near wall, across the mortise, and ¼″ into the far wall. Mark the tenon. Seat the tenon fully, put the bit back into the leg hole and tap it so the point dimples the tenon cheek. Offset and drill the tenon. Pull the tenon, move the mark 1/32″ toward the shoulder, and drill at that new mark. A drill press with a fence keeps it square to the cheek; clamp scrap behind to prevent blowout. Make the pins. Straight-grain cherry or 1/8″ hardwood dowel, with a 3/8″ taper at the tip so it finds the offset hole. Glue-up. Glue on the tenon cheeks and shoulders, none on the pins. Seat the joint, then drive the pin until it stops; you should feel the shoulder draw in. When the glue has set, saw the pins flush and scrape them clean.
data.why-these-proportions#Why these proporti: The shallow 14" depth is the point of a hallway piece — it hugs the wall and stays out of the traffic path. 34" tall sits at about waist height, comfortable for setting things down (anywhere 30–34" works; taller reads more console-like). 42" long gives presence without dominating a corridor. Legs are 1½" square — slender but honest for this span; go to 1¾" if you want it chunkier. The lower shelf earns its keep both as storage and as a structural tie that stiffens the whole frame.

data:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Furniture Designs Heartwood Shaker 3-Drawer Nightstand (product page, archive), with the proportions taken from the maker’s photos and drawing. Three equal drawers stacked under a top that flares out past the case at the ends, four straight legs, an arched apron across the front, and frame-and-panel sides.
Provenance of the numbers. The maker publishes only the overall size and the construction notes. (stated) = from the maker’s page. (derived) = worked out from other numbers here so everything closes. (est.) = measured off the maker’s front photo, dimensioned drawing and three-quarter photo — good to about ±¼″ at best. The front/back overhang in particular is borrowed from a sibling model (the Heartwood Shaker End Table), because it cannot be read from a front view. Check the (est.) items before cutting.
data.build-sequence#Build sequence: Mill the 8/4 for legs, then the 4/4 in stages, resting between passes. Cut mortises and tenons for the legs. Cut the two arches on the front apron and the bottom side rails before assembly. Groove the side rails, muntins and legs for the panels. Make the four panels, finish them before assembly so no bare wood shows when they move. Glue up each side frame (legs + top rail + bottom rail + muntin + two panels). Drawbore the leg joints if you like. Join the two sides with the front apron, the two front rails and the back rails. Dry-clamp first; the opening must be 16″ and the case 19″ × 15½″. Slide the back panel into its grooves before the last rail goes in. Screw on the slide spacers, then build and dovetail the three drawers and hang them on the slides. Make and fit the knobs. Finish with hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax (cherry), matching the maker. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Centre it: 2½″ at each end, 1¼″ front and back.

data.domino-option#Domino option:
A Domino is a poor fit for the leg joints on this piece, and a good fit for the muntins.
Why: the 1½″ legs take several joints at the same height. At each back corner, the back top rail and the top side rail both enter at the top; at every corner the arched aprons and bottom rails (2⅝″ tall) meet at the same level. Two Domino mortises from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so they would have to be staggered in height, and 1½″ and 2⅝″ parts don’t have room to stagger. The hand-cut plan avoids the collision by mitering tenon tips.

data:
A proposed build — a copy of the Vermont Woods Studios / Vermont Furniture Designs Modern Craftsman 2-Drawer Console Table (product page, archive), with the proportions held to the maker’s published numbers. A long, low console: a wide, thin top that overhangs the leg frame by a lot at the ends, two shallow drawers hung right under the top, and a narrow lower shelf carried on chunky side rails.
Provenance of the numbers. Dimensions marked (stated) come straight from the maker’s Dimensions and Construction Details panels. Dimensions marked (derived) are worked out from the stated ones so everything closes. Dimensions marked (est.) are measured off the maker’s front and three-quarter photos — good to roughly ±¼″ — and are the ones to sanity-check against the real piece, or against your own taste, before cutting.
data.build-sequence#Build sequence: Mill legs from 8/4 and everything else to size; let stock sit between passes — cherry moves. Cut mortises and tenons (5/16″–⅜″ mortises, 1″ deep). Miter tenon tips where two meet inside a leg. Dry-fit the two end frames: leg pair + side apron + shelf side rail. Confirm the 10½″ shoulder distance and that the rail sits flush to the leg outer face. Glue up the ends, then join them with the front and back aprons and the lower front rail. Dry-clamp first and check the 40½″ opening and the 44″ × 14″ frame for square. Drawbore if you like — optional here, since the top and drawers add little racking load. Fit the center runner and divider and check the two drawer openings are equal (≈ 19⅞″ each with 1/16″ reveals). Screw on the slide spacers, add the shelf cleats and drop in the shelf. The shelf carries load, so keep the cleats glued and screwed. Build and dovetail the drawers, fit the slides, then trim the fronts to a 1/16″ reveal. Make the walnut pulls and fit them. Finish: hand-rubbed linseed oil and wax for cherry and walnut (tung oil and wax for maple), matching the maker. Scrape off all squeeze-out first. Attach the top with buttons so it can move seasonally. Center it: 8″ at each end, 1″ front and back.

data.domino-option#Domino option:
A Festool Domino can cut most of the joints instead of hand-cut tenons. The 5/16″ mortise in this plan matches an 8 mm Domino; a 40 mm Domino goes 20 mm (¾″) into each part, a 50 mm Domino 25 mm (1″).
Rule at a leg corner: two mortises entering from adjacent faces cross inside the leg, so no two Domino mortises in a leg may be at the same height — stagger them. (The hand-cut plan avoids this by mitering tenon tips, which a loose tenon can’t do.)

data: Printable jigs and shop tools for woodworking projects — the woodworking counterpart to the rodmaking tool set.

A proposed shop jig for cutting long, accurate scarf bevels in strip stock: the 4½" splice on Rod 002’s bamboo sections, and also scarfed trim, bow and paddle laminations, and anything else that needs a feathered lap joint. It’s a permanent tool, not a one-off. One knob sets any ratio from 1:8 to 1:40, and the setting doesn’t depend on the stock’s thickness.
How it works. Two hard-maple rails form a flat reference plane. A sanding beam rides on them and can’t cut below that plane. Between the rails is a tilting bed hinged so that its top surface pivots on the rail plane. Clamp the stock with its end on the hinge line and drop the far end of the bed. The stock then rises above the rails by exactly the wedge you want removed. Sand until the beam rides the rails, and the bevel feathers out precisely at the end of the stock. The only setting is the ratio: the bed’s drop at the 12″ mark is d = 12″ ÷ ratio, for any thickness of stock.
data.3d-printed-parts#3D-printed parts:
A 3D printer makes several of the fiddly parts easier, and repeatable. Print them in PETG, which is tougher than PLA and doesn’t creep under a clamp, at 4+ perimeters and 40% infill.
Part Why print it Ratio setting gauges A stepped block whose steps are the drop d for 1:8, 1:12, 1:16, 1:20, 1:23.3 and 1:24. Set it on the bed at the 12″ line and raise the bed until the step for your ratio touches a straightedge across the rails. No calipers needed, and the setting repeats. Print it on its side so the steps are accurate, and check them with calipers once. Hold-down clamps Low-profile cam clamps or bars with a TPU pad, sized to sit under the beam’s path where they can. For narrow stock, a bar with a shallow relief so it presses on the center of the top flat. Fence strip A thin printed fence with tabs that key into the insert holes, so it registers square to the hinge line every time instead of being taped on. End-alignment gauge A small block that rests on both rails and drops a lip exactly to the hinge line. Push the stock’s end against the lip, then lift the gauge away. It’s faster and more accurate than sighting with a square. Beam handles A comfortable handle (and a short-beam version) bolted to the MDF or aluminum beam. The rails, bed and base should stay wood: their flatness and stiffness are the whole tool. Printed parts only hold, locate and set.
data.build#Build: Mill the rails and bed from the same quartersawn board. Plane them to final thickness together so they move together. Glue and screw the rails to the base’s long edges, with their outside faces flush. Put the screws in from underneath so nothing is near the rail tops. Add the feet. Drill the hinge together. Shim the bed so its top is flush with the rail tops, and clamp everything. Then drill one ¼″ hole straight through rail, bed, and rail at X = 5″, 3/8″ below the top. That’s 2-5/8″ above the base’s top. Drilling it in one pass is what keeps the bed’s top surface pivoting on the rail plane. The pin goes through the bed. The hole is centered in the bed’s ¾″ thickness, with ¼″ of wood above and below the pin. Leave 3/8″ of bed behind the hole and round that nose to a 3/8″ radius about it. Because the nose is centered on the pin, its highest point stays at the rail plane at every tilt, so it never sticks up into the beam’s path. Fits: the pin is a press fit in the rails. Open the bed’s hole just enough for the bed to turn without play, with a ¼″ reamer or 320 grit wrapped on a dowel. A sloppy 17/64″ hole would let the feather point wander. Flatten the reference plane. With the bed shimmed flush and clamped, sand the rail tops and the bed top together on a flat surface, such as PSA paper on a jointer bed, a cast-iron wing, or glass. They must be one continuous plane. Check with a straightedge: the bed flush to the rails within 0.002″ is d = 0. Lift screw: install the T-nut under the base at X = 17″. Epoxy the brass pad under the bed at that spot, and thread in the thumb screw and jam nut. Marks: scribe the hinge line (X = 5″) and the 12″ setting line (X = 17″) across both rail tops, and ink them. Hold-down: install the two inserts in the bed, and make the bar and the fence strip. Sanding beam: flatten the MDF, stick on the PSA paper, and add a handle. Wax the rail tops so the beam glides.

data.holding-the-work#Holding the work:
A C-clamp won’t work on the bed itself. The bed sits recessed in a 3″ channel between 3″-tall rails, with the base underneath, so a clamp’s lower jaw has nowhere to go. Anything sticking up above the rail plane inside the scarf would also be hit by the beam. The hold comes in three layers instead:
Double-sided tape under the scarf zone (the primary hold). Use thin cloth carpet tape or turner’s tape, along the whole scarf and a few inches past it. It’s the only thing that can hold the feather, the last thin inch that no clamp can reach. On bamboo, press the section down hard for a minute. Release it afterward with a putty knife and a little naphtha. The hold-down bar goes across the stock’s top flat, knobbed into the nearest insert pair past the beam’s travel. It resists the pull of each stroke. For a scarf of length L, use the first pair beyond L + 3″, and use a short beam (6″ long) on short scarfs so it stops short of the bar. For the 4½″ bamboo splice, that’s the 9″ pair. Pad the bar so it doesn’t mark the enamel side. The outboard end gets the C-clamp. A rod section is 39″ long and leaves the jig sloping gently downhill (2.5° at 1:23). Support it on a block or roller stand at that height, and C-clamp it there. That’s where a C-clamp is useful: it keeps the long lever arm from rocking the stock on the bed. Sand with light strokes toward the feather. That pulls the stock toward the hinge, against the tape and the bar, and keeps bamboo fibers from lifting at the thin end.

data.rod-002-splice-worked-example#Rod 002 sp: Joint: 4½″ scarf at the 39″ joint, where the hex measures 0.193″ across the flats. Ratio: r = 4.5 ÷ 0.193 = 1:23.3, so d = 12 ÷ 23.3 = 0.515″. Tip section: lay it flat-side down on the bed with its end on the hinge line. A hex rests stably on a flat, so the bevel runs across the flats. Tape it and hold it down at the far end, then sand with light strokes. Bamboo fibers want to lift at the feather: finish with 220 and keep strokes going toward the feather. Butt section: same setting, same procedure. Mate them: rotate one section 180° about its axis so the bevels face each other. Line up the guide flats, whip the feather ends, and tape the joint, as described on the Rod 002 page.
data.settings#Settings:
Drop d is measured at the 12″ setting mark, from a straightedge laid across the rails down to the bed’s top. Use a depth gauge or the depth rod of your calipers.
Ratio d at 12″ mark Bed angle Max stock thickness (L ≤ 15″) 1:8 1.500″ 7.1° 1.88″ 1:10 1.200″ 5.7° 1.50″ 1:12 1.000″ 4.8° 1.25″ 1:16 0.750″ 3.6° 0.94″ 1:20 0.600″ 2.9° 0.75″ 1:23.3 (Rod 002 splice) 0.515″ 2.5° 0.64″ 1:24 0.500″ 2.4° 0.62″ 1:30 0.400″ 1.9° 0.50″ Any other ratio: d = 12 ÷ r. For a scarf of length L on stock of thickness t, r = L ÷ t. Capacity: stock up to 2-3/4″ wide. Scarf length L up to 15″, so the maximum thickness is 15 ÷ r. Ratio range: at 1:8 the bed’s far end still clears the base by 0.27″, which sets the steep limit (~1:7.5). Shallow ratios are only limited by how small a d you can measure.
data.using-it#Using it: Zero: with d = 0, a straightedge should lie flat across rails and bed. Set the ratio: turn the lift screw until d at the 12″ line matches the settings table, then lock the jam nut. Load the stock: lay it on the bed against the fence, with its end exactly on the hinge line. Sight down the scribed line with a square, then hold it as described in Holding the work. Sand: take long, light strokes along the jig, starting with 80 grit. Keep the beam flat on both rails. You’re done when the beam rides the rails along the whole scarf and the end has feathered to nothing. Finish with 120 and then 220. The mating piece gets the same setting and the same procedure. Joined face to face, the two bevels restore the full section. Accuracy. The pin sits 3/8″ below the bed’s top surface, so the pivot line moves very slightly as the bed tilts. At 1:8 the feather point shifts 0.05″ along the stock and drops 0.003″; at 1:23 it’s about a third of that. That’s well inside the material you trim off the feathered tip anyway.
data.variations#Variations: Router sled for thick stock. A 6″ × 12″ sled spanning the rails can carry a trim router with a flat-bottom bit set flush with the sled’s underside. Run it back and forth along the rails. It’s faster than sanding on 1″+ hardwood. Take conventional (not climb) passes, and use a full hold-down. Longer scarfs: lengthen the rails and bed together. Keep the 12″ setting mark, and capacity grows with the bed. Metric: scribe a second mark 300 mm from the hinge; d = 300 mm ÷ r there.

data.design-at-a-glance#Design at a glance: Material: white oak, S3S, 4/4 (posts 8/4); panels are 3/4" plywood Slope: 35.3° (measured), assuming a 7-1/16″ riser and 10″ tread — verify on the actual stair Run: 98″ (8′-2″) along the slope; 80″ clear between posts, 87″ overall including posts Top rail: 1-5/8″ × 3″ (two 4/4 boards face-glued), laid flat; top of rail 36″ above the nosing line Posts: 4×4 (8/4 stock) Infill: 5 panels, 12″ wide, with gaps of 3-1/3″ (all under 4″) Panel mounting: single-4/4 oak cleats (13/16″) hidden behind the panels, set 3/4″ in from the rail’s outside edge so the panel face is flush with the rail edge; the panel butts the rail underside, outside the cleat, and is screwed into the cleat (three 1-5/8″ screws per cleat) Cleat fastening: glued to the rail, plus a 2″ stainless screw every 12″ driven up through the cleat into the rail; the bottom rail is the mirror image (cleat on top) Panel opening: 29-1/64″ vertical between the rails
